title: Ali Tajer, "Causal Representation Learning" (Thursday, October 1, 2026)
text:
Ali Tajer, "Causal Representation Learning" takes place on Thursday, October 1, 2026 at 3:30 PM at Benedum Hall, 102.
Event: Ali Tajer, "Causal Representation Learning"
Date: Thursday, October 1, 2026 at 3:30 PM to 4:30 PM
Venue: Benedum Hall, 102, 3700 O'Hara Street, Pittsburgh, PA 15261
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Department of Industrial Engineering
Description: Abstract: Building reliable world models for physical systems is a central challenge in modern AI, with broad implications for scientific discovery, robotics, autonomy, and control. Unlike purely statistical prediction, world models for physical environments must capture the underlying causal structure of the system: which latent factors correspond to genuine physical mechanisms, how these factors evolve under interventions, and how they govern future observations across changing environments. This motivates a fundamental question: how can an agent learn representations that are not merely predictive, but causally meaningful and therefore suitable for reasoning, planning, and adaptation in the physical world?

In this talk, we will discuss causal representation learning (CRL) as a principled foundation for building world models of physical systems. CRL aims to uncover latent variables that correspond to the system’s underlying generative factors and to organize them in a way that reflects causal relationships, invariances, and intervention effects. Such representations can enable models that extrapolate more reliably beyond the training regime, support counterfactual and interventional reasoning, and provide a pathway toward more interpretable and transferable decision-making. title: Bioengineering Seminar Series - Damion Shelton (Thursday, October 1, 2026)
text:
Bioengineering Seminar Series - Damion Shelton takes place on Thursday, October 1, 2026 at 4:00 PM at Benedum Hall, 157.
Event: Bioengineering Seminar Series - Damion Shelton
Date: Thursday, October 1, 2026 at 4:00 PM to 5:00 PM
Venue: Benedum Hall, 157, 3700 O'Hara Street, Pittsburgh, PA 15261
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Department of Bioengineering
Description: Damion Shelton, Associate Vice President and Executive Director of the Swartz Center for Entrepreneurship at Carnegie Mellon University, will present "What do we want from our machines?"

Abstract

The purpose of this talk is twofold. First, general purpose robots, including humanoids - since they look like us, occupy our spaces, and are able to perform tasks in a manner similar to us - have the ability, at least in theory, to completely replace the majority of human-performed tasks. What are the ethical, legal, and social implications of this sort of technology? It’s tempting to think that humanity has always faced these sorts of labor pressures, but is that actually true? Secondly, humans are not passive observers of our technical decisions and deployments. Most of us welcome some level of automation in our lives (we’re not washing our clothes in boiling cauldrons these days), but also push back against non-human content in the form of “AI slop” on YouTube. We have the opportunity to ask a more general question: “What do we want from our machines?”. The hard part is answering it, but this is something that it won’t be possible to be on the sidelines for. While I’ll provide my own answer as part of this presentation, the main takeaway will be this: form your own opinion, and hold politicians, industry, and yourselves accountable.

Description: South American Summer Monsoon variability and water balance from the Lake Junín (Central Peruvian Andes) molecular isotopic record over glacial-interglacial timescales

Presented by Laura Lopera Congote | GES PhD Candidate, University of Pittsburgh

Talk Abstract:

We are experiencing a period of rapid climate change driven by fossil fuel use, leading to unprecedented environmental change. I aim to understand the climate variability of the Andes and Amazon basin to better constrain future climate change scenarios. While meteorological records rarely extend beyond the past 100 years, we can use lake sediment records to expand our knowledge of how climate has changed over much longer timescales (700,000 years in the case of Lake Junin). Over the past 2.6 million years, the Earth’s climate has oscillated between cold periods (glacials) and warm periods (interglacials). Yet, most paleoclimate records focus on the Holocene (~12,000 years BP), but much less is known beyond this time, because reliable paleorecords of climate extending that far back into time are scarce, especially in tropical South America. However, long sediment cores from Lake Junin in the central Peruvian Andes, offer the opportunity to reconstruct climate, (i.e. temperature, precipitation, and water stress) over several glacial interglacial cycles, providing an unprecedented perspective on tropical climate change. Description: We often think that we need a vacation or large blocks of time in our days to feel refreshed, but it may just be that we need to learn how to capture small doses of well-being where we can in each day. Little “wins” can make a big difference and can be the catalyst to shift our mood/perspective in a positive direction.

The goal of these sessions is to use the time as a gentle nudge toward helping you explore your own interior world through the journal prompt of the day or time to just be still and enjoy the relaxing music. Instead of waiting for the world to stop so we can catch up, let’s slow down on purpose. Make a commitment to show up for yourself; to begin your day from a more centered place. Because, after all, mindset matters.

Description: The Center for Philosophy of Science invites you to our Featured Former Fellow online lecture presented by:

Featured Former Fellow: Jessica Pfeifer

Friday, October 2nd @ 12:00 pm - 1:30 pm EST

Title: An Alternative Account of Objective Probabilities in Evolution

Abstract:

Strevens, Abrams, and Rosenthal have independently developed accounts of objective probability consistent with determinism grounded in the theory of arbitrary functions. In this talk, I focus on Strevens’ way of developing and describing the approach in terms of microconstancy and macroperiodicity. These accounts face (at least) two major problems: (1) the problem of initial conditions; and (2) the question of whether systems studied by scientists satisfy the conditions required for these accounts to work, in particular whether the systems are microconstant and macroperiodic.

The aim of the talk is to outline an alternative account of physical probability in a deterministic system that is grounded in the dynamics of that system, without requiring that the system is microconstant or macroperiodic, and without being dependent on the actual distribution of initial conditions in some form or other. Like Strevens, Abrams, and Rosenthal, I think objective probabilities in deterministic systems can be grounded in facts about the dynamics of the actual world. Description: Join Pitt Alumnus Dr. Mahmood Mamdani (Herbert Lehman Professor of Government, Columbia University)for a conversation with Dr. Christel Temple about his time as a undergraduate student at Pitt during the Civil Rights era.

Mamdani came to the University of Pittsburgh from Uganda in 1963, one of the hundreds of East African students who enrolled in American universities as part of the "Kennedy Airlift." As an undergraduate he joined the civil rights struggle,boarding a bus with fellow Pitt students for Montgomery, Alabama, where he was arrested. After returning to Pitt, he completed his degree in 1967 and went on to become one of the pre-eminent postcolonial scholars of his generation. On October 2, he returns to campus to talk to the Pitt community about his undergraduate days.

Titles and Abstracts

Jillian Herr
Title: Defining the signaling mechanisms of protein trafficking in 2-deoxyglucose-induced metabolic toxicity
Abstract: Cancer cells depend on rapid nutrient uptake through plasma membrane (PM) transporters. Many undergo the Warburg effect (shifting from aerobic respiration to aerobic glycolysis) making them heavily reliant on glucose due to reduced ATP generation per glucose molecule. This glycolytic dependence creates a therapeutic window, where cancer cells are metabolically distinct from healthy cells. 2-deoxyglucose (2DG), a toxic glucose analog that slows glycolysis, explodits this therapeutic vulnerability in cancer cells. 2DG has orphan drug status for treating glioblastomas, aggressive brain cancers with a median survival of 14.6 months post diagnosis. Despite clinical use, the full scope of 2DG’s cytotoxicity remains unclear. Earlier studies from our lab discovered that 2DG triggers rapid endocytosis of glucose transporters, starving cells of glucose. α-Arrestins, a dynamic and understudied class of trafficking adaptors, regulate this 2DG-induced enocytosis of glucose transporters. How widespread is 2DG-induced, alpha-arrestin-mediated endocytosis? We conducted a high-content imaging screen of all yeast PM proteins to identify which respond to 2DG and alpha-arrestins. Remar

Description: The 2026 M. Michael Barmada Memorial Lecture, presented by Eleanor Feingold, PhD, Dean, College of Science, Oregon State University

Genetic Studies of Down Syndrome and Meiotic Recombination
Aneuploidy in human gametes, embryos, and even live births is surprisingly common. The maternal age effect is well known, but both genetic and environmental effects can contribute to risk of aneuploidy. Many of these effects are mediated through phenotypes related to genetic recombination, as physical crossovers stabilize chromosomes during meiosis. This talk traces several decades of genetic epidemiological work on genetic and other risk factors for human aneuploidy.

Dr. Feingold has spent her scientific career as a statistical geneticist and genetic epidemiologist, studying traits as varied as dental caries, Alzheimers, and oral cancer, as well as developing methods for new types of genomic data over a number of generations of technology development. The one constant has been the study of traits related to human reproduction, particularly meiotic recombination and aneuploidy. She spent most of her professional career in the Department of Human Genetics at Pitt, where her colleagues were a constant source of inspiration, education, and friendship. Key among those was Mike Barmada, whose perspectives on computational issues in genomic studies and genomic medicine were formative. Description: Data management and sharing plans (DMSPs) are short documents that outline how a research team will organize, store, preserve, and share their research data during and after data collection. Two major funders changed how these plans are submitted in 2026: the National Science Foundation (NSF) now collects the plan through a structured webform in Research.gov that is tailored to your directorate, and the National Institutes of Health (NIH) replaced its narrative format with a shorter, mostly yes/no format page. The underlying expectations have not softened; the National Science Foundation (NSF) requires that data supporting funded publications be shared at the time of publication, with any exceptions justified in the plan itself.

Attend this workshop to learn how DMPTool, a free online resource, can help you draft, collaborate on, and get feedback on your data management and sharing plan (DMSP) before you enter it into a funder system. DMPTool now offers templates that mirror the Research.gov webform, including directorate-specific versions, along with the 2026 National Institutes of Health (NIH) format.

title: Reasoning over Sets: Toward Consistent LLM Systems (Friday, October 2, 2026)
text:
Reasoning over Sets: Toward Consistent LLM Systems takes place on Friday, October 2, 2026 at 2:00 PM at Sennott Square, 5317.
Event: Reasoning over Sets: Toward Consistent LLM Systems
Date: Friday, October 2, 2026 at 2:00 PM to 3:30 PM
Venue: Sennott Square, 5317, 210 South Bouquet Street, Pittsburgh, PA 15260
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Department of Computer Science
Description: Abstract:
Modern large language models (LLMs) increasingly operate not on single inputs, but over sets of information—collections of generated statements, retrieved documents, or intermediate reasoning steps. However, existing frameworks largely treat these elements independently, overlooking the fact that correctness and reliability often emerge at the set level, where interactions such as contradictions, redundancy, or joint relevance become critical. In this talk, I argue that reasoning over sets is a fundamental challenge for building reliable and controllable LLM systems, and present a unified perspective centered on set-level verification, retrieval, and editing.

Bio:

Jay-Yoon Lee is an Associate Professor in the Graduate School of Data Science at Seoul National University (SNU). His research focuses on improving the reliability and controllability of AI systems, particularly large language models, by enabling them to reason over sets of information such as generated thoughts and retrieved documents. His work spans structured prediction, constraint-based learning, and retrieval-augmented generation.

Prior to joining SNU, he was a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, working with Andrew McCallum. He received his Ph.D. in Computer Science from Carnegie Mellon University under the supervision of Jaime Carbonell, and his B.S. in Electrical Engineering from KAIST. He serves as an Area Chair for ACL, EMNLP, NeurIPS, ICLR, and COLM.

“Back to the Future: Phage Therapy for Treating Antibiotic-Resistant Infections”

title: Mindset Matters Series (Monday, October 5, 2026)
text:
Mindset Matters Series takes place on Monday, October 5, 2026 at 8:30 AM at Online.
Event: Mindset Matters Series
Date: Monday, October 5, 2026 at 8:30 AM to 8:50 AM
Venue: Online
Category: Trainings & Workshops, Virtual
Organizer: Office of Human Resources
Description: We often think that we need a vacation or large blocks of time in our days to feel refreshed, but it may just be that we need to learn how to capture small doses of well-being where we can in each day. Little “wins” can make a big difference and can be the catalyst to shift our mood/perspective in a positive direction.

The goal of these sessions is to use the time as a gentle nudge toward helping you explore your own interior world through the journal prompt of the day or time to just be still and enjoy the relaxing music. Instead of waiting for the world to stop so we can catch up, let’s slow down on purpose. Make a commitment to show up for yourself; to begin your day from a more centered place. Because, after all, mindset matters.

Testimonials:
“I was distracted this morning, but the music in the background and the deep breaths helped ease me into the day.”

“I was on vacation for over a week and really missed the journal prompts. They are great to really put things in perspective and make you think. Thank you!!"

Description: The Center for Philosophy of Science at the University of Pittsburgh invites you to join us for our Lunch Time Talk. Attend in person at 1117 Cathedral of Learning or visit our live stream on YouTube at https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCrRp47ZMXD7NXO3a9Gyh2sg.

LTT: Aditya Jha

Tuesday, October 6th @ 12:00 pm - 1:30 pm EST

Title: The Anatomy of Thermal Equilibrium and Fluctuation Theorems

Abstract:

In this talk, I explore the relationship between various fluctuation theorems and the Second Law in statistical thermodynamics and argue against a commonly held perception, namely that fluctuations somehow constitute a "violation" of the Second Law. I instead suggest that the Second Law restricts the statistical form of fluctuations not only in equilibrium regimes but also in far-from-equilibrium regimes. This restriction, I show, emerges from the anatomy of statistical (thermal) equilibrium, which, properly understood, is a conjunction of three conditions: the stationarity of an ensemble, its detailed balance, and a compositional condition on energies and probabilities, grounded in the operational content of the Second Law, that forces probability to be logarithmically linear in energy. I demonstrate how fluctuation theorems exploit this anatomy: in equilibrium through the global detailed balance of the system itself, and in far-from-equilibrium regimes through local detailed balance, a condition that the thermal environment imposes locally on a system's coarse-grained transiti

What is the GAO? GAO is a nonpartisan, independent agency that works for Congress. Event: Introduction to Text Mining & Analysis (Online)
Date: Wednesday, October 7, 2026 at 1:00 PM to 2:30 PM
Venue: Online
Category: Trainings & Workshops
Organizer: University Library System
Description: This workshop will introduce participants to some essential methods and techniques used for computational text analysis. We will explore the difference between "text mining" and "text analysis," as well as discuss common text processing tasks such as tokenization and computing term and document frequencies (TF-IDF). Finally, we will look at some natural language processing methods such as named entity recognition, sentiment analysis, and topic modeling.

No prior experience with text mining or analysis is required; all are welcome to attend - bring your questions and ideas! The workshop will also introduce some recommended tools and learning resources for getting started with text analysis, including a hands-on demo of Voyant Tools (https://voyant-tools.org/).

Can't make it to this workshop? You can always contact us with your questions about this or other digital scholarship and publishing topics! Read more about Digital Scholarship & Publishing support.

Please check in with the workshop or contact ULS-DigitalScholarshipServices@pitt.edu if you have any pre-event questions. All are welcome at our online events!

title: Fusionism: Liberty, Virtue, and the Future of the American Right - Book Talk by Stephanie Slade (Wednesday, October 7, 2026)
text:
Fusionism: Liberty, Virtue, and the Future of the American Right - Book Talk by Stephanie Slade takes place on Wednesday, October 7, 2026 at 4:30 PM at Wesley W. Posvar Hall, 3911.
Event: Fusionism: Liberty, Virtue, and the Future of the American Right - Book Talk by Stephanie Slade
Date: Wednesday, October 7, 2026 at 4:30 PM to 6:00 PM
Venue: Wesley W. Posvar Hall, 3911, 230 S Bouquet St, Pittsburgh, PA 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Center for Governance and Markets
Price: 0
Description: A book talk with Stephanie Slade, senior editor at Reason

Wednesday, October 7 | 4:30 PM ET | Posvar 3911

Register here — the first attendees get a free copy of the book.

Postwar American conservatism rested on "fusionism," a pairing of liberty and virtue. The Trump-era right has traded that for a muscular, will-to-power approach to governing, upending assumptions about the whole political landscape. Slade traces where the fusionist movement began, how it broke from its founding commitments, and what the country loses if fusionism is abandoned for good. She will discuss:

What it means to be a conservative in the American context, and how that differs from conservatism elsewhere

How the right of the postwar decades compares to the right of today

Q&A with the author follows the talk.

Register

Part of the Pluralism360 series at the Center for Governance and Markets.

Venue: Online
Category: Trainings & Workshops
Organizer: University Center for Teaching and Learning
Description: Online Teaching and Learning encompasses different modalities with one common element: instruction requires access to the internet. Pitt’s official learning management system (LMS) is called Canvas, and all instructors have access to a Canvas course “shell” each semester; a virtual space in which to build their course. During this session, we will review four basic principles of online course design using Canvas to support your in-person and/or remote course to and to enhance your and your students’ educational experiences.

So that we may devote our time to thinking together about the pedagogical rationale that guides our use of Canvas’ features (i.e., Modules, Pages, Assignments/Assessments), we expect you to have completed either of these ~60 minute long, pre-workshop activities:

Option 1: Complete the Introduction to Canvas: Foundations course, orOption 2: Watch the recorded webinar Introduction to Canvas: Getting StartedThis workshop may be counted toward the Online Teaching concentration of the Achievement in Pedagogy Badge, offered through the Graduate Student Teaching Initiative. For more information, visit the Achievement in Pedagogy Badge website or contact teaching@pitt.edu.

By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

Organize important communication and expectation information in CanvasChoose which course layout is best for the materialArrange the course materials consistently throughout the course shellUtilize tools to check course accessibility

title: What Is Aboutness? What Is Agency? What Are Persons? (Thursday, October 8, 2026)
text:
What Is Aboutness? What Is Agency? What Are Persons? takes place on Thursday, October 8, 2026 at 12:30 PM at Cathedral of Learning, 602.
Event: What Is Aboutness? What Is Agency? What Are Persons?
Date: Thursday, October 8, 2026 at 12:30 PM to 2:00 PM
Venue: Cathedral of Learning, 602, Fifth Ave at Bigelow, Pittsburgh, 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Humanities Center
Description: Hosted by the Humanities Center and featuring Visiting Fellow, Josh Berson. Josh will be in conversation with the Center's co-director, Carla Nappi.

A gull alights on the beach and you find yourself adjusting your posture to match theirs. Your body has made itself about the gull, but in one sense you had nothing to do with it. But one evening you squat down and sketch the gull’s likeness in the sand. Now you’ve added something reflexive. We tend to view the two responses as phenomena of different orders. What if we viewed them as regions on a continuum? What if we viewed agency, the felt capacity to act in the world, as a continuation of taxis, the motor responsiveness common to all life?

For this event, Josh Berson and Humanities Center co-director Carla Nappi consider this and neighboring possibilities, building on Berson’s recent work on the contextual quality of such things as meanings and selves. At the root of their conversation stands this premise: experiential qualities like agency or first-personhood are historical phenomena. We should expect them to vary depending on when and where we look. And we might even hope to ask: how are they changing now?

This event will be hybrid, so you can attend it either in person in 602 CL or via Zoom as you prefer. Precirculated material for this colloquium will be available here about two prior to the event.

Josh Berson will also visit on October 29 for an event called Borrowed Places.

Abstract: With the advancement of technology, there is an increasing demand for multifunctional materials that combine optical, electronic, mechanical, and ionic properties. Hybrid metal halide semiconductors (MHS) have emerged as promising candidates for a wide range of optoelectronic applications, including solar cells, light-emitting diodes (LEDs), photodetectors, and lasers. title: Vikram Krishnamurthy, "Adversarial Sensing: Infer, Reveal, and Conceal" (Thursday, October 8, 2026)
text:
Vikram Krishnamurthy, "Adversarial Sensing: Infer, Reveal, and Conceal" takes place on Thursday, October 8, 2026 at 3:30 PM at Benedum Hall, 102.
Event: Vikram Krishnamurthy, "Adversarial Sensing: Infer, Reveal, and Conceal"
Date: Thursday, October 8, 2026 at 3:30 PM to 4:30 PM
Venue: Benedum Hall, 102, 3700 O'Hara Street, Pittsburgh, PA 15261
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Department of Industrial Engineering
Description: Abstract:
In sophisticated sensing and inference systems, such as cognitive radars or networks of interacting LLMs, observations can reveal far more than the physical state: actions and responses also expose hidden beliefs, strategies, and objectives. An adversary can exploit these observed actions and responses to infer the underlying belief. This talk presents a unifying perspective on sensing as an adversarial inference problem.

We first consider how hidden beliefs can be reconstructed from observed actions using inverse filtering, and how information is fused across networks through word-of-mouth learning. Extending this viewpoint to networks of interacting large language models reveals a striking phenomenon: endogenous information exchange can create a persistent “glass ceiling” in influence. We then discuss how revealed preference theory and inverse reinforcement learning serve as principled tools for inferring utility from sensing actions. Finally, we reverse the perspective: how can a sensing system conceal its objectives from an adversarial observer while preserving operational effectiveness? We discuss utility masking and information-theoretic approaches that degrade identifiability while maintaining performance.

Bio:
Vikram is a professor in Electrical and Computer Engineering at Cornell University. His research interests are in statistical signal processing, inverse reinforcement learning, stochastic optimization and partially observed Markov decision processes.

Description: Dr. Vikram Chib will present "Fatigue and the State-Dependent Valuation of Effort in Health and Disease."

Abstract

Our decisions about whether to act depend not only on the costs and rewards of actions in our external environment, but also on our internal state. Physical fatigue provides a powerful example: the same action can feel easy when rested but prohibitively costly when fatigued, even though its objective requirements are unchanged. In this talk, I will present a framework for understanding fatigue as an internal state that reshapes the subjective valuation of physical effort and, consequently, decisions about whether to act. Using behavioral experiments, computational modeling, and neuroimaging, I will show that changes in neuromuscular state systematically increase the subjective cost of effort, biasing individuals away from exertion. I will present evidence that a distributed neural network, including the prefrontal and insular cortices, integrates information about the body's state into the valuation of effortful actions. I will then describe how we are extending this framework to long COVID, a condition in which persistent fatigue is among the most debilitating symptoms. Individuals with long COVID exhibit heightened sensitivity to effort costs, providing a potential mechanism linking persistent fatigue to reduced engagement in everyday activities. Description: NASA’s Airborne and Satellite Thermal Views of Urban Heat Risk

Dr. Glynn Hulley| Carbon Cycle and Ecosystems group at JPL

Talk Abstract:

Extreme heat is becoming the deadliest, costliest climate threat facing cities, and most of it is invisible to the naked eye. Using high-resolution thermal infrared data from NASA's ECOSTRESS satellite (70m) and the airborne HyTES sensor (5m), we map the urban heat island effect down to the level of individual buildings and streets. This talk shows how combining space- and air-based thermal imaging reveals who swelters and who doesn't across Los Angeles by exposing how diurnal heat patterns, mitigation efforts, and decades of geopolitical segregation intersect to create starkly unequal heat exposure. With next-generation missions (EAGLE-TIR, TRISHNA, LSTM) poised to make this kind of data globally available on a daily basis, we're entering a new era of seeing, and addressing, urban heat inequity from above.

Biography:

Dr. Hulley is a member of the Carbon Cycle and Ecosystems group at JPL with 20 years of experience in thermal infrared remote sensing. His research interests include multi- and hyperspectral thermal infrared remote sensing of Earth surface properties, urban climate science, and investigating links between extreme heat and public health. Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Medieval & Renaissance Studies Program
Description: Over the course of the seventeenth century, the North Atlantic and Arctic oceans would occupy a spectral position in English literature and drama even as great numbers of workaday fisherman began to sail between England, Iceland, and Newfoundland in pursuit of cod. This talk brings together these extremes, to investigate not only the practices of map-making and Arctic navigation, but also the oceanic political fictions that emerged around them throughout the seventeenth century.

Benjamin VanWagoner lives in New York and teaches at Columbia University. He is the author of Imperial Ventures: Maritime Drama and the Invention of Risk (Penn Press, 2025) which won the Renaissance Society of America’s First Book Prize. His writing on enslavement, piracy, oceans, colonialism, and precarity has appeared in edited volumes and journals including PMLA and Shakespeare Quarterly. With Jane Hwang Degenhardt, he was co-editor of “Local Oceans,” a special issue of the Journal for Early Modern Cultural Studies, where he now serves on the Advisory Board. He has taught Shakespeare, postcolonial and world literature, Romanticism, theory and criticism, oceanic studies, and composition at Columbia University; Baruch College, CUNY; Taconic Correctional Facility (NY) and Orange High School (NJ).

Description: A workshop for graduate students and jobseekers in the humanities.

Benjamin VanWagoner lives in New York and teaches at Columbia University. He is the author of Imperial Ventures: Maritime Drama and the Invention of Risk (Penn Press, 2025) which won the Renaissance Society of America’s First Book Prize. His writing on enslavement, piracy, oceans, colonialism, and precarity has appeared in edited volumes and journals including PMLA and Shakespeare Quarterly. With Jane Hwang Degenhardt, he was co-editor of “Local Oceans,” a special issue of the Journal for Early Modern Cultural Studies, where he now serves on the Advisory Board. He has taught Shakespeare, postcolonial and world literature, Romanticism, theory and criticism, oceanic studies, and composition at Columbia University; Baruch College, CUNY; Taconic Correctional Facility (NY) and Orange High School (NJ). From 2009–11, he taught high school math in St. Louis.

Category: Trainings & Workshops, Virtual
Organizer: Office of Human Resources
Description: We often think that we need a vacation or large blocks of time in our days to feel refreshed, but it may just be that we need to learn how to capture small doses of well-being where we can in each day. Little “wins” can make a big difference and can be the catalyst to shift our mood/perspective in a positive direction.

The goal of these sessions is to use the time as a gentle nudge toward helping you explore your own interior world through the journal prompt of the day or time to just be still and enjoy the relaxing music. Instead of waiting for the world to stop so we can catch up, let’s slow down on purpose. Make a commitment to show up for yourself; to begin your day from a more centered place. Because, after all, mindset matters.

Testimonials:
“I was distracted this morning, but the music in the background and the deep breaths helped ease me into the day.”

“I was on vacation for over a week and really missed the journal prompts. They are great to really put things in perspective and make you think. Thank you!!"

Description: All maps inevitably distort reality. They project a complex, three-dimensional world onto a flat, two-dimensional plane. Mapmakers use generalization and symbols to highlight the points they want to make. This workshop will briefly trace the role of the map in the history of humanity take a closer look on how we lie with maps.

Eric Spiegel has spent 35+ years in technology. He started as a software developer, moved into leadership, and went on to build and lead teams at startups and Fortune 100 companies. He spent 6 years at Amazon Web Services, where he led a global partner team and conducted 250+ interviews as a hiring manager.

Today, Eric is the Life Design Educator for Computer Science students at Johns Hopkins University, where he advises undergraduates on internships, first jobs, and career strategy in a market reshaped by AI. He also runs First Move Advisory, an independent career advisory practice for early-career students and professionals.

Students advised by Eric have landed internships and full-time roles at OpenAI, Google, Amazon, and other leading employers. He has also seen a growing number of new grads choose startups over big tech, and he can explain what is driving that shift.

Eric is a Pitt alumnus (BS, Information Science, '88), has MS from Johns Hopkins, and has mentored Pitt
students for decades.

Join this roundtable to learn:

How AI is changing entry-level software engineering hiring, and which skills employers screen for now

What separates candidates who get offers from those who apply into the void

Why more graduates are joining startups, and how to evaluate one before you accept

What to build, publish, and practice this year to stand out to recruiters and hiring manage

title: Hiding Patterns: Evasion and Postwar Justice between Romania and the Soviet Union (Friday, October 9, 2026)
text:
Hiding Patterns: Evasion and Postwar Justice between Romania and the Soviet Union takes place on Friday, October 9, 2026 at 4:00 PM at Carnegie Mellon University, Baker/Porter Hall, 246A.
Event: Hiding Patterns: Evasion and Postwar Justice between Romania and the Soviet Union
Date: Friday, October 9, 2026 at 4:00 PM to 5:30 PM
Venue: Carnegie Mellon University, Baker/Porter Hall, 246A
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Center for Russian, East European, and Eurasian Studies, Jewish Studies Program, World History Center
Description: This lecture is part of the Socialist Studies Seminar.

As Soviet forces returned to Bessarabia in 1944, many Holocaust perpetrators sought to evade postwar accountability through flight, concealment, or crossing the Romanian border. This paper follows forty perpetrators implicated in the July 1941 massacre of over 300 Jews in a Bessarabian village, who were split between Romanian and Soviet jurisdictions by the postwar border. What determined whether evasion succeeded: citizenship, mobility, local ties, or the structures of the pursuing states? One crime, one cohort, divided by a single border. What accounted for their radically different fates?

Co-sponsored by the World History Center and Jewish Studies Program at Pitt and the Department of History at Carnegie Mellon University

text:
Poem Plus Prompt: Envisioning Home, with Dilruba (Ruba) Ahmed takes place on Saturday, October 10, 2026 at 1:30 PM at Hillman Library, Text & conText Lab (310 Hillman).
Event: Poem Plus Prompt: Envisioning Home, with Dilruba (Ruba) Ahmed
Date: Saturday, October 10, 2026 at 1:30 PM to 2:30 PM
Venue: Hillman Library, Text & conText Lab (310 Hillman), 3960 Forbes Avenue, Pittsburgh, PA 15260
Category: Trainings & Workshops
Organizer: Center for Creativity
Description: Join us for an hour of reading, discussion, and writing focused on the idea of "home," led by poet Dilruba Ahmed, author of Bring Now the Angels and Dhaka Dust (winner of the Bakeless Prize).

Is home another place, remembered or longed for? A community, a language, or a feeling rather than a location? Is it coming back to yourself, to your body or your history? What does it mean to make home in a place where you're told you don't belong? These questions are at the heart of Envisioning a Just Pittsburgh, a regional call for art inviting Pittsburghers to respond to the idea of home; they’ll also guide our work together.

We'll start with a close read and discussion of one poem that centers "home," exploring and unpacking key craft elements. Then we'll move into quiet, shared writing time with a prompt inspired by the poem, and close by setting a small, achievable personal writing goal to help sustain your ongoing practice.

Open to everyone in the University and wider Pittsburgh communities, no experience necessary. Come prepared to write!

On the poet: Dilruba (Ruba) Ahmed is the author of Bring Now the Angels (Pitt Poetry Series, University of Pittsburgh Press, 2020). Her debut book of poetry, Dhaka Dust (Graywolf Press), won the Bakeless Prize. Her poems have appeared in American Poetry Review, Kenyon Review, New England Review, Ploughshares, and Poetry. She holds degrees from the University of Pittsburgh and Warren Wilson College’s MFA Program for Writers.

Description: We often think that we need a vacation or large blocks of time in our days to feel refreshed, but it may just be that we need to learn how to capture small doses of well-being where we can in each day. Little “wins” can make a big difference and can be the catalyst to shift our mood/perspective in a positive direction.

The goal of these sessions is to use the time as a gentle nudge toward helping you explore your own interior world through the journal prompt of the day or time to just be still and enjoy the relaxing music. Instead of waiting for the world to stop so we can catch up, let’s slow down on purpose. Make a commitment to show up for yourself; to begin your day from a more centered place. Because, after all, mindset matters.

Testimonials:
“I was distracted this morning, but the music in the background and the deep breaths helped ease me into the day.”

“I was on vacation for over a week and really missed the journal prompts. They are great to really put things in perspective and make you think. Thank you!!"

Description: Title: A Redesigned Approach to Accessing Cationic Intermediates

Abstract: Efforts in the Musacchio research group are on the development of enabling chemical transformations to accessing valuable cationic intermediates using mild catalysis from unconventional functional groups. In the past few years, we have successfully established a visible-light photoredox catalysis platform to orchestrate the generation of carbocations directly from C(sp3)–H bonds to avoid the harsh requirements of classical SN1 conditions from organohalides, protected alcohols, etc. The key mechanistic strategy is the combination of two steps: a hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) followed by a radical-polar crossover (RPC), to ultimately provide a net hydride removal from a C–H bond. A recent discovery in our lab demonstrates that this platform can also be used to generate alkene radical cations from homobenzylic C–X motifs (i.e. alkyl halides, protected and unprotected alcohols, and alkyl azides). Computational studies reveal a concerted HAT and spin-center shift (SCS) process to access the radical cation intermediate. We leverage this mechanism to establish a 1,2-difunctionalization of C(sp³)–X motifs. text:
Pitt-CMU Colloquium: Regina Demina (University of Rochester) takes place on Monday, October 12, 2026 at 3:30 PM at Thaw Hall, 321.
Event: Pitt-CMU Colloquium: Regina Demina (University of Rochester)
Date: Monday, October 12, 2026 at 3:30 PM
Venue: Thaw Hall, 321, 3943 O'Hara Street, Pittsburgh, PA 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Department of Physics and Astronomy
Description: Quantum observables at colliders

The behavior of elementary particles is governed by quantum field theory, yet demonstrating their quantum nature experimentally is far from straightforward. Until recently, such demonstrations were either performed at relatively low energies or involved only composite particles. Recent results from the LHC have challenged this status quo by demonstrating entanglement in a system of the heaviest known fundamental particles—the top quarks.

A top-antitop quark pair produced at high energies constitutes a two-qubit system. The top quark has an extremely short lifetime of approximately 5 × 10−25 s, shorter than the characteristic hadronization timescale, 1/ΛQCD ≈ 10−24 s. Consequently, the top quark decays before hadronization, transferring its spin information to the angular distributions of its decay products. This unique feature has been exploited by both the ATLAS and CMS experiments to measure spin correlations between the top and antitop quarks. In certain regions of phase space, these correlations are strong enough to satisfy the Peres–Horodecki criterion for entanglement.

Near the threshold for top-antitop production, an enhancement of the spin correlations beyond theoretical predictions has been observed, pointing to the possible formation of a bound state, commonly referred to as toponium. Detailed studies of the kinematics in this region are consistent with the presence of such a bound-state contribution.

Date: Tuesday, October 13, 2026 at 8:00 AM to 9:00 AM
Venue: Online
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Institute for Bioethics, Jewish Studies Program, Department of Religious Studies
Description: Healthcare and Religion Lecture

Hannah Zaves-Greene, PhD
Author, Able to Be American: Disability in US Immigration Policy and the American Jewish Response

Epilepsy. Heart disease. Varicose veins. “Feeble-mindedness.” In 1891, Congress unambiguously codified the popular sentiment that “defects” like these should preclude admission to the United States. Expanding the eugenics-rooted restrictions of the 1882 Immigration Act, the new law conflated illness, poverty, and disability with criminality and “moral turpitude,” starkly revealing Congress’s vision of the “ideal” American. Simultaneously, American Jews sought security and acceptance in the United States. In confronting this American culture of exclusion, rooted fundamentally in eugenic evaluations of immigrants’ bodies and minds, American Jewish women and men boldly asserted that they too had the right, knowledge, and ability to shape the meaning of American national belonging and, indeed, the fabric of the country itself.

Continuing medical education credit will be available for those in attendance.

Description: A lunch and learn from Prevention at Pitt presented by Karen Jakubowski. Intimate partner violence encompasses a range of harmful behaviors, including physical and sexual violence and coercive control. Sleep is an unexplored behavior that abusive partners may attempt to abuse, manipulate, or control. In our ongoing NIH-funded research, we have identified ways that abusive partners directly interfere with or restrict sleep, which we have termed “sleep coercion and abuse.” We will present results from a series of qualitative interviews and focus groups with IPV survivors, advocates, clinicians, and researchers to discuss key aspects of sleep coercion and abuse. title: LTT: Shimin Zhao - From probability raising to actual causation (Tuesday, October 13, 2026)
text:
LTT: Shimin Zhao - From probability raising to actual causation takes place on Tuesday, October 13, 2026 at 12:00 PM at Cathedral of Learning, The Center for Philosophy of Science  - Room 1117  - 11th Floor.
Event: LTT: Shimin Zhao - From probability raising to actual causation
Date: Tuesday, October 13, 2026 at 12:00 PM to 1:00 PM
Venue: Cathedral of Learning, The Center for Philosophy of Science  - Room 1117  - 11th Floor, Fifth Ave at Bigelow, Pittsburgh, 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Center for Philosophy of Science
Description: The Center for Philosophy of Science at the University of Pittsburgh invites you to join us in person for our upcoming presentations. Due to technical issues, this talk will not be livestreamed. If possible, a recording will be made available on our YouTube channel: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCrRp47ZMXD7NXO3a9Gyh2sg.

LTT: Shimin Zhao

Tuesday, October 13th @ 12:00 pm - 1:30 pm EST

Title: From probability raising to actual causation

Abstract:

In this talk, I address an epistemic gap between statistical causal models and actual causal inquiries. First, I illustrate the gap with two cases: radiation cancer and coin bending. In both cases, the actual causes are empirically undecidable, leading to a deadlock of intuitions. Then, I propose a methodological shift. Rather than relying on unverifiable assumptions, I analyze the functions of causal concepts: why are we interested in causes even when actual causal inquiries cannot be answered? I argue that the answer is: guiding future actions and assigning responsibility. Crucially, for both purposes, a probability-raiser (under interventions) is sufficient. Thus, for practical purposes, a probability-raiser functions exactly as a cause. This crosses the gap from probability raising to actual causation, without dissolving the difference. A metaphysics-free interpretation of the legal “probability of causation” metric is also provided, as an application of my account.

title: Food for Thought with Dr. César Briones (Tuesday, October 13, 2026)
text:
Food for Thought with Dr. César Briones takes place on Tuesday, October 13, 2026 at 1:00 PM at Wesley W. Posvar Hall, 4303 - Center for Urban Education.
Event: Food for Thought with Dr. César Briones
Date: Tuesday, October 13, 2026 at 1:00 PM to 2:30 PM
Venue: Wesley W. Posvar Hall, 4303 - Center for Urban Education, 230 S Bouquet St, Pittsburgh, PA 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Center for Urban Education
Description: Join the Center for Urban Education for "Beyond Nini: If Not School or Work, Then What? A Developmental Reading of Youth Exclusion in Central America" by Dr. César Briones, Assistant Professor of Practice at the University of Pittsburgh School of Education.

Across the capital cities of Central America, millions of young people are labeled "nini," (ni estudia ni trabaja) neither studying nor working, a term that describes a structural condition while quietly judging the people living inside it. This talk asks the question the label avoids: if not school or work, then what? Drawing on Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory, Erikson's identity formation, and Marcia's identity status model, we posit that adolescent identity formation is not optional, only its content is. When institutions fail to offer young people agency, mastery, and consequence, those developmental needs do not disappear. They get met elsewhere, inside whatever structures the urban environment actually makes available. In this framework, gang membership, immigration, and criminality function less like identity confusion and more like identity achievement, built from the materials on offer when legitimate ones close off. While the roots of exclusion reach back to early childhood, adolescence and youth are a second window of opportunity, a developmental period second only to early childhood in its capacity to build the socioemotional skills and sense of agency a young person needs. Description: Brigadier General (Ret.) Choi Wan-kyu is a distinguished expert in the ROK-US alliance, military strategy, and the revolution in military affairs. He retired from the Republic of Korea Army after 38 years of dedicated service.

BG (Ret.) Choi was commissioned as an Infantry Officer upon graduating from the Korea Military Academy in 1988. His academic achievements include a Bachelor of Arts degree from the Korea Military Academy, a Master of Arts in International Relations from Korea University, and a Ph.D. in International Politics from Kyong-gi University.

He furthered his professional education by attending the U.S. Army Infantry School at Fort Benning, Georgia, and the U.S. Army Command and General Staff College at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.

BG (Ret.) Choi had the honor of leading and serving alongside members of all military branches, inter-agency colleagues, and coalition partners throughout his career, from platoon-level units to the ROK-US Combined Forces Command. Notably, he served as the Director for ROK-US Policy in the Ministry of National Defense.

He also participated in multiple overseas deployments, including Operation Enduring Freedom in Afghanistan and Operation Iraqi Freedom.

Currently, BG (Ret.) Choi teaches courses on the history of modern warfare and operational art at the Korea Military Academy.

Description: In partnership with the American-Hellenic Foundation of Western Pennsylvania and the European Art Center in Greece (EUARCE), the Greek Nationality Room's commemoration and celebration of the 250th Anniversary of America unearths previously unknown and underdiscussed facets of its founding. From Revolution to Constitution, Greeks played direct and indirect roles on land and at sea even before 1776.

As we celebrate those unknown Greeks, we also consider the 250th Anniversary of Thomas Paine’s landmark essay “Common Cause”. How ancient Greek thought shaped it, but also how ancient Greek thought tempered it. This synthesis culminated in the Constitution of the United States of America.

With the contribution of distinguished invited guests, this synthesis is discussed, distilled and debated. Is it stable in a modern America facing internal and international challenges?

Last, the distinguished invited guests are asked to consider if and how this synthesis travelled back to a nascent modern Greek state following the Revolutionary War and how the Greek Church acted as the bridge to stabilize the synthesis between the Fire and the Pillar, represented by Paine and Aristotle/Kapodistrias.

With the overarching theme “America 250: The Aegean Arc”, we invite you this October to a first-in-history exploration of the unknown Greeks in the American Revolution, the “Fire” of Paine’s “Common Cause” and what it means to America 250 years lager. Venue: Alumni Hall, 815, 4227 Fifth Avenue, Pittsburgh, PA 15260
Category: Trainings & Workshops
Organizer: University Center for Teaching and Learning
Description: In an age of constant distraction, attention is a precious and limited resource. Designing for learning is also designing for attention—an opportunity to nurture, protect, and sustain it. This workshop will explore strategies for engaging students across the entire learning journey: from piquing curiosity by framing a course around a big question, to modeling engagement and creating a classroom climate that invites participation. We’ll examine practical methods for “warming the course,” and sustaining focus through interactive content. Drawing on insights from theatre and learning science— with examples of how tools like Top Hat can bring these strategies to life—participants will walk away with practices to foster connection and design learning experiences that resonate in an attention-scarce world.

Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.

Description: Talk Title - "From Surviving to Thriving: Development of Psychosocial Interventions to Empower Cardiac Arrest and Neurocritical Care Survivors and Caregivers"

Dr. Alexander Presciutti is a clinical health psychologist and Assistant Professor in the Brain Injury Research Center of Mount Sinai. His research has elucidated post-ICU sequelae faced by survivors and their caregivers, and their downstream impacts on long-term health and quality of life. He is currently funded by the NIH to test survivorship interventions among cardiac arrest survivors and their caregivers, and caregivers of patients with severe acute brain injury.

Dr. Presciutti holds several national leadership roles focused on improving critical care survivorship, including as Chair of the American Heart Association’s (AHA) Emergency Cardiovascular Care Systems of Care Survivorship Committee, Lead of the Survivorship Chapter of the AHA’s 2025 Guidelines for Post-Cardiac Arrest Care, and Chair of the Scientific Advisory Board of the Sudden Cardiac Arrest Foundation.

In January 2023, Dr. Presciutti co-launched the Cardiac Arrest Survivor Alliance, an online peer support community for all those impacted by cardiac arrest. Later that year, he was inducted into the Citizen CPR Foundation’s “Top 40 Under 40” class in recognition of his work in cardiac arrest survivorship.

Prior to joining Mount Sinai, Dr. Presciutti was an Assistant Professor at Harvard Medical School and Staff Psychologist in the Center for Health

title: Foundations of Quantitative Study Deisgn (Wednesday, October 14, 2026)
text:
Foundations of Quantitative Study Deisgn takes place on Wednesday, October 14, 2026 at 3:00 PM at Online.
Event: Foundations of Quantitative Study Deisgn
Date: Wednesday, October 14, 2026 at 3:00 PM to 5:00 PM
Venue: Online
Category: Trainings & Workshops
Organizer: Office of Academic Career Development
Description: Many research publications are rejected due to weak or inappropriate study design and analysis plan. This course offers a structured introduction to core principles of designing rigorous quantitative studies, helping researchers avoid common pitfalls and strengthen their work from the ground up. A well-thought-out study design is essential for successful analysis and interpretation.

Participants will learn how to conceptualize a research study, develop testable hypotheses, select appropriate variables and sampling methods, and apply foundational statistical analyses. The course will also address key methodological considerations, including bias, confounding, and scientific rigor.

Part 1: Conceptualizing a Quantitative Study

Identifying a research topic and problem statementDefining the significance of the studyFormulating clear hypothesesUnderstanding variable types and levels of measurementOperationalizing variables for analysisOverview of sampling methods, including strengths and limitationsPart 2: Study Design, Bias, and Analytical Approaches

Overview of observational and experimental study designsCommon sources of error: bias, confounders, mediators, moderatorsIntroduction to statistical methodsEnsuring scientific rigorBy the end of the lecture, participants will have a stronger foundation for designing quantitative studies that are methodologically sound, analytically robust, and well-suited for grant submissions and manuscript publications.

title: The Flame, the Pillar, and the Bridge: A Core Theoretical Framework for the 250th Anniversary of Thomas Paine's "Common Sense" (Thursday, October 15, 2026)
text:
The Flame, the Pillar, and the Bridge: A Core Theoretical Framework for the 250th Anniversary of Thomas Paine's "Common Sense" takes place on Thursday, October 15, 2026 at Online.
Event: The Flame, the Pillar, and the Bridge: A Core Theoretical Framework for the 250th Anniversary of Thomas Paine's "Common Sense"
Date: Thursday, October 15, 2026
Venue: Online
Category: Virtual
Organizer: Nationality Rooms and Intercultural Exchange Programs
Description: In partnership with the American-Hellenic Foundation of Western Pennsylvania and the European Art Center in Greece (EUARCE), the Greek Nationality Room's commemoration and celebration of the 250th Anniversary of America unearths previously unknown and underdiscussed facets of its founding. From Revolution to Constitution, Greeks played direct and indirect roles on land and at sea even before 1776.

As we celebrate those unknown Greeks, we also consider the 250th Anniversary of Thomas Paine’s landmark essay “Common Cause”. How ancient Greek thought shaped it, but also how ancient Greek thought tempered it. This synthesis culminated in the Constitution of the United States of America.

With the contribution of distinguished invited guests, this synthesis is discussed, distilled and debated. Is it stable in a modern America facing internal and international challenges?

Last, the distinguished invited guests are asked to consider if and how this synthesis travelled back to a nascent modern Greek state following the Revolutionary War and how the Greek Church acted as the bridge to stabilize the synthesis between the Fire and the Pillar, represented by Paine and Aristotle/Kapodistrias.

With the overarching theme “America 250: The Aegean Arc”, we invite you this October to a first-in-history exploration of the unknown Greeks in the American Revolution, the “Fire” of Paine’s “Common Cause” and what it means to America 250 years lager. title: Using Practice and Policy to Support Rural Students' College Access and Success (Thursday, October 15, 2026)
text:
Using Practice and Policy to Support Rural Students' College Access and Success takes place on Thursday, October 15, 2026 at 9:00 AM at Wesley W. Posvar Hall, 2500.
Event: Using Practice and Policy to Support Rural Students' College Access and Success
Date: Thursday, October 15, 2026 at 9:00 AM to 4:00 PM
Venue: Wesley W. Posvar Hall, 2500, 230 S Bouquet St, Pittsburgh, PA 15213
Category: Trainings & Workshops
Organizer: Office of the Provost
Description: Dr. Ty C. McNamee is an Assistant Professor of Educational Policy Studies & Evaluation at the University of Kentucky. Growing up as a gay, working-class student in rural Wyoming influenced Ty's research interests. He studies higher education access, success, and equity for rural students, particularly those from poor and working-class backgrounds and those who are queer, as well as college teaching and learning and faculty development at rural postsecondary institutions.

Outside research, Ty co-founded the Rural Education and Healthcare Coalition, a Teachers College, Columbia University network focused on rural education and healthcare programming and research. He also serves in the Association for the Study of Higher Education (ASHE), the American Educational Research Association (AERA), Student Affairs Administrators in Higher Education (NASPA), and College Student Educators International (ACPA).

Ty holds his EdD in Higher and Postsecondary Education from Teachers College, Columbia University, MA in Higher Education and Student Affairs from the University of Connecticut, and BA in English from the University of Wyoming.

Schedule:

9:30-10 a.m. - Check-in 10 a.m.-noon - Introductions, Literature Review/Discussion, Review of Practice and Policy for Rural Students (offered virtually)Noon-1 p.m. - Lunch with Open Networking and Mingling1-3:30 p.m. - Workshop on Developing Practice and Policy Ideas Register to attend by September 31, 2026.

text:

Category: Trainings & Workshops

Description: Omeka ("Oh-meh-kah") is a free, open source platform for creating digital exhibits. Omeka is best for projects focusing on objects and curation, and it can be a powerful tool for sharing research, showcasing archival materials, and teaching.

This workshop will provide an overview of Omeka's basic functions and features and demonstrate how to build and manage your own site.

This event is the second in a two-part series of workshops on Digital Exhibits. Attendance at the first workshop is not necessary.

Can't make it to this workshop? You can always contact us with your questions about this or other digital scholarship and publishing topics! Read more about Digital Scholarship & Publishing support.

Location: This is a hybrid workshop; you are welcome to attend in-person at Hillman Library or online via Zoom. The in-person portion of the event will take place in Hillman Library's Digital Scholarship Lab (room G30), located just past the main service desk on the ground floor of the library. Look for the glass double-doors after entering through the ground floor atrium entrance; if you enter on the first floor, take the elevator down to the ground floor and turn right out of the elevator.

Software: This workshop does not require any specialized software.

title: Designing Assignment Instructions and Grading (Thursday, October 15, 2026)
text:
Designing Assignment Instructions and Grading takes place on Thursday, October 15, 2026 at 12:00 PM at Online.
Event: Designing Assignment Instructions and Grading
Date: Thursday, October 15, 2026 at 12:00 PM to 1:15 PM
Venue: Online
Category: Trainings & Workshops, Virtual
Organizer: University Center for Teaching and Learning
Description: This beginner-level workshop introduces foundational concepts in student assessment and guides you through creating clear, aligned assignment instructions. You will learn the differences between assessment types, explore characteristics of effective and equitable assessment, and walk through the key steps in the grading process. Using the alignment model, you will have the opportunity to review and revise an assignment prompt and connect it with appropriate grading criteria.

This workshop may be counted toward the Pedagogy concentration of the Achievement in Pedagogy Badge, offered through the Graduate Student Teaching Initiative. For more information, visit the Achievement in Pedagogy Badge website or contact teaching@pitt.edu.

As a result of completing this workshop, participants will be able to:

Define assessment.Articulate the difference between formative and summative assessment.Describe characteristics of effective, equitable assessment.Explain the steps in the grading process.Create an assignment prompt that aligns with a learning objective and clearly communicates grading criteria.

Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Humanities Center
Description: Hosted by the Humanities Center and featuring graduate fellow, Hebah Uddin.

This project engages with horror as a place of survival for Black girls, challenging the presumption that horror as a genre can only further traumatize this jeopardized demographic, and instead framing it as a source of empowerment and strength. Rather than treating horror as shock or spectacle, it focuses on how it functions over time, as a way for young readers to name fear, confront violence, and imagine themselves as capable of enduring it. By recovering a neglected archive of Black women’s children’s and young adult horror, this project offers a radical rethinking of literary history, bringing attention to traditions that have long existed outside the canon.

Respondents include Kaliane Ung, from French and Italian + Dr. Lashon Daley, Director of Children's Literature Program and Director of National Center for the Study of Children's Literature, and Assistant Professor, Department of English & Comparative Literature, San Diego State University. This event will be hybrid, so you can attend it either in person in 602 CL or via Zoom as you prefer. Precirculated material for this colloquium will be available here about two prior to the event.

Description: Dr. Shalini Prasad, Head of Department of Bioengineering at The University of Texas at Dallas, will present "Wearable Sweat Biosensing: Decoding Hormonal, Circadian, and Inflammatory Health in Real Time."

Abstract

Human physiology unfolds in dynamic rhythms, yet conventional diagnostics largely rely on isolated measurements that can miss critical hormonal and inflammatory transitions. This seminar will present wearable electrochemical biosensing technologies designed to continuously and non-invasively measure biomarkers in passive sweat. The talk will highlight two applications. The first examines continuous monitoring of estradiol and progesterone across the menstrual cycle, to resolve individualized hormonal trajectories that discrete blood, saliva, and urine measurements may not capture. The second explores the concurrent monitoring of cortisol, melatonin, interleukin-6, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha to characterize circadian regulation, stress responses, inflammation, and age-associated changes. In a 48-hour study, sweat-based cortisol and melatonin measurements showed strong agreement with salivary reference measurements. Together, these studies illustrate how wearable biosensors can move health assessment from episodic testing toward continuous, multidimensional phenotyping. title: Geology & Environmental Science Colloquium: Dr. Rachel Glade | University of Rochester (Thursday, October 15, 2026)
text:

Event: Geology & Environmental Science Colloquium: Dr. Rachel Glade | University of Rochester
Date: Thursday, October 15, 2026 at 4:00 PM to 5:00 PM
Venue: Thaw Hall, 104, 3943 O'Hara Street, Pittsburgh, PA 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Department of Geology and Environmental Science
Description: How do solifluction patterns form? A journey through icy, drippy, wavy Arctic hillslopes

Presented by Dr. Rachel Glade | Assistant Professor of Earth and Environmental Sciences and Assistant Professor of Mechanical Engineering, University of Rochester

Talk Abstract:

Slowly flowing soil in some of the coldest places on Earth produces large scale features called solifluction patterns that strongly resemble a variety of different fluid patterns, like rainwater flowing down window glass or icing dripping down a cake. We found that despite their striking similarity, the physical ingredients needed to form solifluction patterns are distinct from those found in everyday fluids. Perhaps the closest analogous fluid pattern was only recently discovered—waves formed in oobleck (cornstarch mixed with water). This requires unique behavior in which the flow stiffens at the downhill side of bumps, causing a buildup of material behind it and the ultimate formation of waves. Our work, which includes mathematical theory and computer modeling, shows that solifluction patterns form in a similar way due to spatial differences in soil moisture at the front of bumps on the landscape. This demonstrates how patterns in everyday fluids can be compared and contrasted with complex patterns in sediment to better understand how Earth's surface evolves.
.

Biography:

Dr. Rachel Glade is a geomorphologist who studies sediment transport and landscape evolution using a combination of fieldwork, experiment

Description: Explore the art of decorative bookbinding in this relaxed, hands-on workshop. Learn the fundamentals of Japanese stab binding, a traditional technique known for its beautiful, visible stitching. With roots in centuries-old East Asian bookmaking, stab binding offers a distinctive combination of structure and ornament, making the stitching itself an integral part of the design.

Learn variations and experiment with colorful threads and papers to create your own small softcover notebooks. Along the way, you’ll gain an introduction to basic bookbinding tools, materials, and techniques while discovering how simple changes in stitching create striking geometric patterns.

Designed with beginners in mind, this workshop is an opportunity to slow down, make something by hand, and explore your creativity in a welcoming, informal setting. No previous bookbinding experience is necessary! Just bring your curiosity and a willingness to experiment.

Description: In partnership with the American-Hellenic Foundation of Western Pennsylvania and the European Art Center in Greece (EUARCE), the Greek Nationality Room's commemoration and celebration of the 250th Anniversary of America unearths previously unknown and underdiscussed facets of its founding. From Revolution to Constitution, Greeks played direct and indirect roles on land and at sea even before 1776.

As we celebrate those unknown Greeks, we also consider the 250th Anniversary of Thomas Paine’s landmark essay “Common Cause”. How ancient Greek thought shaped it, but also how ancient Greek thought tempered it. This synthesis culminated in the Constitution of the United States of America.

With the contribution of distinguished invited guests, this synthesis is discussed, distilled and debated. Is it stable in a modern America facing internal and international challenges?

Last, the distinguished invited guests are asked to consider if and how this synthesis travelled back to a nascent modern Greek state following the Revolutionary War and how the Greek Church acted as the bridge to stabilize the synthesis between the Fire and the Pillar, represented by Paine and Aristotle/Kapodistrias.

With the overarching theme “America 250: The Aegean Arc”, we invite you this October to a first-in-history exploration of the unknown Greeks in the American Revolution, the “Fire” of Paine’s “Common Cause” and what it means to America 250 years lager. Abstract

The manufacture of cement is responsible for roughly 7% of global CO2 emissions; if the cement industry were a country, it would rank among the four largest emitters in the world. Decarbonizing concrete is therefore one of the major materials challenges of this century. This lecture examines that challenge from two perspectives separated by nearly 2,000 years. Synchrotron-based techniques are revealing how ancient Roman concretes developed long-term durability and continued to evolve over centuries, absorbing atmospheric CO2 and locking it into the binder as stable minerals. Description: Spirals in Galaxies: Physics and Observations

The iconic spiral arms that decorate the disks of massive galaxies (like our own Milky Way) have been studied observationally and theoretically since they were first recorded nearly 200 years ago, nevertheless the exact details of their physical nature remains elusive. I will review the basic physics of spiral galaxy dynamics, with an emphasis on what is known observationally about spiral arms, including results from the citizen science project Galaxy Zoo (www.galaxyzoo.org) and the large galaxy survey “MaNGA” (Mapping Nearby Galaxies at Apache Point Observatory - part of the SDSS). I will discuss how these and other observational data are currently being used to constrain the variety of different physical models which have been proposed to explain spiral arms in galaxies.

title: LTT: Jamee Elder - The Secret Lives of Mass Gap Black Holes (Friday, October 16, 2026)
text:
LTT: Jamee Elder - The Secret Lives of Mass Gap Black Holes takes place on Friday, October 16, 2026 at 12:00 PM at Cathedral of Learning, The Center for Philosophy of Science  - Room 1117  - 11th Floor.
Event: LTT: Jamee Elder - The Secret Lives of Mass Gap Black Holes
Date: Friday, October 16, 2026 at 12:00 PM to 1:00 PM
Venue: Cathedral of Learning, The Center for Philosophy of Science  - Room 1117  - 11th Floor, Fifth Ave at Bigelow, Pittsburgh, 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Center for Philosophy of Science
Description: The Center for Philosophy of Science at the University of Pittsburgh invites you to join us for our Lunch Time Talk. Attend in person at 1117 Cathedral of Learning or visit our live stream on YouTube at https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCrRp47ZMXD7NXO3a9Gyh2sg.

LTT: Jamee Elder

Friday, October 16th @ 12:00 pm - 1:30 pm EST

Title: The Secret Lives of Mass Gap Black Holes

Abstract:

Recent LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA observations indicate black holes in the “mass gap” where pair-instability supernovae prevent black hole formation. One leading explanation is hierarchical mergers: merging black holes that are themselves products of prior mergers. I examine the evidence for this proposal and draw two methodological lessons. First, the high spins of mass-gap black holes serve as a “smoking gun” signature of merger origin. Second, such inferences rely on narrative models which scaffold epistemic iteration as new information is incorporated. This supports an optimistic view of astrophysical methodology and its capacity to uncover even the darkest objects’ histories.

This talk will also be available live streamed on:

YouTube at https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCrRp47ZMXD7NXO3a9Gyh2sg.

Rita Ononiwu
Title: Elucidating the pathogenic mechanism of polycystin-2 missense mutations in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
Abstract: Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD) is a genetic disease that affects 1 in 400 to 1 in 1,000 people globally. By the time the symptoms of this disease appear, half of all patients are already on the path to kidney failure. Despite the high prevalence of this disease, there is still no specific treatment. We know that ~85% of ADPKD cases are caused by mutations in PKD1 and PKD2, the genes that encode the essential proteins PC1 and PC2. PC1 and PC2 form a heteromeric complex in a 3:1 ratio (PC2:PC1). The function of the polycystin complex in regulating calcium signaling at the cilia of kidney cells is critical to prevent cyst formation in the kidney. However, how disease-associated mutations disrupt the function of the polycystin complex and lead to ADPKD pathogenesis is not fully understood. My research aims to elucidate the pathogenic mechanism of missense mutations in PKD2 that lead to ADPKD. Description: The Clinical and Translational Science Institute's (CTSI) Responsible Conduct of Research (RCR) Center serves as a resource for researchers at the University of Pittsburgh. Our objective is to provide education so that you can learn to effectively recognize and avoid research misconduct and understand the resources that are available to support your research. Click here for more information or to view upcoming workshops.

Presented by Shirley Longinotti, BA, Research Education Facilitator

The International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) was assembled to reduce divergence in regulatory and technical requirements across countries. Harmonized guidelines on Quality, Safety, and Efficacy—along with common terminology and data standards—support consistent global expectations followed by FDA, NIH, and international sponsors.

This session spotlights the ICH E6(R3) revision with a dedicated focus on Annex 2, which provides additional GCP considerations for diverse interventional trial designs such as:

Pragmatic trials that embed research in routine care settings

Decentralized and hybrid trials leveraging emerging technologies

Studies that generate or leverage Real-World Data and Real-World Evidence

Annex 2 guides day‑to‑day GCP decisions on pragmatic and decentralized designs, vendor and DHT oversight, credible use of RWD/RWE, and inspection‑ready monitoring and records

title: Mindset Matters Series (Monday, October 19, 2026)
text:

Event: Mindset Matters Series
Date: Monday, October 19, 2026 at 8:30 AM to 8:50 AM
Venue: Online
Category: Trainings & Workshops, Virtual
Organizer: Office of Human Resources
Description: We often think that we need a vacation or large blocks of time in our days to feel refreshed, but it may just be that we need to learn how to capture small doses of well-being where we can in each day. Little “wins” can make a big difference and can be the catalyst to shift our mood/perspective in a positive direction.

The goal of these sessions is to use the time as a gentle nudge toward helping you explore your own interior world through the journal prompt of the day or time to just be still and enjoy the relaxing music. Instead of waiting for the world to stop so we can catch up, let’s slow down on purpose. Make a commitment to show up for yourself; to begin your day from a more centered place. Because, after all, mindset matters.

Testimonials:
“I was distracted this morning, but the music in the background and the deep breaths helped ease me into the day.”

“I was on vacation for over a week and really missed the journal prompts. They are great to really put things in perspective and make you think. Thank you!!"

title: Foucault and Hayek: On Power, Knowledge, and Freedom - Book talk by Mark Pennington (Monday, October 19, 2026)
text:
Foucault and Hayek: On Power, Knowledge, and Freedom - Book talk by Mark Pennington takes place on Monday, October 19, 2026 at 12:00 PM at Wesley W. Posvar Hall, 3911.
Event: Foucault and Hayek: On Power, Knowledge, and Freedom - Book talk by Mark Pennington
Date: Monday, October 19, 2026 at 12:00 PM to 2:00 PM
Venue: Wesley W. Posvar Hall, 3911, 230 S Bouquet St, Pittsburgh, PA 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Center for Governance and Markets
Price: 0
Description: A talk by Mark Pennington, Professor of Political Economy and Public Policy, King's College London

Monday, October 19 | 12:00 PM ET | Posvar 3911

Register here — the first attendees get a free copy of the book.

Foucault and Hayek are rarely read together, but Pennington argues they should be. Drawing on his new book, Foucault and Liberal Political Economy: Power, Knowledge and Freedom (Oxford University Press, 2025), he shows how Foucault's critique of power can sharpen Hayek's liberalism into a "post-modern liberalism" equipped to identify and challenge illiberalism and over-government in contemporary societies. He will discuss:

Where Foucault's account of power and knowledge complements, rather than contradicts, Hayek's case for freedom

What a post-modern liberalism offers for diagnosing un-freedom today

Q&A follows the talk.

Register to reserve your seat: link

Part of the Pluralism360 series at the Center for Governance and Markets.

Description: The next Aging Institute Research in Progress is scheduled for next Monday, October 19th from 12:00pm–1:00pm!

Presenter Shweta Yadav, PhD (Parkhitko Lab) will be speaking on Methionine restriction promotes stress resistance and longevity through PRMT5

Location (In-Person ONLY):
5th Floor Board Room
100 Technology Drive, Pittsburgh, PA 15219

FREE PARKING: Guest parking is located at the front of the building. Please register your license plate at the security desk.
FREE Pitt Shuttles
FREE PIZZA in conference room

Abstract: Methionine restriction (MetR) extends lifespan and improves metabolic health across species, but clinical translation is limited by poor dietary compliance and palatability. Methionine and ATP are the precursors for the production of S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), the principal and rate-limiting methyl donor used by methyltransferases (MTs). To determine which MTs exert beneficial effects similar to those of MetR, we performed a genetic screen of all MTs predicted in the Drosophila melanogaster genome. Notably, the top 10% of hits were enriched for protein arginine methyltransferases (PRMTs), implicating arginine methylation as a key regulatory node downstream of methionine metabolism. Among these, knockdown of PRMT5 significantly extended lifespan and enhanced resistance to starvation stress, and these effects were conserved in yeast and mammalian cells.
