title: LTT: Caterina Sisti - Ramsey on conditionals and variable hypotheticals (Tuesday, October 20, 2026)
text:
LTT: Caterina Sisti - Ramsey on conditionals and variable hypotheticals takes place on Tuesday, October 20, 2026 at 12:00 PM at Cathedral of Learning, The Center for Philosophy of Science  - Room 1117  - 11th Floor.
Event: LTT: Caterina Sisti - Ramsey on conditionals and variable hypotheticals
Date: Tuesday, October 20, 2026 at 12:00 PM to 1:00 PM
Venue: Cathedral of Learning, The Center for Philosophy of Science  - Room 1117  - 11th Floor, Fifth Ave at Bigelow, Pittsburgh, 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Center for Philosophy of Science
Description: The Center for Philosophy of Science at the University of Pittsburgh invites you to join us for our Lunch Time Talk. Attend in person at 1117 Cathedral of Learning or visit our live stream on YouTube at https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCrRp47ZMXD7NXO3a9Gyh2sg.

LTT: Caterina Sisti

Tuesday, October 20th @ 12:00 pm - 1:30 pm EST

Title: Ramsey on conditionals and variable hypotheticals

Abstract:

The standard view in the contemporary literature on conditionals reads Ramsey as evaluating indicative conditionals by conditional probability, while offering only a few remarks on counterfactuals. This interpretation is associated with the so-called “Ramsey Test”, a procedure for evaluating conditionals developed by later authors from a short footnote in Ramsey’s General Propositions and Causality (1929). Drawing on his broader writings, I argue that the picture is not quite accurate: counterfactuals occupy a much more central place in Ramsey’s account than is usually recognized, and conditional probability is not meant to apply to all indicative conditionals. I present Ramsey’s overall view of conditionals and show how it is connected to his conception of variable hypotheticals — a distinctive form of generalization.

Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Department of Chemistry
Description: Title: Chemistry Innovation and Biological Discovery through Natural Product Total Synthesis

Abstract: This talk will focus on our recent efforts in function and efficiency-driven total synthesis of medicinally important natural products. The target molecules include macrolides, alkaloids, and polycyclic diterpenoids. Novel and enabling synthetic strategies and methodologies including skeletal editing, radical retrosynthesis, and catalytic carbonylation toward these target molecules will be highlighted. Biological evaluation and target identification of the selected natural products and their analogs will be discussed as well. These biological endeavors have led us to the exciting territories of targeting the previously undruggable disease proteins for novel therapeutic development. Overall, this talk will emphasize how we use natural product total synthesis to achieve chemistry innovation and biological discovery.

Biosketch: Dr. Mingji Dai grew up in a small village in Sichuan, China and received his B.S. degree from Peking University in 2002 under the mentorship of Professors Zhen Yang and Jiahua Chen. After working as a research associate in the same laboratory for two more years, he went to New York City in 2004 and earned his Ph.D. degree with distinction from Columbia University in 2009 under the mentorship of Professor Samuel J. text:
The Flame, the Pillar, and the Bridge: A Core Theoretical Framework for the 250th Anniversary of Thomas Paine's "Common Sense" takes place on Wednesday, October 21, 2026 at Online.
Event: The Flame, the Pillar, and the Bridge: A Core Theoretical Framework for the 250th Anniversary of Thomas Paine's "Common Sense"
Date: Wednesday, October 21, 2026
Venue: Online
Category: Virtual
Organizer: Nationality Rooms and Intercultural Exchange Programs
Description: In partnership with the American-Hellenic Foundation of Western Pennsylvania and the European Art Center in Greece (EUARCE), the Greek Nationality Room's commemoration and celebration of the 250th Anniversary of America unearths previously unknown and underdiscussed facets of its founding. From Revolution to Constitution, Greeks played direct and indirect roles on land and at sea even before 1776.

As we celebrate those unknown Greeks, we also consider the 250th Anniversary of Thomas Paine’s landmark essay “Common Cause”. How ancient Greek thought shaped it, but also how ancient Greek thought tempered it. This synthesis culminated in the Constitution of the United States of America.

With the contribution of distinguished invited guests, this synthesis is discussed, distilled and debated. Is it stable in a modern America facing internal and international challenges?

Last, the distinguished invited guests are asked to consider if and how this synthesis travelled back to a nascent modern Greek state following the Revolutionary War and how the Greek Church acted as the bridge to stabilize the synthesis between the Fire and the Pillar, represented by Paine and Aristotle/Kapodistrias.

With the overarching theme “America 250: The Aegean Arc”, we invite you this October to a first-in-history exploration of the unknown Greeks in the American Revolution, the “Fire” of Paine’s “Common Cause” and what it means to America 250 years lager. Title: Genotyping Bd Across Spatial and Temporal Scales and Investigating Strain Specific Susceptibility in Bullfrogs
Abstract: Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) is a fungal pathogen responsible for an ongoing epizootic that is causing catastrophic losses to amphibian populations (Scheele et al. 2019). Bd is thought to have dispersed rapidly and recently due to global trade, but hypotheses on Bd origins are extremely conflicted (Byrne et al. 2019). The Fluidigm Access Array platform utilizes Bd extracts from previously collected amphibian skin swabs to amplify many specifically selected regions of the Bd genome using a microfluidic multiplex PCR platform to prepare samples for Illumina sequencing. Since Bd in culture is not required for this assay, Fluidigm provides a unique opportunity to genotype Bd to analyze its range and spread from both a spatial scale as well as a temporal scale using swabbed amphibian museum specimens. Findings from previous similar studies have found that bullfrogs in Pennsylvania appear to exhibit strain specific susceptibility in which they are infected with the Bd-GPL1 sub lineage despite the presence of other lineages (Byrne et al. 2022), but further investigation is needed to decipher why this is. title: Entangled with the River: The making of Safavid Isfahan from Watershed to Body (HAA Colloquium) (Wednesday, October 21, 2026)
text:
Entangled with the River: The making of Safavid Isfahan from Watershed to Body (HAA Colloquium) takes place on Wednesday, October 21, 2026 at 12:00 PM at Frick Fine Arts Building, 202.
Event: Entangled with the River: The making of Safavid Isfahan from Watershed to Body (HAA Colloquium)
Date: Wednesday, October 21, 2026 at 12:00 PM to 12:50 PM
Venue: Frick Fine Arts Building, 202, 650 Schenley Drive, Pittsburgh, PA 15260
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Department of History of Art and Architecture
Description: The usual story of seventeenth-century Isfahan is a story of land: a capital remade by Shah Abbas I (r.1588-1629) and his Safavid successors through squares, gardens, promenades, and monumental structures, making the city a rival to the great cities of the early modern world. This talk proposes a shift of lens, from land to water, and asks what that shift offers to the study of the familiar. If the city is read outward from its famed river, the Zayandehrud, what new questions arise, which new actors enter the story, which overlooked spaces come into view, and what fresh interpretations of well-known buildings emerge?

Moving between scales, from the watershed to the body of a single structure, the talk argues that the Zayandehrud was never a neutral backdrop to the city’s development. Its properties were carefully considered, its potentials were put to work, and its limits and threats were managed. Each of these engagements left traces in Isfahan’s built environment: from gardens and urban spaces, to ambitious infrastructural projects, to the physical structure of its bridges. Read together, they reveal a city shaped in continuous dialogue with its river.

About the Speaker: Sahar Hosseini is an Assistant Professor in the Department of History of Art & Architecture. Read her faculty profile.

title: Dissertation Defense: Krysta Beam (Wednesday, October 21, 2026)
text:
Dissertation Defense: Krysta Beam takes place on Wednesday, October 21, 2026 at 5:00 PM at Online.
Event: Dissertation Defense: Krysta Beam
Date: Wednesday, October 21, 2026 at 5:00 PM to 7:00 PM
Venue: Online
Category: Defenses
Organizer: Department of History
Description: Join the History Department in support of Krysta Beam, who will defend her dissertation, "Transnational Child-Saving, Hogar Bíblico Roblealto, and Latin America Mission in Costa Rica, 1921-1980," on Wednesday, October 21 from 5-7PM EST over Zoom.

Founded in 1932 by missionaries of the Latin America Mission, Hogar Bíblico Roblealto, a children's residential home in Heredia, Costa Rica, serves as a compelling case study for examining twentieth-century evangelical engagement in Latin America. Its significance is heightened by the Costa Rican context: a nation defined by strong political mobilization and a burgeoning welfare state. This study traces transnational encounters, exchanges and negotiations between missionaries, international financial supporters, local workers, state reformers, and children. Employing a multi-scalar approach, the study addresses methodological and theoretical challenges in the history of childhood. By pairing adult-curated archival records with oral history interviews, it recovers the voices of former child-residents, highlighting how their memories were informed by spiritual experiences and religious identities. Ultimately, this work demonstrates that while Protestant mission in Latin America shifted from career missionaries to youth-focused short-term mission trips, the imperative of child-saving consistently anchored evangelical presence through residential homes, schools, clinics, and summer camps.

Description: In partnership with the American-Hellenic Foundation of Western Pennsylvania and the European Art Center in Greece (EUARCE), the Greek Nationality Room's commemoration and celebration of the 250th Anniversary of America unearths previously unknown and underdiscussed facets of its founding. From Revolution to Constitution, Greeks played direct and indirect roles on land and at sea even before 1776.

As we celebrate those unknown Greeks, we also consider the 250th Anniversary of Thomas Paine’s landmark essay “Common Cause”. How ancient Greek thought shaped it, but also how ancient Greek thought tempered it. This synthesis culminated in the Constitution of the United States of America.

With the contribution of distinguished invited guests, this synthesis is discussed, distilled and debated. Is it stable in a modern America facing internal and international challenges?

Last, the distinguished invited guests are asked to consider if and how this synthesis travelled back to a nascent modern Greek state following the Revolutionary War and how the Greek Church acted as the bridge to stabilize the synthesis between the Fire and the Pillar, represented by Paine and Aristotle/Kapodistrias.

Organizer: Center for Latin American Studies
Description: Please register to attend. Lunch will be served.

CLAS Speaker Series: "The Necropolitics of Silence: Sound, Protest, and State Power in Colombia (2019-2021)"

Abstract:

Between 2019 and 2021, Colombia’s Paro Nacional (National Strike) established sound and music as central instruments of political protest. This lecture examines two significant instances of this phenomenon: the viral 2019 Cacerolazo Nacional, in which banging pots and pans spread across the country as a spontaneous form of dissent, and the 2021 Cacerolazos Sinfónicos, in which orchestral musicians brought their instruments into public demonstrations. Reading mediated sources, including videos, WhatsApp communications, press coverage, and human rights reports, as situated representations rather than transparent evidence of lived experience, this analysis develops a theoretical framework that extends Achille Mbembe's concept of necropolitics from lethal exposure to what might be termed aural governance. This framework, theorized here as a necropolitics of silence, accounts for how states render certain voices, communities, and experiences inaudible as a means of fragmenting and managing populations. In response to this imposed silence, citizens mobilized practices of noising and musicking to form ephemeral sonic communities that contested state-imposed inaudibility and briefly redistributed the sensible, reclaiming urban space for democratic claim-making. Organizer: Health Sciences: Office of the Senior Vice Chancellor
Description: Antonio D’Amore
Associate professor of surgery,
School of Medicine

“Observe, Understand, Develop: Structural Biomimicry in Cardiovascular Tissue Engineering”

Cardiovascular implants can restore function and save lives, but most cannot grow, repair themselves or remodel as living tissues do. D’Amore’s laboratory investigates whether structural biomimicry—reproducing the organization and mechanics of native tissues—can make implant architecture an active cue for tissue formation. Using engineered heart valves, chordae tendineae and blood vessels as complementary test beds, he will show how advanced manufacturing, quantitative tissue mapping, bioreactors, computational modeling and preclinical studies can reveal design rules linking structure, function and tissue remodeling. This integrated platform connects fundamental discovery with reproducible manufacturing, commercial translation, industry partnerships and a credible path toward patient impact.

Description: Annual Variations in Carbon, Nitrogen, and Nitrate in Trophic Endmember Freshwater Lake Systems

Presented by Timothy Suder | PhD Candidate, Geology and Environmental Science, University of Pittsburgh

Talk Abstract:

With the increased prevalence of drought-like conditions in many areas of the world, freshwater has become a critically significant resource. Thus, not only is the presence of freshwater important, but the health of those aquatic ecosystems becomes increasingly consequential. One aspect of this is the impact of algae on lacustrine ecosystems. While algae is usually beneficial to the ecosystem in which it is present, as it is a major primary producer, it can become harmful to the same ecosystem if it grows out of control into what is known as a harmful algal bloom (HAB). These blooms can shade out other photosynthesizing organisms, deoxygenate the water, and, in the case where the HAB is made up predominantly of cyanobacteria, produce toxins that get released into the water column. HABs are largely the result of anthropogenic input of key nutrients, including nitrate and ammonia, and the shifts in climate resulting from anthropogenic climate change. With this, it becomes important to not only look at the modern algal communities, but to also understand historic changes in algal communities that allow a window into how algal populations have changed and are likely to change in a lacustrine system. Description: Join us to celebrate the work of our Unleashed Wonder grant recipients, Divya Tase and Zora Borde-Perry. Come meet them and check out their work, and enjoy an evening of unleashed creativity!

A project by Divya Tase (Biology & Public Health '28) explored creativity, reflection, and community service. The Street Medicine at Pitt One-Word Workshop invited participants to reflect on their experiences through art, creating space for connection and well-being beyond street rounds. Meals that Matter brought together students and faculty to explore how thoughtful culinary practices can be a creative expression of empathy and equity. Together, these events highlighted creativity and community as meaningful forms of service and connection.

Petals of Persistence by Zora Borde-Perry (Social Work '27) began with a question: How can culturally significant flowers represent beauty and resilience in places experiencing sociopolitical hardship? Zora’s project transformed broken fragments of glass into a series of floral mosaics, creating art that echoes the fracture and reassembly of histories. Each work honors a place navigating sociopolitical strain while centering its living symbol of continuity. She views her project as an offering, a reminder that even in turbulent climates, something sacred continues to bloom.

Description: Westmoreland Reads welcomes Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist and author Eliza Griswold to campus to discuss her book, Amity and Prosperity: One Family and the Fracturing of America. The event is free and open to the campus community and the public.

Griswold tells the story of the energy boom’s impact on a small town in Washington County (PA). The fracking boom in the early 2000s forced Stacey Haney, a local nurse, to become an unlikely activist as she grappled with the negative changes to her children’s health and the health of the animals on her farm. Griswold based the book on seven years of immersive reporting and reveals what happens when an imperiled town faces a crisis of values, and a family wagers everything on an improbable quest for justice. (from https://us.macmillan.com/books/9781250215079/amityandprosperity/)

Westmoreland Reads selected Griswold's book as the 2026 common read. Print and audio copies of the book are available (while supplies last) at no cost, as are chapter-by-chapter reading questions and a discussion guide. Visit the Westmoreland Reads page for details.

Venue: Benedum Hall, 102, 3700 O'Hara Street, Pittsburgh, PA 15261
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Department of Chemical and Petroleum Engineering
Description: Abstract: Living systems self-regulate by operating at dynamic optima through feedback loops between mechanics and chemical kinetics, an ability largely missing in synthetic matter. Realizing next-generation materials with analogous capabilities requires exploring these feedback loops outside of purely biological settings. To motivate this core idea, I will first present an integrated theory of cell migration bridging force generation, mechanics, and biochemical signaling, revealing how the mechanics of filopodial protrusions regulates chemical polarization to sustain locomotion. I will then propose a passive physical feedback loop that utilizes the fluid mechanics of viscous flow vortices to design minimal artificial analogs of cell filopodia. Next, I will introduce theory and experiments on "hydrogel diffusiophoresis," a soft deformation pathway driven by solute gradients discovered by my group. I will show how it can potentially close the chemomechanical feedback loop to enable truly active, tissue-like materials. Finally, I will present a first-principles geometric theory of elastic filaments constrained on curved surfaces in a frustrated state. Our solution to this problem paves the way for understanding chemomechanical coupling in biological systems like contractile actin rings on the cell membrane during cytokinesis.

"Jobsite of the Near Future: Simulation as the Decision Engine for Agentic AI in Construction"

Abstract:

Imagine a haul truck breaking down at 9:40 a.m. By 9:50, the site engineer has three options on screen, each with its expected effect on the day’s production, along with a recommendation and one clarifying question from an AI assistant. What would have to be true for that to work?

This talk argues that the answer is simulation. Construction operations are stochastic, resource-coupled, and constantly disturbed, which is why a schedule alone cannot tell an engineer what will happen next. Discrete-event simulation can, by representing how crews, equipment, and materials interact over time and by answering “what if” before a decision is made. Yet simulation has largely stayed in the lab, because building and updating a model has always cost more time than a jobsite has.

Agentic AI changes that equation. Large language model agents can read the changing world into the model, run the right computational experiments, and translate outcome distributions into timely recommendations, while knowing when to ask a human. Description: "Statistical Methods for the Design and Analysis of Circadian Omics Studies", School of Public Health Department of Biostatistics and Health Data Science.

Advisor and Committee Chair: George Tseng

Abstract:

Circadian rhythms coordinate daily physiology and influence health and disease. Advances in high-throughput
technologies have expanded circadian omics studies across tissues, species, and molecular modalities. Limited
sample sizes and uneven sampling times require careful power analysis and study design. Comparisons
between conditions help distinguish conserved from altered rhythmic programs and assess how well animal
models recapitulate human circadian biology. Integrating evidence across tissues further reveals the temporal
organization of these programs across organs and their conservation across species. This dissertation develops
three statistical frameworks to address these connected needs.

In Chapter 2, we develop Simulation-based Circadian Power (SCP), a framework for power analysis and sample
size planning in circadian omics studies. SCP uses pilot-derived distributions of amplitude, phase, sampling time,
and noise to capture transcriptome-wide signal heterogeneity. It estimates power under false discovery rate

title: Machine Learning You Can Maintain: Observable, Editable, and Modular Models (Friday, October 23, 2026)
text:
Machine Learning You Can Maintain: Observable, Editable, and Modular Models takes place on Friday, October 23, 2026 at 12:00 PM at Sennott Square, 5317.
Event: Machine Learning You Can Maintain: Observable, Editable, and Modular Models
Date: Friday, October 23, 2026 at 12:00 PM to 2:00 PM
Venue: Sennott Square, 5317, 210 South Bouquet Street, Pittsburgh, PA 15260
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Department of Computer Science
Description: Talk Abstract

Modern machine learning remains dependent on a paradigm in which considerable up-front effort produces models that are monolithic, opaque, and costly to change once trained. In this talk, I will discuss three active lines of research from the AI Division at the Software Engineering Institute that aim to make ML models easier to maintain. First, I will present analytic methods that propagate uncertainty from a neural network’s inputs through to its outputs without sampling. These methods enable applications ranging from efficient online Bayesian updates to assessing how a model responds to rare events. Second, I will describe a machine unlearning method for mixture-of-experts models that isolates the influence of subsets of training data within dedicated experts, so that specific training examples can be removed without retraining from scratch. Finally, I will present techniques for modularizing neural networks that perform end-to-end autonomous control, decomposing them into components for subtasks such as perception and navigation. This approach retains much of the performance of end-to-end learning while allowing individual components to be inspected, tested, and replaced. Together, these efforts point toward ML systems that can be monitored, corrected, and evolved after deployment.

Alex Spittel

Title: Investigating a novel embryonic gene with potential roles in transposon defense
Abstract: During embryonic development, dynamic gene regulation underlies the rapid differentiation from stem cell to subsequent specialized cell types. Chromatin regulatory factors play a pivotal role during this process. Enzymes such as lysine methyltransferases (KMTs) selectively deposit methyl groups on histones, the proteins that make up the nucleosomal core around which DNA is wrapped. This correlates with gene expression activation or repression depending on which histone residues are modified. How these enzymes coordinate and interact with their substrates to modulate gene expression during early development remains to be fully characterized. The Lee lab investigates gene expression and chromatin dynamics across animals, to better understand the evolution of convergent and divergent regulatory mechanisms guiding early embryonic development. title: When did Greek astronomy start looking like Ptolemy's astronomy? (Friday, October 23, 2026)
text:
When did Greek astronomy start looking like Ptolemy's astronomy? takes place on Friday, October 23, 2026 at 4:00 PM at Cathedral of Learning, 332.
Event: When did Greek astronomy start looking like Ptolemy's astronomy?
Date: Friday, October 23, 2026 at 4:00 PM
Venue: Cathedral of Learning, 332, Fifth Ave at Bigelow, Pittsburgh, 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Department of Classics
Description: Click for event flyer

Ptolemy’s astronomical writings, and in particular his Almagest, defined for many centuries of later astronomers in the Byzantine, Islamic, and Latin traditions what the central goals and practices of astronomy were, namely the deduction and quantification of geometrical models for the heavenly bodies through mathematical analysis of observations, and the production of predictive tables based on those models. In this talk I will explore the questions—made the more challenging by the loss of most of the Greek astronomical literature by his predecessors—how much of Ptolemy’s scientific program was original to himself and to what extent, and since when, earlier Greek astronomy followed the same agenda.

Description: In partnership with the American-Hellenic Foundation of Western Pennsylvania and the European Art Center in Greece (EUARCE), the Greek Nationality Room's commemoration and celebration of the 250th Anniversary of America unearths previously unknown and underdiscussed facets of its founding. From Revolution to Constitution, Greeks played direct and indirect roles on land and at sea even before 1776.

As we celebrate those unknown Greeks, we also consider the 250th Anniversary of Thomas Paine’s landmark essay “Common Cause”. How ancient Greek thought shaped it, but also how ancient Greek thought tempered it. This synthesis culminated in the Constitution of the United States of America.

With the contribution of distinguished invited guests, this synthesis is discussed, distilled and debated. Is it stable in a modern America facing internal and international challenges?

Last, the distinguished invited guests are asked to consider if and how this synthesis travelled back to a nascent modern Greek state following the Revolutionary War and how the Greek Church acted as the bridge to stabilize the synthesis between the Fire and the Pillar, represented by Paine and Aristotle/Kapodistrias.

With the overarching theme “America 250: The Aegean Arc”, we invite you this October to a first-in-history exploration of the unknown Greeks in the American Revolution, the “Fire” of Paine’s “Common Cause” and what it means to America 250 years lager. Description: Workshop on the Naturalized Metaphysics of Physics

October 24 @ 8:30 am - 5:30 pm EDT

Venue and Date: Center for Philosophy of Science, University of Pittsburgh - October 24, 2026

In light of radical ontological revision demanded by relativity and quantum mechanics, naturalized metaphysics of physics seeks to develop metaphysical accounts by taking the content, practice, and empirical successes of contemporary physical theories as the primary evidence and constraint. It rejects approaches that rely primarily on a priori reasoning or intuitions disconnected from scientific practice, while recognizing the study of the topics traditionally under the purview of metaphysics (ontology, fundamentality, laws, space and time, etc.) as critical for understanding of the picture of the world entailed by our best physical theories.

Speakers will share research exploring questions related to the following key themes.

1. text:
America 250: George Hubbard Clapp: A Life of Curiosity, Collecting, and Contributions takes place on Saturday, October 24, 2026 at 2:00 PM at Cathedral of Learning, 332.
Event: America 250: George Hubbard Clapp: A Life of Curiosity, Collecting, and Contributions
Date: Saturday, October 24, 2026 at 2:00 PM
Venue: Cathedral of Learning, 332, Fifth Ave at Bigelow, Pittsburgh, 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Nationality Rooms and Intercultural Exchange Programs
Description: George Hubbard Clapp, longtime Board Member of the University of Pittsburgh, supporter of the school through its transition to Oakland, was a Renaissance-man who endowed public collections with his wide-ranging interests in mollusk shells, coins, art, and the preservation of history. The commemorative lecture will highlight George Hubbard Clapp's many contributions to the liberal arts and sciences in Pittsburgh and reveal a man whose drive was one of abundant curiosity and support.

George Hubbard Clapp donated the Early American Room to the University of Pittsburgh in the late 1930’s. Mr. Hubbard Clapp also gave funding support to each of the Nationality and Heritage Rooms that were being constructed during that time period.

At 2:00 pm, Michael Walter, Manager of Education Programs for the Nationality Rooms and Intercultural Exchange Programs, will share details on the life and contributions of George Hubbard Clapp.

Following the lecture, representatives of the Pittsburgh Chapter of the Pennsylvania Society Sons of the American Revolution will recognize George Hubbard Clapp posthumously with the PSSAR Silver Good Citizenship Award as a recognition of his outstanding and unusual patriotic achievement and service to the Pittsburgh region.

Private, small group tours will be led in the Early American Room during the Q&A section of the lecture.

A reception will be held in the Braun Room on the 12th floor of the Cathedral of Learning immediately following the talk.

Description: Dedicated to promoting peace through music and sound, violinist Monique Mead joins 30 sound practitioners and musicians to envelop you in an immersive soundscape unlike any other.

title: When to Let Students Use AI—and When to Say No (Monday, October 26, 2026)
text:
When to Let Students Use AI—and When to Say No takes place on Monday, October 26, 2026 at 10:30 AM at Online.
Event: When to Let Students Use AI—and When to Say No
Date: Monday, October 26, 2026 at 10:30 AM to 12:00 PM
Venue: Online
Category: Trainings & Workshops
Organizer: University Center for Teaching and Learning
Description: AI can be a valuable tool for teaching and learning. It is also becoming ubiquitous in the workplace. But it brings risks if not used correctly and in the appropriate context. Students who outsource their thinking to AI tools before mastering core skills will struggle to think independently and evaluate information critically. These same skills are also needed for effective AI use after graduation. Like a conductor who tries to lead an orchestra before knowing how to play an instrument, a student needs a strong foundation to be able to leverage AI's potential ethically and effectively. In this workshop we'll focus on a scaffolded framework for managing AI in higher-education courses. We'll explain how instructors can decide if, when, and how to deploy AI tools in their teaching. We'll discuss appropriate scaffolding and how it applies across the spectrum—from no-use or restricted-use zones to sophisticated applications at the capstone level. You'll leave with a concrete decision checklist, an approach to integrating AI into your teaching, and ready-to-use AI guidance for students. The goal is teaching that supports foundational skills and prepares graduates to command AI rather than be commanded by it.

Description: Taiwan's fledgling plastic industry faced immense cost pressures and mounting losses, after crude oil prices skyrocketed following the Oil Crises of 1973 and 1979 and multi-national petrochemical companies withdrew in the 1980s. Description: Active Matter: The Physics of Self-Organization

Birds flock, bees swarm and fish school. These are just some of the remarkable examples of collective behavior found in nature. Physicists have been able to capture some of this behavior by modeling organisms as ``flying spins’’ that align with their neighbors according to simple but noisy rules. Successes like these have spawned a field devoted to the physics of active matter – matter made not of atom and molecules but of entities that consume energy to generate their own motion and forces. Through interactions, collectives of such active particles organize in emergent structures on scales much larger than that of the individuals. Living systems are the paradigm of such behavior, but same behavior has also been mimicked in the lab through the engineering a variety of ``active particles’’ that self-assemble to form smart materials.

In this lecture I will introduce the field of active matter and highlight ongoing efforts by physicists, biologists, engineers and mathematicians to model the complex behavior of these systems, with the goal of identifying universal principles. I will specifically focus on two examples of active behavior. Description: Icy, unpredictable, and treacherous, the dangers of the Yalu River between Korea and China were heightened in the twentieth century when it became part of the longest non-maritime border of the Japanese Empire. Border of Water and Ice (Cornell University Press, 2024) focuses on the river at this critical juncture, analyzing how imperial Japan attempted to harness and control this fluid border. By examining both human and nonhuman actors — including water, ice, timber cutters, smugglers, and anti-Japanese guerrillas — Joseph Seeley shows how the Yalu determined how borders were drawn, how imperial power was exerted, and how local resistance was enacted.

Dr. Joseph Seeley is an Associate Professor at the University of Virginia's Corcoran Department of History. A specialist in the histories of Korea, the Japanese Empire, and the East Asian environments and borderlands, Seeley is the author of the recently-published Border of Water and Ice (shortlisted for the ACLS Open Access Book Prize) as well as articles on such topics as cattle disease control in colonial Korea, Japanese colonial zoos in Seoul and Taipei, North Korean hydraulic engineering, Korean tiger-human relations, and US-Korea relations. He is currently working on two new book projects: one a solo-authored work on the environmental history of North Korea, the other a co-authored project (with Aaron Skabelund and Lisa Yoshikawa) on the history of hunting in the Japanese Empire. title: LTT: Nick Huggett - The Highs and Lows of Particle Physics (work with Mike Schneider) (Tuesday, October 27, 2026)
text:
LTT: Nick Huggett - The Highs and Lows of Particle Physics (work with Mike Schneider) takes place on Tuesday, October 27, 2026 at 12:00 PM at Cathedral of Learning, The Center for Philosophy of Science  - Room 1117  - 11th Floor.
Event: LTT: Nick Huggett - The Highs and Lows of Particle Physics (work with Mike Schneider)
Date: Tuesday, October 27, 2026 at 12:00 PM to 1:00 PM
Venue: Cathedral of Learning, The Center for Philosophy of Science  - Room 1117  - 11th Floor, Fifth Ave at Bigelow, Pittsburgh, 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Center for Philosophy of Science
Description: The Center for Philosophy of Science at the University of Pittsburgh invites you to join us for our Lunch Time Talk. Attend in person at 1117 Cathedral of Learning or visit our live stream on YouTube at https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCrRp47ZMXD7NXO3a9Gyh2sg.

LTT: Nick Huggett

Tuesday, October 27th @ 12:00 pm - 1:30 pm EST

Title: The Highs and Lows of Particle Physics (work with Mike Schneider)

Abstract:

Recent work on the philosophy of high-energy physics experiments has considerably advanced our understanding of their epistemology, for instance, concerning measurements by the ATLAS collaboration at the large hadron collider (Beauchemin 2017). In this talk I aim to highlight and analyze complementary low energy ‘tabletop’ experiments in particle (and other kinds of fundamental) physics. In particular, I contrast ATLAS measurements with high precision measurements of the electron magnetic moment. We find, for instance, that the simplicity of the latter experiment allows for uncertainties to be minimized materially, in the very construction of the apparatus; it promises to probe new ‘regimes’ of physics found in ‘increased significant figures’ rather than higher energies. We finally suggest that a better appreciation of the capacities of such comparatively ‘frugal’ experiments broadens our conception of ‘cutting edge’ physics, and ultimately helps to inform value judgments about possible research programs in the field.

This talk will also be available live streamed on Y

Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Department of Chemistry
Description: Title: Design and Synthesis of Organometallic Compounds for Magneto-Optical Thermometry

Abstract: Luminescence thermometry offers remote, non-invasive temperature readout with high spatial resolution, and lanthanide ions are ideal probes. Unlike the sharp, environment-insensitive 4f–4f emission of LnIII ions, the Laporte-allowed 5d→4f emission of EuII is broad and strongly dependent on the ligand field, enabling band-shift thermometry. Here, a BH4-bridged Cp*EuII complex is the first discrete organometallic EuII band-shift thermometer, with an emission shift of 1899 cm−1 over 60–320 K and the highest absolute thermal sensitivity reported to date. A systematic study of analogues bearing different cyclopentadienyl ligands and coordinating solvents, combined with variable-temperature single-crystal X-ray diffraction, reveals that near-identical structures can give vastly different emission properties, with the Eu···Eu′ separation, the Eu–Cp plane distance, and metal–ligand rigidity governing performance. Building on this, we developed a new family of phosphine chalcogenide-functionalized cyclopentadienides, K[C5Me4(PCh(NMe2)2)] (Ch = S, Se, Te), which form homoleptic europocenes in which the pendant P=Ch arms also coordinate the metal. Description: Tuesday, October 27th English Room, CL 144 5:30 pm

Reception Croghan Schenley Room, CL 156 6:30 pm

Legacy of Hungarians in the United States: People, Places, Pathways is an interdisciplinary heritage initiative developed in connection with the 250th anniversary of the United States. It brings together historians, ethnographers, archivists, cultural institutions, and community partners from Hungary and the United States to present more than two centuries of Hungarian migration and life in America. The project approaches this history from three perspectives: migration periods and journeys, important locations in Hungarian-American history, and personal and family stories. Alongside the traveling exhibition, a bilingual online exhibition provides an expanding resource for education, research, and community use.

The exhibition will be introduced by a short video following which a walkthrough will be led by Balázs Balogh, the Director General of the ELTE Research Centre for the Humanities and the Director of the Institute of Ethnology, Budapest.

A reception will be held after the exhibition walkthrough in the Croghan Schenley Ballroom CL156. Guests can also view a 2015 Hungarian ethnographic documentary titled “Boarding House” or in Hungarian "Burdosház Amerikából," narrated by Dr. Balogh and which shares the story of a Hungarian mining settlement in Vintondale, Pennsylvania. Tours of the Hungarian Room CL 121 will be available starting at 6:30 pm.

40 years ago, Ray Barnett was on a humanitarian trip to war-torn Uganda when he gave a small boy a ride from his decimated home to the safety of another village.

Under Ray’s leadership, the Choir has gained international recognition and has raised the funds and sponsorship needed to educate over 53,000 children in 38 years.

Ray who resides in White Rock, British Columbia, has been the subject of two television documentaries and has received numerous awards and honors for his work. These include the prestigious Cross of Nails, awarded by the Coventry Cathedral in England to recognize his widespread efforts to promote peace throughout the world, and the Heart of Gold Award bestowed by Esther Ranson at the BBC.

In the early 1970’s, Ray connected with Suzanne Nelson who became a founding member of the African Children’s Choir.

Description: Why do queer audiences embrace horror? The monsters? The camp? Maybe it's the chance to see versions of ourselves in stories about otherness, transformation, and challenging fear?

text:
Panther Rehab Rounds – Lifespan, Healthspan, Playspan with Jiří Dvořák, MD takes place on Wednesday, October 28, 2026 at 7:00 AM at UPMC Mercy Pavilion, 4th Floor, Room 4.221.

Venue: UPMC Mercy Pavilion, 4th Floor, Room 4.221, 1622 Locust St, Pittsburgh, PA 15219
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Department of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation
Description: Join the Department of PM&R for a monthly-invited lecture in the field of physical medicine and rehabilitation. Topics will be of interest to our Residents, Fellows, and Post-docs, but the event is open to trainees and faculty of all departments.

October's topic: Lifespan, Healthspan, Playspan.

Presented by: Jiří Dvořák, MD

Dr. Jiří Dvořák is one of the world’s most renowned soccer medicine experts, having worked as FIFA’s Chief Medical Officer for over twenty years. In his years at FIFA, he mainly focused on spinal disorder prevention and sport injuries. Making use of the sport’s widespread popularity, he then co-founded the FIFA 11 for Health educational program for children, where well-known players, such as Lionel Messi or Carles Puyol, made appearance in educational videos. Together with Professor Manohar Panjabi from the Yale School of Medicine, Dvořák has helped expand the frontiers of knowledge in biomechanics of the spine, later assisting in the development of Intraoperative Neuromonitoring used in difficult spinal surgeries. He was involved in the founding of Eurospine (the spine society of Europe), the world’s largest organization of its kind.

Today Dr. Dvořák works as senior consultant to the Board of Schulthess Clinic Zurich and as co-founder and executive adviser at the Bangkok Wellness Clinic, a part of the Bangkok Dusit Medical Services hospital network in Asia.

Description: Publishing research is one of the most important ways to share scientific discoveries, build visibility, and support career growth. However, with an increasing number of journals, evolving expectations around research transparency, and the rapid emergence of AI tools, researchers face new questions about how to publish responsibly and effectively.

In this webinar, we will discuss manuscript preparation, journal selection, peer review, and how editors evaluate submissions. We will also explore research integrity topics including data management, open data, data reuse, data visualization best practices, and ethical considerations surrounding image manipulation. A dedicated session will examine the responsible use of AI in research and publishing, including current policies, disclosure requirements, and the responsibilities of authors, reviewers, and editors.

Description: The Global Appalachia Faculty Reading Series brings Appalachia into conversation with regions around the world that share similar histories and challenges. Through fiction, history, and global scholarship, participants explore themes of extraction, economic transition, migration, environmental justice, Indigenous land rights, cultural identity, and the future of rural communities. The series encourages participants to consider what Appalachia can teach us about global challenges and what the experiences of communities elsewhere can teach us about Appalachia.

Description: Madison Thomas - Final Dissertation Defense - HUGEN PhD Candidate

Department of Human Genetics Doctoral Candidate, Madison Thomas, will defend the following dissertation on “Inhibiting Smad2 Signaling in Adult Hyperglycemic Mice Enhances β-Cell Resilience”

COMMITTEE CHAIR: George K, Gittes, MD

Committee Members:

F. Yesim Demirci, MDKrishna Prasadan, PhDBeth L. Roman, PhD

ABSTRACT:

Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is a common chronic metabolic syndrome clinically characterized by dysregulation of blood glucose levels. Current treatments for T2D alleviate the symptoms of hyperglycemia but do not treat the underlying mechanism of β-cell failure. Transforming growth factor-beta (TGFB) signaling is essential in orchestrating the expansion, growth, and function of mouse pancreatic β-cells. TGFB signaling is a broad pathway, but it can be modified with precision by manipulating downstream SMAD2 signaling. This dissertation examined inhibition of Smad2 as a target for improving diet-induced hyperglycemia in mice, with the translational goal of an rAAV-mediated gene therapy for T2D.

First, I used a tamoxifen-inducible β-cell-specific mouse model (Smad2βKO) to suppress Smad2 mRNA in the β-cells of adult mice after hyperglycemia was established. Smad2βKO improved glucose physiology in vivo and islet function ex vivo. Next, I defined the mechanism behind this recovery. The rescue was distal. Organizer: Global Studies Center
Description: Crescent Over Another Horizon: Islam in Latin America, the Caribbean, and Latino USA traces the story of Islam from Spanish colonial rule through today, covering Muslim and Morisco communities in colonial Spanish America, enslaved African Muslims, indentured South Asian laborers in Suriname, and contemporary Muslim communities in Argentina, Brazil, Mexico, Cuba, Martinique, and Trinidad. It closes with a look at the United States, including Muslim communities in South Florida and the experiences of Latina converts to Islam.

Rather than treating Muslims as a small, separate "minority," the book shows how religion and ethnicity have intertwined across the region to shape identity and belonging in diverse ways.

Discussion will be led by Dr. Keila Grinberg, Global Studies Center Faculty Fellow, Professor of History, and Director of the Center for Latin American Studies, with special guest author Paulo Pinto, Professor of Anthropology at Universidade Federal Fluminense, Brazil.

A free copy of the book is available to participants who register and attend the discussion.

text:

Description: Hosted by the Humanities Center and featuring visiting fellow, Josh Berson.

Berson works best in borrowed places, and by this he means in three senses. First, he has observed that the times when writing feels effortless, when the days slip by in a sustained waking dream, when he senses he is not the source but the channel, when he hears the text whispered in his ear as he writes and wakes in the night with passages fully formed in his head, are those when he has but the most tenuous claim to the place where he’s living, where the bedding is borrowed and the garden view, the morning birdsong, the dusk chorus, the petrichor that follows rain, the kitchen utensils (save for his Kuhn-Rikon carbon steel y-peeler, which accompanies him everywhere, notwithstanding the overzealous efforts of Berlin airport security); when he’s been living out of a knapsack for six months. It is in borrowed places that the world recedes, and it is in borrowed places that Berson feels the sense of openness that encourages risk-taking.

Second, he has observed that his most gratifying work is that where the writing process itself acquires a quality of dislocation. Writing, for Berson, is like wandering out on a tidal flat at dusk only to find, as the light goes and the tide returns, that he’s lost his sense of direction and stepped on something stinging.

Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Description: Dr. Jason Szafron, Assistant Professor, Biomedical Engineering at Carnegie Melon University, will present "Computational biomechanics in vascular treatment planning for cardiopulmonary disease."

Abstract

Many forms of cardiopulmonary disease require interventions with a vascular component. The biomechanical environment prior to intervention can have implications for the success of a procedure, and the post-intervention hemodynamics can lead to long-term pulmonary remodeling that exacerbates the risk for future complications. In this talk, I will discuss our work using computational fluid dynamics to predict the success of mechanical thrombectomy in acute pulmonary embolism patients and the resulting biomechanical environment with lung transplant in pulmonary arterial hypertension. I will also outline our approach to using multiscale simulations of the pulmonary vasculature to predict changes in clinically relevant metrics of disease progression.

Description: How can AI improve spaceborne thermal volcano monitoring?

Presented by Dr. Sophie Pailot-Bonnétat | Postdoctoral Research Associate, University of Pittsburgh

Talk Abstract:

Volcanic eruptions pose significant hazards to human populations and infrastructure, threatening millions of lives and billions of dollars in economic losses annually worldwide. Thermal precursors often accompany volcanic unrest, making spaceborne thermal infrared (TIR) remote sensing a critical tool for monitoring active and dormant volcanic systems, particularly in remote or inaccessible regions lacking ground-based instrumentation. Satellite TIR sensors can detect a diverse range of volcanic thermal manifestations, including summit crater lakes, lava lakes, active lava flows, dome effusion and extrusion, fumarolic fields, hot springs, diffuse degassing areas, and subtle ground-surface heating associated with hydrothermal alteration. Despite decades of satellite thermal monitoring, traditional detection algorithms often struggle with cloud contamination, atmospheric interference, low-magnitude thermal anomalies, and the sheer volume of data generated by modern sensors, limiting timely hazard assessment. Recent advances in machine learning and deep learning offer new opportunities to overcome these limitations by enabling automated, scalable, and more sensitive detection of thermal anomalies across large volcanic datasets. Title: Next-Generation Wearable Health Sensors: How Materials Chemistry Enables Continuous Electrochemical Monitoring

Abstract: Chemical sensors for use in human body fluids, environmental waters, and industrial process monitoring are highly sensitive and selective analytical tools that offer a variety of advantages, such as simplicity of measurement, high analysis throughput, rapid detection, continuous on-line monitoring, and low cost of analysis. While such sensors are used in clinical laboratories for billions of measurements every year, applications in continuous health monitoring still pose many challenges. The Buhlmann group has contributed to the development of such sensors with new design principles and quantitative theory as well as the introduction of new materials to meet the needs of real life applications. This talk will address the long-term sensor stability of wearable and implantable sensors, challenges and opportunities of calibration-free measurements, miniaturization and low-cost design for point-of-care analysis, and—in view of long-term monitoring in the human body and the environment—robust design and resistance to chemical and biological fouling.

Understanding Proton-Coupled Electron Transfer on Polyoxometalates

Abstract:

Catalysis is essential to efficient chemical reactions, and improving its performance is key to meeting the challenges of global demand and sustainability while supporting our quality of life. Copious efforts pursue enhanced and innovative catalytic capabilities; however, their development still faces myriad complexities with incomplete understanding, slowing progress. Investigation via molecular models promises to unlock deeper understanding of the underlying physics, particularly when theoretical modelling is aligned with experiments and developed to general principles.

The mechanics of proton and electron transfers are essential to many commercially relevant systems and offer fundamental descriptors for chemical behavior, especially the dynamics that arise with Proton-Coupled Electron Transfer (PCET). Metal oxides are an indispensable class of catalytic materials with potent and versatile abilities to influence PCET and other chemical activities. Many phenomena in these systems are rooted in their thermodynamics. Unifying them is the foundational descriptor of Bond Dissociation Free Energy, i.e. the BDFE(O–H), of hydroxide bonds on metal oxides.

Description: Where do stars explode in the ISM? A new constraint on stellar feedback models

In this talk, I will present the first set of direct observational constraints on where stars explode in the interstellar medium (ISM) from high-resolution surveys of nearby galaxies with JWST, HST, VLA, ALMA and VLT/MUSE. Explosions of stars, i.e. supernovae (SNe) are the main regulators of star-formation in galaxies. They achieve this most directly by launching winds, which remove cold star-forming gas from the ISM, and creating pressure in the ISM by supplying heat, turbulence and cosmic rays. The efficiency of these processes depend sensitively on the environments where SNe occur, particularly the correlation between SNe and dense gas clouds. While there is evidence of SN shocks interacting with molecular clouds, the ionizing radiation and stellar winds from massive stars can quickly unbind and disperse dense clouds before SNe occur. How these different feedback channels limit star-formation in molecular clouds and launch winds is one of the biggest open questions in galaxy evolution. I will discuss how we can address this topic with the novel method of observations of evolved massive stars and supernova remnants in the Local Volume, supplied by high-resolution multiwavelength surveys like PHANGS, LGLBS and SDSS. I will also show preliminary comparisons with hydrodynamical simulations of galaxies to show how these observations can serve as valuable checks on the underlying stellar feedback mod

Title: Perceptual Discrimination and Necessary Laws of Appearance

Abstract:

Perceptual experience varies dramatically across sensory modalities and species. Humans, sharks, butterflies, and countless other animals inhabit perceptual worlds structured by radically different sensory capacities. Does this diversity imply that the ways things appear are governed entirely by contingent laws? I argue that it does not. Beneath the contingent diversity of perceptual modalities lie metaphysically necessary laws governing appearance itself. I ground this claim in the operations of perceptual discrimination. First, I argue that the exercise of perceptual discrimination capacities is necessary for things to appear. I then advance three necessary laws of appearance grounded in those operations. These laws identify aspects of appearance that remain invariant across differences in sensory modality and species, distinguishing necessary constraints from the contingent forms appearance takes in particular perceptual systems. Description: Title:

Electric-Field-Driven Ion Trapping and Tunable Relaxation Kinetics in Two-dimensional Transistors for Edge Computing

Abstract:

Two challenges that modern electronics face include processing sensor data directly on local devices (i.e., edge computing) and protecting hardware from reverse engineering. These two applications demand different memory behaviors: processing time-dependent signals requires a short-term, fading memory, whereas protecting hardware requires programmable doping that persists without constant power. One way to achieve time-dependent memory is through the use of ions in an electric-double-layer (EDL). EDL gating provides ultra-high interfacial capacitance density (µF/cm²) by drifting mobile ions in an electrolyte to a semiconductor surface under an applied voltage. This dissertation first characterizes the time-dependent pulse dynamics of a well-studied PEO:LiClO₄ electrolyte on graphene and WSe₂ transistors. In a dual-gate configuration, pulsed inputs generate a fading memory for processing ECG signals, where 30/30 ms pulse timing at 305 K maintains baseline stability (+1.57% net retention) and current modulation up to 21%. Next, this work demonstrates the use of electric fields generated by the EDL (~V/nm) to trigger localized chemistry in a custom solid polymer electrolyte, enabling both programmable relaxation kinetics and non-volatile doping in 2D transistors. The increasing availability of electronic health records (EHRs), clinical narratives, and large-scale healthcare datasets provides new opportunities to understand clinical decision-making and improve patient outcomes. My research applies and integrates biostatistical methods, machine learning, natural language processing (NLP), causal inference, and artificial intelligence (AI) to address clinically meaningful questions using complex real-world healthcare data.

In this presentation, I will describe the evolution of my research program and highlight applications across emergency care, organ transplantation, and aging and dementia research. I will first discuss a series of studies integrating structured EHR data with clinical narratives using machine learning, NLP, transformer-based models, and large language models to predict clinical outcomes and healthcare decisions. I will then describe research examining disparities in healthcare access, utilization, and outcomes, and how this work has evolved toward causal modeling and fairness-aware AI to better understand mechanisms underlying observed disparities. Oleksii Dorohan is a Ukrainian expert in law, public policy, regulatory reform, and digital transformation. He began his career with Baker & McKenzie and Coca-Cola HBC, as a practicing lawyer, before transitioning into policy-making. Since 2019, he has served as CEO of BRDO, the biggest independent think tank of Ukraine with a team of more than 100 professionals, including lawyers, analysts, and software engineers. Over the past decade, BRDO has helped develop more than 350 regulatory acts, contributed to the adoption of over 250 draft laws and government resolutions, created 15 digital systems and registries, produced more than 100 analytical studies, and contributed to the review of more than 1,300 regulatory acts, over 300 of which were subsequently repealed. BRDO works across a broad range of sectors and policy areas, including construction, energy, infrastructure, agriculture, IT and telecommunications, digital development, regulatory policy, anti-corruption, and justice reform.

The lecture will explore how legal reform, public policy, and govtech can work together to modernize government and improve public services.

Description: Dr. Emerson Cram, an associate professor in the Departments of Communication Studies and Gender, Women’s & Sexuality Studies at the University of Iowa, brings expertise in frameworks of critical environmental justice that center recursive relationships between race, disability, sexuality and the environment.

Their first book, Violent Inheritance: Sexuality, Land, and Energy in Making the North American West (University of California Press, 2022) examines the history of sexuality in the US as a story about energy to contextualize the regenerative and land-based practice of queer ecology today. Written for scholars in queer studies and the environmental/energy humanities, this book highlights how various regional communities engage cultural and environmental legacies of harm to reimagine violent ecologies through practices of care, healing, and regeneration. The Wesley C. Salmon Memorial Lecture takes place on Friday, October 30, 2026 at 3:30 PM at Cathedral of Learning, 1008.

Venue: Cathedral of Learning, 1008, Fifth Ave at Bigelow, Pittsburgh, 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Department of History and Philosophy of Science, Department of Philosophy
Description: Presenting the Wesley C. Salmon Memorial Lecture, Friday, October 30, 2026, at 3:30 PM

Cathedral of Learning 1008

The Department of History and Philosophy of Science, The Department of Philosophy, and The Center for Philosophy of Science, University of Pittsburgh Present:

Michael Strevens, NYU

"Do Large Language Models Understand What They Are Talking About?"

According to certain liberal accounts of meaning, the words produced by a large language model represent the things that they appear to represent. LLMs, in that case, make meaningful statements. But do they understand what they say? This paper uses contemporary accounts of understanding to explore the prospects for a positive answer to the question. A significant obstacle to understanding is LLMs’ isolation from the world that their words (arguably) depict. Nevertheless, an account of what it is for human thinkers to understand esoteric terms in scientific theories holds out the promise that current or future LLMs are capable of some degree of understanding in an interesting and substantive sense.

We are excited to be back again for a joyous day of Slovak culture, music, history, food and education. At Slovak Fest, you can wander through our vendors and informational display tables, explore the Czechoslovak Room, enjoy a lineup of traditional music and dance performances, attend lectures on Slovak culture, and maybe even meet the ambassador! The Slavic Languages and Literatures Department at the University of Pittsburgh is proud to be the home of the only permanent Slovak Studies Program in the United States. There is no better place to do it than right here in Pittsburgh! Thanks to all the organizations and individuals whose combined support has allowed Pitt to serve as a beacon of the Slovak diaspora.

Category: Trainings & Workshops, Virtual
Organizer: Office of Human Resources
Description: We often think that we need a vacation or large blocks of time in our days to feel refreshed, but it may just be that we need to learn how to capture small doses of well-being where we can in each day. Little “wins” can make a big difference and can be the catalyst to shift our mood/perspective in a positive direction.

The goal of these sessions is to use the time as a gentle nudge toward helping you explore your own interior world through the journal prompt of the day or time to just be still and enjoy the relaxing music. Instead of waiting for the world to stop so we can catch up, let’s slow down on purpose. Make a commitment to show up for yourself; to begin your day from a more centered place. Because, after all, mindset matters.

Testimonials:
“I was distracted this morning, but the music in the background and the deep breaths helped ease me into the day.”

“I was on vacation for over a week and really missed the journal prompts. They are great to really put things in perspective and make you think. Thank you!!"

text:

Event: Settling Cities in Modern Hokkaido
Date: Monday, November 2, 2026 at 4:30 PM to 6:00 PM
Venue: Wesley W. Posvar Hall, 3703, 230 S Bouquet St, Pittsburgh, PA 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Department of History, World History Center, Asian Studies Center
Description: Sapporo, today the capital of Japan’s northernmost island, Hokkaido, was built as Japan’s first modern colonial city in 1869. This talk explores how salmon and the Indigenous societies that depended on them shaped the ecological and social conditions that led to the city’s founding. When Japanese settlers began colonizing the region in the late nineteenth century, they partnered with Western sojourners passing through the area, forging links to new imperial and transnational networks and helping turn Sapporo into a laboratory of Japanese colonial urbanism.

Michael Thornton is Assistant Teaching Professor in the Department of History at Northeastern University. His research focuses on the history of Japanese cities from the seventeenth century onwards. His current projects include a study of Sapporo and its role in turning Hokkaido into a Japanese colony as well as a co-authored historical guidebook to Tokyo that shows how ordinary people have contested power and place across the metropolis. Born and raised in Japan, he now splits time between New York and Boston

title: From Jerusalem to Côte d'Ivoire-Rachel Feldman Talk (Monday, November 2, 2026)
text:
From Jerusalem to Côte d'Ivoire-Rachel Feldman Talk takes place on Monday, November 2, 2026 at 5:00 PM at Barco Law Building, 107.
Event: From Jerusalem to Côte d'Ivoire-Rachel Feldman Talk
Date: Monday, November 2, 2026 at 5:00 PM to 6:30 PM
Venue: Barco Law Building, 107, 3900 Forbes Avenue, Pittsburgh, PA 15260
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Department of Religious Studies, Jewish Studies Program
Description: From Jerusalem to Côte d'Ivoire:The Post-Colonial Afterlives of Rebbe Nachman and the Theo-Politics of Hasidic Joy

Feldman explores the postcolonial afterlives of Rebbe Nachman of Breslev (1772–1810) through ethnographic research conducted with communities reviving Breslev Hasidism in Montréal, Paris, Jerusalem, and Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire. In the twenty-first century, digital platforms have facilitated the emergence of a transnational Francophone Breslev movement, generating new religious identities among French Sephardic Jews and West African converts alike—communities shaped by the enduring legacies of French colonial rule.

Across these settings, Rebbe Nachman’s eighteenth-century teachings are reinterpreted as practices of spiritual repair that respond to histories of religious and cultural erasure, whether through French laïcité, racialization, or Christian missionization. Breslev joy (simḥah) is discursively configured as “anti-Occident,” imagined as the antithesis of French secular modernity and mobilized as a theo-political resource. Dr. Rachel Z. Feldman is an Associate Professor of Religion at Dartmouth College. She specializes in the anthropology of Judaism, messianic movements, digital religion, contemporary Israel/Palestine, and gender studies.

title: The Visibility Dilemma: Investigating the Intermediating Role of Platform Algorithms in Government Communication, Kayla Schwoerer, Ph.D. (Tuesday, November 3, 2026)
text:
The Visibility Dilemma: Investigating the Intermediating Role of Platform Algorithms in Government Communication, Kayla Schwoerer, Ph.D. takes place on Tuesday, November 3, 2026 at 11:30 AM at Wesley W. Posvar Hall, 3911.

Date: Tuesday, November 3, 2026 at 11:30 AM to 12:30 PM
Venue: Wesley W. Posvar Hall, 3911, 230 S Bouquet St, Pittsburgh, PA 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Institute for Cyber Law, Policy, and Security
Description: Join SPIA and Pitt Cyber as we welcome Kayla Schwoerer, Ph.D., to share with us her research on how government agencies increasingly rely on X, Instagram, and other commercial platforms to share information about public services, policies, and crises. But these platforms are not neutral channels. Proprietary algorithms designed to maximize attention, engagement, and monetization rather than public values shape which government messages become visible, to whom, and when. To reach citizens, agencies may therefore feel pressure to adjust their communication strategies to fit the affordances and logics of platforms, e.g., leveraging meme formats, emotional narratives, ephemeral trends, and pop culture. While these strategies may increase (algorithmic) visibility, they can also sit uneasily with expectations that government communication be neutral, professional, and trustworthy. Hence, the visibility dilemma.

This 3-year comparative research project was recently funded by the NWO’s (Dutch Research Council) Veni grant (€ 320000) as part of the NWO Talent Programme to study how algorithmic intermediation is reshaping the relationship between citizens and the state. The project combines conceptual research, computational and qualitative analysis of government social media, and survey experiments across the United States, United Kingdom, Netherlands, Germany, and Sweden. Description: Egypt, the Sterling Zone, and the Long Road
to the Suez Crisis, 1916–1956

Aaron Jakes

ASSOCIATE PROFESSOR OF MODERN MIDDLE EASTERN HISTORY
University of Chicago

Aaron Jakes is the author of the prize-winning Egypt’s Occupation: Colonial Economism and the Crises of Capitalism (Stanford University Press, 2020), which explores the relationship between financial capitalism, imperial governance, and Egyptian nationalist thought. His current research project, tentatively titled Tilted Waters: The World the Suez Canal Made, investigates how the Suez Canal has shaped global capitalism. Spanning more than two centuries, from the earliest European proposals to excavate a channel through the Isthmus of Suez to the Egyptian military regime’s current efforts to remake the waterway and its environs into a major processing hub and free trade zone, the book will explore the many and shifting roles that the Suez Canal has played in the production of global inequalities.

The event is co-sponsored by the Atlantic History seminar, the Early Modern Worlds Initiative, and the Center for African Studies.

For more information, please contact Niklas Frykman

Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Department of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation
Description: Join the Department of PM&R for a monthly-invited lecture in the field of physical medicine and rehabilitation. Topics will be of interest to our Residents, Fellows, and Post-docs, but the event is open to trainees and faculty of all departments.

November's topic: Exploring the biology and symptom burden associated with allostatic load after TBI

Presented by: Amy Wagner, MD

Dr. Wagner is a leading investigator in the use of biomarkers developing prognostic models and clinical decision algorithms as well as optimizing individualized treatment outcomes, in an effort to “personalized rehabilitation medicine.” She has coined the term “Rehabilomics” to define this relatively new field of study that involves clinical and preclinical studies involving rehabilitation-relevant biomarkers as related to function, prognosis, treatment, and recovery.

Her research also focuses on the neurobiology of neuroplasticity and recovery after TBI and how commonly used therapeutic agents impact neurobiological and neurobehavioral processes associated with neuroplasticity and recovery. She is especially focused on dopaminergic systems and brain injury recovery, and her experimental TBI work also includes the study of rehabilitation relevant cognitive training paradigms to better understand the substrates and mechanisms of learning and memory recovery.

10 am to 12 pm PDT (Las Vegas) 1 pm to 3 pm EST (Pittsburgh)15 hrs to 17 hrs (São Paulo)Zoom Link: Available upon request. Contact Renata de Almeida Ramos at RAR137@pitt.edu.

Dissertation Title: "The Felted Web - The Continuous Process of Becoming a Critical Teacher among Experienced Pedagogues in the Early Years of Elementary Education in Brazil and the United States"

Dissertation Description:

This study travels alongside five experienced early elementary public educators in São Paulo, Portland, and Washington, D.C., to understand how becoming a reflective-critical pedagogue is lived, struggled with, and reinvented in daily praxis. Grounded in Freire (1970, 1998), Lugones (2003), and Ciampa (1987), we learn that these pedagogues embody a living web of relationships, enacting praxis through humility, empathy, love, esperançar, and freedom. Curriculum is both a contested space, where corporate education logic and ethical praxis collide, and a territory of emancipatory praxis that pedagogues negotiate daily. Their praxis, Freirean in grammar, is often decolonial in practice, centering territory, place-based epistemology, and collective conscientização as conditions for transformation.

Dissertation Committee: Dr. Michael Gunzenhauser (advisor), Dr. Kari Kokka, Dr. Edwin Mayorga, Dr. Leigh Patel

title: Finding the Human: The Social Theories of Early Cold War Memoranda (Thursday, November 5, 2026)
text:
Finding the Human: The Social Theories of Early Cold War Memoranda takes place on Thursday, November 5, 2026 at 12:30 PM at Cathedral of Learning, 602.
Event: Finding the Human: The Social Theories of Early Cold War Memoranda
Date: Thursday, November 5, 2026 at 12:30 PM to 2:00 PM
Venue: Cathedral of Learning, 602, Fifth Ave at Bigelow, Pittsburgh, 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Humanities Center
Description: Hosted by the Humanities Center and featuring faculty fellow, Paul Johnson.

Following the death of Franklin Roosevelt, Harry S. Truman was thrown into the complex and unfamiliar caldron of the Second World War's end and the murmurings of a new global conflict with the Soviet Union. Accordingly, he commissioned a number of reports evaluating the character of the Soviet threat, among them George Kennan's famous "The Sources of Soviet Conduct" and Clark Clifford and George Elsey's "American Relations with the Soviet Union." These, along with other reports, offer interpretations of Soviet regime behavior informed by the author's own interpretations of figures like Karl Marx, G.W.F. Hegel, and Gottlob Frege (among others). This paper looks at the rhetorical contours of the world iterated in some of these memos to understand the philosophical assumptions about the world that drove early Cold War decisionmaking, and ultimately how the war would in part be conducted by the aggressive construction of a globalist consumer citizen.

Respondents include Neepa Majumdar from Film & Media Studies + Dr. Kyong-Min Son, Associate Professor, Political Science & IR at the University of Delaware. This event will be hybrid, so you can attend it either in person in 602 CL or via Zoom as you prefer. Precirculated material for this colloquium will be available here about two prior to the event.

text:

Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Department of Chemistry
Description: Title: Boronic Ester Design Enables Rapid, Stereospecific B-Alkyl Suzuki-Miyaura Cross-Coupling

Abstract: In the past decades, the Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling (SMCC) has been well renowned as the premier method for the facile and selective construction of C(sp2)–C(sp2) bonds. In recent years, B-alkyl SMCC has gained considerable intrigue as a method for creation of C(sp2)–C(sp3) linkages for drug discovery and development. Despite advances made in both ligand and boronate design, these challenging cross-coupling reactions typically suffer from poor yields and long reaction times, stemming from slow transmetalation of alkylboronates and rapid -hydride elimination of alkylpalladium(II) complexes. Previous work using neopentyl glycol boronic esters and potassium trimethyl silanolate (TMSOK) enabled primary alkyl SMCC to numerous aryl halides. Unfortunately, these conditions were unsuccessful with secondary alkylboronic esters due to deleterious protodehalogenation arising from the boronic ester backbone. Investigation of many sec-butylboronic esters indicated that substitution proximal to the oxygens on the ester skeleton was crucial for circumventing protodehalogenation and enabling productive cross-coupling. Thus, there was a need for a highly reactive boronic ester scaffold without the capability to undergo -hydride elimination. Further experimentation led to the identification of a boronate generated in situ from tetramethyl-N-methyliminodiacetic acid (TIDA) alkylboronate

Description: Dr. Adele Moatti, Assistant Professor in the Department of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine and Adjunct Assistant Professor of Biomedical Engineering at Carnegie Mellon University, will present "Rebuilding the Translational Pipeline for Inner Ear Therapies."

Abstract

A major barrier in inner ear therapeutics is not a single limitation, but a broken pipeline, where clinically relevant models, targeting strategies, and delivery mechanisms fail to align. Here, we rebuild this pipeline by integrating complementary translational advances. We establish a porcine model of cochlear synaptopathy that captures key features of human pathology, enabling meaningful evaluation of therapeutic interventions. In parallel, we generate a comprehensive map of AAV expression in the pig inner ear, providing a critical bridge between mouse studies and clinically relevant gene therapy design. We further demonstrate that extracellular vesicles (EVs) can be harnessed to enhance safe local AAV delivery, improving transduction efficiency while reducing immune responses. Finally, we uncover an unexpected biological lever of drug delivery: sensory-driven formulation effects. We show that modulation of taste receptor signaling can extend drug retention within the inner ear, revealing a new axis for therapeutic control. Talk Abstract:

Very high-resolution (VHR) satellite topography derived from commercial electro-optical line-scan imagery enables detection of subtle Earth surface changes at high spatio-temporal resolution. In this talk, I discuss the development of satellite photogrammetry workflows to measure seasonal glacier dynamics in Nepal Himalaya and volcanic flows in Mauna Loa, Hawaii, demonstrating both the scientific promise and practical limitations of current methods. I show how unmodeled satellite attitude variations (jitter) introduce systematic small-scale elevation artifacts (>50 cm) that preclude small-magnitude topographic change detection, and present new correction algorithms that resolve these errors. Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Department of Chemical and Petroleum Engineering
Description: From Electrically Conductive MOFs to Sustainable Batteries

Abstract: The emergence of electrically conductive metal-organic frameworks (c-MOFs) has been one of the most paradoxical developments in the field in the last few years. Indeed, how can one transport charges through a material that is mostly “empty” space? In this sense, MOFs made from layers of organic ligands connected by (typically) square-planar metal ions have shown particularly good electrical conductivity. However, a precise mechanism for charge transport is still the subject of debate, with various experimental and computational reports describing these materials as metals, semiconductors, or semimetals. This lecture will describe the latest efforts from our group to understand the intrinsic properties of 2D c-MOFs, especially as related to single-crystal electrical measurement studies and will discuss in particular the unexpectedly large influence of out-of-plane transport. The seminar will also discuss how these fundamental studies have led directly to the discovery of a sustainable, organic cathode material that is competitive with incumbent oxides in Li-ion and Na-ion rechargeable batteries.

Short Bio Sketch: Mircea Dincă is the Alexander Stewart 1886 Professor of Chemistry at Princeton University.
