text:
LTT: Caterina Del Sordo - Was Early Carnap a Machian Neutral Monist? takes place on Friday, November 6, 2026 at 12:00 PM at Cathedral of Learning, The Center for Philosophy of Science  - Room 1117  - 11th Floor.
Event: LTT: Caterina Del Sordo - Was Early Carnap a Machian Neutral Monist?
Date: Friday, November 6, 2026 at 12:00 PM to 1:00 PM
Venue: Cathedral of Learning, The Center for Philosophy of Science  - Room 1117  - 11th Floor, Fifth Ave at Bigelow, Pittsburgh, 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Center for Philosophy of Science
Description: The Center for Philosophy of Science at the University of Pittsburgh invites you to join us for our Lunch Time Talk. Attend in person at 1117 Cathedral of Learning or visit our live stream on YouTube at https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCrRp47ZMXD7NXO3a9Gyh2sg.

LTT: Caterina Del Sordo

Friday, November 6th @ 12:00 pm - 1:30 pm EST

Title: Was Early Carnap a Machian Neutral Monist?

Abstract:

In this talk, I defend the thesis that early Carnap is a Machian neutral monist. To support this thesis, I mediate between two opposing readings of the relation between Mach and early Carnap: Textor (2021), who advances a neutral monistic reading of Carnap’s Aufbau, and Banks (2003, 2014), who regards Carnap’s Aufbau and Mach’s neutral monism as divergent projects. I argue that the Aufbau does not satisfy the main conditions of Machian neutral monism and that the comparison between Mach and early Carnap with respect to ontological neutrality remains largely underdetermined. I further argue that Carnap’s pre-Aufbau works satisfy the main conditions of Machian neutral monism and support a reading according to which Mach and early Carnap are aligned in their account of ontological neutrality.

This talk will also be available live streamed on

Description: Hear directly from curator Hiroyuki Good about his exhibit, "From Noh to Kabuki: Reimagined Stories in Ukiyo-e"

During this talk, you will see original Ukiyo-e (Japanese woodblock prints) from Archives & Special Collections at the University of Pittsburgh Library System. These prints, created in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, depict both Noh and Kabuki plays. The Japanese theatre tradition of Noh emerged in the fourteenth century and was associated with the samurai elite. Kabuki theatre developed in the Edo period (1600 and 1868) as a form of popular theatre for a broader audience. See the representations of characters, themes, and theatrical expressions in Noh performances and how Kabuki reimagined and expanded these stories.

title: Is Vibe Coding Safe? Benchmarking, Aligning, and Exploiting AI Coding Agents (Friday, November 6, 2026)
text:
Is Vibe Coding Safe? Benchmarking, Aligning, and Exploiting AI Coding Agents takes place on Friday, November 6, 2026 at 12:00 PM at Sennott Square, 5317.
Event: Is Vibe Coding Safe? Benchmarking, Aligning, and Exploiting AI Coding Agents
Date: Friday, November 6, 2026 at 12:00 PM to 2:00 PM
Venue: Sennott Square, 5317, 210 South Bouquet Street, Pittsburgh, PA 15260
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Department of Computer Science
Description: Talk Abstract

Software development is undergoing a major shift from human coding to AI generation. While the rise of “vibe coding” promises massive productivity gains, it introduces severe security risks. Our study on the SusVibes benchmark reveals that while frontier coding agents achieve 60% functional correctness, only 10% of their solutions are secure. To bridge this gap, we present AuraForge, a scalable method to synthesize comprehensive security tests. We further develop SecureVibe, a security alignment framework to train coding agents for better security planning, generation, supervision, and self-improvement. Finally, we present agentic systems for security auditing and vulnerability exploitation. This talk provides a clear demonstration of AI coding risks, practical approaches to train secure agents, and insights into the future of autonomous security defense.

Biography

Lei Li is an Associate Professor in Language Technologies Institute at Carnegie Mellon University. His research focuses on AI agents, AI security, machine translation, and AI-powered drug discovery. He received Ph.D. from CMU School of Computer Science in 2011. He is a recipient of the ACL 2021 Best Paper Award and the 2012 ACM SIGKDD dissertation award (runner-up), and is recognized as Notable Area Chair of the ICLR 2023. Venue: Online
Category: Trainings & Workshops
Organizer: University Library System
Description: Data management and sharing plans (DMSPs) are short documents that outline how a research team will organize, store, preserve, and share their research data during and after data collection. Two major funders changed how these plans are submitted in 2026: the National Science Foundation (NSF) now collects the plan through a structured webform in Research.gov that is tailored to your directorate, and the National Institutes of Health (NIH) replaced its narrative format with a shorter, mostly yes/no format page. The underlying expectations have not softened; the National Science Foundation (NSF) requires that data supporting funded publications be shared at the time of publication, with any exceptions justified in the plan itself.

Attend this workshop to learn how DMPTool, a free online resource, can help you draft, collaborate on, and get feedback on your data management and sharing plan (DMSP) before you enter it into a funder system. DMPTool now offers templates that mirror the Research.gov webform, including directorate-specific versions, along with the 2026 National Institutes of Health (NIH) format.

Upon attending this presentation, you should be able to:

List the components of a data management and sharing plan (DMSP) and identify which funder requires which format.Access DMPTool with your University of Pittsburgh credentials.Select the right template for your funder and create a draft.Transfer your draft into the Research.gov webform or the National Institutes of Hea

Description: In 1979, during a regular workday at the Center for Latin American Studies (CLAS), Director Carmelo Mesa-Lago, Assistant to the Director June Belkin, and Assistant Director Shirley Kregar were discussing upcoming programming and asked a simple but powerful question: How can we promote greater cultural awareness of Latin American cultures in Pittsburgh while meaningfully involving Latin American communities in the region? Shirley Kregar proposed the idea of a Latin American Festival. While the concept began modestly, no one could have anticipated the scale, longevity, and regional impact the festival would ultimately achieve. Although Shirley originated the idea, Alan Adelman organized and implemented the first festival, establishing a foundation of core elements—many of which remain integral to the event today.

The Latin American and Caribbean Festival has experienced more than four decades of sustained success, with continuous growth in attendance, artistic quality, community participation, and media visibility. As Pittsburgh’s Latino and Hispanic populations have continued to expand, the festival has become one of the largest and most significant gatherings of Latin American and Latinx communities in Western Pennsylvania, drawing students, families, artists, and visitors from across the region.

text:

Event: Kristallnacht: The 1938 Reich's Pogroms, The End of the Beginning, the Beginning of the End and its Echoes Today
Date: Sunday, November 8, 2026 at 4:00 PM to 5:30 PM
Venue: Beit Kulanu (Formally Rodef Shalom), 4905 Fifth Avenue, Pittsbugh, PA 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: European Studies Center
Description: Kristallnacht, or the “Night of Broken Glass,” was a pogrom that occurred November 9-10, 1938. It was the first organized, government-sanctioned act of violence against the Jews in Germany. It marks the start of the systematic violence against Jews during the Holocaust. Each year, the Holocaust Center of Pittsburgh holds an event to commemorate this important turning point in history. These programs are generously supported by Edgar Snyder.

Dr. Michael Berenbaum is a writer, lecturer, and teacher consulting in the conceptual development of museums and the development of historical films. He is director of the Sigi Ziering Institute: Exploring the Ethical and Religious Implications of the Holocaust at the American Jewish University (formerly the University of Judaism) where he is also a Distinguished Professor of Jewish Studies.

A co-sponsored event by the European Studies Center, German Studies Program, and Jewish Studies Program at the University of Pittsburgh.

Venue: Online
Category: Trainings & Workshops, Virtual

Description: We often think that we need a vacation or large blocks of time in our days to feel refreshed, but it may just be that we need to learn how to capture small doses of well-being where we can in each day. Little “wins” can make a big difference and can be the catalyst to shift our mood/perspective in a positive direction.

The goal of these sessions is to use the time as a gentle nudge toward helping you explore your own interior world through the journal prompt of the day or time to just be still and enjoy the relaxing music. Instead of waiting for the world to stop so we can catch up, let’s slow down on purpose. Make a commitment to show up for yourself; to begin your day from a more centered place. Because, after all, mindset matters.

Testimonials:
“I was distracted this morning, but the music in the background and the deep breaths helped ease me into the day.”

“I was on vacation for over a week and really missed the journal prompts. They are great to really put things in perspective and make you think. Thank you!!"

title: Pitt-CMU Colloquium: Michel Janssen (University of Minnesota) (Monday, November 9, 2026)
text:
Pitt-CMU Colloquium: Michel Janssen (University of Minnesota) takes place on Monday, November 9, 2026 at 3:30 PM at Thaw Hall, 102.
Event: Pitt-CMU Colloquium: Michel Janssen (University of Minnesota)
Date: Monday, November 9, 2026 at 3:30 PM
Venue: Thaw Hall, 102, 3943 O'Hara Street, Pittsburgh, PA 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Department of Physics and Astronomy
Description: Arch and Scaffold: Jordan’s statistical transformation theory and von Neumann’s Hilbert space formalism

In early 1927, Paul Dirac and Pascual Jordan, independently of one another, published their versions of a general formalism tying the various forms of the new quantum theory together and giving the theory’s statistical interpretation in full generality. This formalism has come to be known as the Dirac-Jordan (statistical) transformation theory. A few months later, in response to these publications, John von Neumann published his Hilbert space formalism for quantum mechanics. The relation between these two formalisms can be captured in terms of a metaphor for theory change in which one theory serves as the scaffold for the arch of another theory. What is unclear in this case is which formalism serves as the scaffold and which one as the arch. Did von Neumann build an arch on the scaffold built by Jordan? Or did von Neumann build a scaffold to prevent the arch built by Jordan from collapsing? Either way, the arch-and-scaffold metaphor is a promising alternative to Thomas Kuhn's paradigm shifts for understanding theory change.

Note: Based on joint work with Anthony Duncan (University of Pittsburgh)

title: AI, Chaplaincy, and the Future of Healthcare (Tuesday, November 10, 2026)
text:
AI, Chaplaincy, and the Future of Healthcare takes place on Tuesday, November 10, 2026 at 8:00 AM at Online.
Event: AI, Chaplaincy, and the Future of Healthcare
Date: Tuesday, November 10, 2026 at 8:00 AM to 9:00 AM
Venue: Online
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Institute for Bioethics, Jewish Studies Program, Department of Religious Studies
Description: Healthcare and Religion Lecture

Mary Moon, MTS
MD candidate, University of Pittsburgh

The Rev. Gaea Thompson, MDiv
Manager, Pastoral Care, UPMC Presbyterian/Montefiore Hospital
Diplomate Supervisor for Clinical Pastoral Education, College of Pastoral Supervision and Psychotherapy

Jonathan Weinkle, MD, FAAP, FACP
Clinical Assistant Professor, Family Medicine, University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine
Chief Medical Officer, Squirrel Hill Health Center

AI is reshaping how patients seek answers, how physicians spend their time, and how we make meaning from illness. But what happens to human presence when the algorithm enters the room?

This talk explores AI at the intersection of healthcare, spirituality, and the search for meaning. We'll open with a brief look at how AI is currently viewed across religious traditions and what the rise of the "digital-first" patient means for the people who sit at the bedside. Then, we'll hear from clinical care and chaplaincy on the front lines: how AI is changing their work, what patients are sharing, and what presence looks like in an age of large language models.

Whether it's a patient turning to a chatbot before a chaplain, or an AI scribe freeing a physician to finally make eye contact — this is a conversation about what technology reveals about what we need most from each other.

Continuing medical education credit will be available for those in attendance.

Co-sponsored by the Department of Religious Studies, Jewish Studies Program

Description: "Retinal AI for Macular Degeneration: Prediction, Image Quality, and Privacy Protection", Department of Biostatistics and Health Data Science, School of Public Health.

Advisors and Committee Chairs: Wei Chen and Qiong Wu

Abstract:

Retinal imaging is fundamental to the diagnosis and monitoring of age-related macular degeneration (AMD), a leading cause of irreversible vision loss in older adults. Because AMD progression is gradual, heterogeneous, and asymptomatic in its early stages, clinical assessment alone is insufficient, creating demand for quantitative methods that leverage retinal imaging data for objective diagnosis and early risk prediction. This dissertation advances retinal AI for AMD across three areas: longitudinal AMD prediction, annotation-efficient image quality assessment, and privacy-preserving image transformation.
The first part addresses longitudinal prediction of AMD progression. We proposed LONGL-Net, which predicts future AMD risk by first synthesizing future fundus appearances through a U-Net-based GAN, then grading disease severity from both observed and predicted images. Building on this, we developed TV-LSTM to integrate longitudinal image embeddings with genetic variants while explicitly modeling irregular follow-up intervals inherent to real-world clinical data. Description: The Center for Philosophy of Science at the University of Pittsburgh invites you to join us for our Lunch Time Talk. Attend in person at 1117 Cathedral of Learning or visit our live stream on YouTube at https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCrRp47ZMXD7NXO3a9Gyh2sg.

LTT: Michel Janssen

Tuesday, November 10th @ 12:00 pm - 1:30 pm EST

Title: Einstein gaining a foothold in the quantum world, 1905–1925

Abstract:

In his early work on quantum theory, Einstein found a number of constraints on a new theory of radiation that would account for various phenomena classical theory could not account for. He found most of these constraints by making sure the thermal behavior of radiation was in accordance with general results in thermodynamics and statistical mechanics. Similar considerations led him to his quantum theory of the ideal gas, which helped pave the way for Schrödinger’s wave mechanics.

This talk will also be available YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCrRp47ZMXD7NXO3a9Gyh2sg.

Description: Join us for our next Food for Thought Talk, What Are Faculty Experiencing in the Anti-DEI Era? by Dr. Linda DeAngelo!

The research program on faculty Dr. DeAngelo will share began in a different political and institutional moment. After decades of national efforts to broaden participation in STEM and engineering, important questions remained about faculty equity-mindedness and readiness to advance equity work. Building on five years of research through two NSF-funded studies, her current research line initially sought to understand engineering faculty's equity-mindedness and readiness to advance transformational change. However, as the study prepared to enter the field, the shifting sociopolitical landscape in the wake of Trump’s election fundamentally altered the conditions under which faculty were being asked to engage in DEI work. These changes also directly affected Dr. DeAngelo's own research, including the termination of one NSF-funded study and required revisions to the public-facing materials of another. This changing context created both a challenge and an opportunity: to examine the relationship between the shifting sociopolitical landscape and faculty perceptions of their responsibility, advocacy, and self-efficacy for advancing equity.

Description: Title: Mimicking Nature: Controlling Charge, Heat, and Spin at Interfaces

Abstract: Many interactions and processes in nature operate at low energy and with critical energy balance, enabling repeated cycling and highly efficient transport. Inspired by these processes, we try to understand them, and to replicate them in synthetic systems. The energies involved are well below those of visible photon energies; thus, we predominantly use tunneling spectroscopies and imaging to probe them. If we could replicate such systems in our devices, we could save most of the energy required to run them. If we could mimic biochemical cycling, we could develop efficient recycling at large scales rather than the extremely labor- and energy-intensive processes of today. We look for underlying principles and what we are currently missing in our understanding. Two of the areas we are exploring are spin conservation in chiral molecules and the roles of polarizability in biological, and now synthetic, systems. Taking this perspective has already led to novel discoveries and inventions, including thermal control with orders of magnitude improvements, in scale, speed, and effect. One of the key advances in nanoscience and nanotechnology has been our increasing ability to reach the limits of atomically precise structures. title: PQI Distinguished Seminar - Cindy Regal (Tuesday, November 10, 2026)
text:
PQI Distinguished Seminar - Cindy Regal takes place on Tuesday, November 10, 2026 at 3:00 PM at Allen Hall, 321.
Event: PQI Distinguished Seminar - Cindy Regal
Date: Tuesday, November 10, 2026 at 3:00 PM
Venue: Allen Hall, 321, 3941 O'Hara Street, Pittsburgh, PA 15213
Organizer: Pittsburgh Quantum Institute, Quantum Science and Engineering
Description: Motional Kerr-Cat States of an Atom in an Optical Tweezer

Abstract

Schrödinger cat states enable quantum information to be encoded in a superposition of classically distinct states, and constitute a powerful resource for quantum computing and enhanced metrology. Creating such states in the phase space of an oscillator requires a nonlinearity, typically inherited from an auxiliary degree of freedom such as atomic spin or a Josephson junction. Neutral atoms trapped in reconfigurable optical tweezer arrays - one leading platform for quantum science and computing - provide an intrinsic nonlinearity via the motion of a single atom in a tightly focused trap. However, this self-Kerr mechanism has not previously been exploited for cat-state generation, and remains largely unexplored as a resource for motional-state control. We realize Schrödinger cat states in the quantized motion of a single neutral atom trapped in an optical tweezer. By modulating the depth and position, we demonstrate parity control of both Kerr-cat and Fock states alongside tunable nonlinearity, establishing a spin- and species-independent framework for controlling motion in tweezers. We further show that the cat-state encoding is intrinsically robust against trap-frequency fluctuations that otherwise limit the fidelity of direct Fock-state transitions. These results establish Kerr-based control of neutral-atom motion as a new paradigm for bosonic-state engineering in optical tweezers.

Description: Title: Evolution of Electrode Interfaces During Electrochemistry

Abstract: Photoelectrochemical reactions have emerged as a direct pathway to harvest solar energy for sustainable chemistry. Understanding and controlling the complex microenvironments of charged electrodes or hybrid inorganic/organic interfaces is critical for optimizing a desired reaction and ensuring electrode/material durability. We utilize in situ electrochemical spectroscopic ellipsometry to measure the complex dielectric constant and index of refraction of the electrolyte interface. Using this approach, we monitor the evolution of the microenvironments of hybrid interfaces and independently measure the properties of the electric double layer, polymer stability, oxide formation and reduction, to disentangle the role of various factors in reaction evolution and electrode degradation. Organizer: European Studies Center, Center for Russian, East European, and Eurasian Studies, Department of Slavic Languages and Literatures, Global Studies Center, World History Center
Description: Join Sean Guillory, host of the Eurasian Knot Podcast, for a live interview with William Chase to launch The Many Faces of Antifascism.

The Many Faces of Antifascism by William Chase and Olga Novikova-Monterde
IN the 1930s, the Popular Front unified international antifascists against the clear and present danger of fascism. The unity, however, proved thin. The Marxist left quickly fractured along sectarian lines. The infighting wasn't just over the nature of fascism and how to combat it. Old battles and rivalries persisted under an antifascist flag.
Why did this fragmentation occur? What drove Marxist militants to fight each other when faced with a common fascist foe? In the Many Faces of Antifascism, William Chase and Olga Novikova-Montero untangle these questions through a series of microhistories of antifascism as a lived experience in the Soviet Union, Germany, Austria, France, England, and Spain.

From June 1981 to mid-1996, just 15 years later, a new and deadly infectious disease, now known as HIV/AIDS, was transformed into a chronic condition that allows those infected to live largely normal lives. Such an achievement was unprecedented in medical history. 2026 marks the 45th anniversary of the first medical publication on HIV/AIDS. To honor the aging physicians, scientists, public health officials, activists, and others who confronted the pandemic, this talk will examine the work that remains to achieve the global end of HIV/AIDS.

Sponsored by the CF Reynolds Medical History Society

Description: This is the 4th workshop of our four-part workshop series “Mastering Single-Cell Analysis with Partek Flow” that will provide in-depth exploration of single cell technologies and their applications. title: Optimizing Your Immigration Portfolio (Wednesday, November 11, 2026)
text:
Optimizing Your Immigration Portfolio takes place on Wednesday, November 11, 2026 at 3:00 PM at Online.
Event: Optimizing Your Immigration Portfolio
Date: Wednesday, November 11, 2026 at 3:00 PM to 4:00 PM
Venue: Online
Category: Trainings & Workshops
Organizer: Office of Academic Career Development
Description: International scholars and employees who may eventually want to apply for permanent residency in the US could benefit from taking steps to compile their immigration portfolio early in their career. An immigration portfolio is an organized system of documents that show a person's ability to meet the criteria necessary to obtain permanent residence in the U.S. based on employment and educational backgrounds. Compiling an immigration portfolio before it’s needed allows for time and space to gather the best documentation without being rushed. It also helps people to identify opportunities that could augment their portfolio, such as conference session reviewing and professional memberships.

This session is geared toward nonimmigrant visa holders in the U.S. We will review the various criteria necessary to obtain permanent residence through several employment-based categories. The participant will learn how to assess their career goals against the green card criteria to better understand how to enhance their immigration portfolio with a desire to obtain permanent residence as early as possible in their career, thus providing stability and ultimate flexibility in their lives.

title: The Educator’s Guide to Non-binary French: Queering the French-Language Curriculum (Thursday, November 12, 2026)
text:
The Educator’s Guide to Non-binary French: Queering the French-Language Curriculum takes place on Thursday, November 12, 2026 at 12:30 PM at Cathedral of Learning, 602.
Event: The Educator’s Guide to Non-binary French: Queering the French-Language Curriculum
Date: Thursday, November 12, 2026 at 12:30 PM to 2:00 PM
Venue: Cathedral of Learning, 602, Fifth Ave at Bigelow, Pittsburgh, 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Humanities Center
Description: Hosted by the Humanities Center and featuring graduate fellow, Elsie Campbell.

Prescriptive tradition dictates that French adhere to a strict binary gender system: masculine, and feminine. That’s how French is often taught: all nouns are gendered along this binary, and student-facing materials tend only to center white cis-hetero-male-Catholic perspectives. Campbell’s project addresses a lack of materials and training, specifically at the intermediate and advanced levels, on how to incorporate LGBTQIAP+ perspectives into the French-language classroom. A mixture of teaching portfolio, queer and trans theory, pedagogy, and personal reflection, their project—like all queer research—is deeply personal and political. At a time when trans folx, and particularly trans folx of color, are being dehumanized and killed, they offer one small but meaningful way we can show up for our students and our community.

Respondents include Ever Osorio Ruiz from English + Dawn E. McCormick, Department of Linguistics, Teaching Professor, TESOL Certificate Advisor, English Language Institute, Director, University of Pittsburgh. This event will be hybrid, so you can attend it either in person in 602 CL or via Zoom as you prefer. Precirculated material for this colloquium will be available here about two prior to the event.

CLAS Speaker Series: "Bound by the Ancestors: Black and Indigenous Garifuna Peoplehood after Land Dispossession in the Central American Caribbean"

Marcela Perdomo is a cultural anthropologist of religion and Teaching Assistant Professor in the Department of Religious Studies at the University of Pittsburgh. She received her PhD from the École des Hautes Études en Sciences Sociales (EHESS) in Paris and holds both an MA and BA from the Sorbonne Nouvelle. She is a member of the Laboratoire d’Anthropologie Sociale (EHESS/CNRS/Collège de France), where she was affiliated during her doctoral research and received support for ethnographic fieldwork. Her research draws on long-term ethnographic and historical research with Garifuna communities in Honduras and examines spirit possession, historical memory, ethnogenesis, race, and the intersections of African diasporic and Carib-Amazonian religious worlds. Her current book project, Chosen by the Ancestors: A Binding Gift. Spirit Possession and Historical Memory in the Garifuna Dugu of Honduras, examines Dugu as a historical-initiatory possession complex through which relationships among ancestors, spirits, kin, and the living transmit histories of displacement, belonging, and Garifuna peoplehood across generations.

Description: CLIFF EVOLUTION THROUGH FEEDBACK BETWEEN DRAINAGE DIVIDE MIGRATION AND WATERFALL RETREAT: MECHANISM, RATES, AND TIMING

Cliffs are steep slopes that separate low-relief highland plateaus from incised lowlands, forming topographic barriers that influence the routing of water and sediment and the spatial patterns of climate and biota. Cliffs whose tops align with drainage divides, where large rivers do not cross the cliff, are expected to retreat slowly and uniformly.

However, such cliffs are often associated with deep embayments (i.e., alcoves) that destroy the cliff front even in landscapes with slow vertical erosion rates. However, the processes that produce and sustain these embayments remain largely unexplored. In such cliffs, embayments typically occur along reversed channels that once flowed away from the cliff but now drain toward it, forming a waterfall (i.e., knickpoint) where the reversed channel crosses the cliff, and a valley-confined drainage divide called a windgap. In this dissertation I explore the hypotheses that (1) a feedback between knickpoint retreat and windgap migration toward the highland can sustain embayments, and (2) that in these settings, the rate of waterfall and cliff can be used to estimate the cliff age and initial location. Description: Title: From the Bottom-Up: Engineering Nanoscale Architectures from De Novo Peptide Building Blocks

Abstract: While proteins serve as nature’s building block of choice for constructing complex and functional architectures, peptides represent an attractive, synthetically accessible alternative. Peptides can mimic several features of proteins, including common protein folding motifs (e.g., alpha helices, coiled coils, collagen triple helices, etc.) and various biological functions (e.g., cell signaling and hormone regulation). Moreover, due to their relatively short sequence length, peptides are amenable to a myriad of bioorganic chemical transformations, which affords the ability to incorporate a broad range of nonnatural moieties into the sequence design. These features position peptides as robust, sequence-programmable building blocks for constructing bioinspired materials with properties and functions that can extend beyond the proteome. However, the advantages afforded by utilizing peptides as molecular building blocks, also play a role in their limitations. Due to their truncated sequence length, peptides cannot encode the same level of structural complexity that can be packaged within proteins. As such, peptides are often relegated to forming lower dimensional, less complex structures via relatively non-specific and non-programmable intermolecular interactions. Description: Hofstadter Hyperorbit Quantization of Landau Levels in twisted-Moiré Systems and Beyond

Dr. Dengyu Yang
National Institute for Standards and Technology (NIST)

Abstract: The Hofstadter butterfly is a striking quantum fractal: the energy spectrum of two-dimensional electrons moving through a periodic potential in a magnetic field. Its intricate structure connects quantum physics with number theory, with successive generations of spectral features organized by the Farey tree of rational numbers. Graphene moiré superlattices bring this physics within reach of laboratory magnetic fields, enabling electrical transport measurements to reveal topological gaps and their associated quantized Hall conductivities. However, transport does not directly resolve the energy bands that form the butterfly’s recursive structure. In this talk, I will present scanning tunneling spectroscopy measurements of a bilayer graphene–hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) moiré superlattice that resolve parent magnetic Bloch bands and their offspring, revealing the Farey-tree hierarchy in the electronic spectrum. I will also discuss our semiclassical analysis connecting the parent bands to their offspring through the quantization of Hofstadter hyperorbits. This analysis highlights the role of quantum geometry, through Berry curvature and the associated orbital magnetic moment, in determining hyperorbit energies. Abstract

Our research advances methods for in vivo neurotransmitter monitoring with high temporal, spatial, and chemical resolution. Building on Ralph Adams' pioneering work, we coupled online microdialysis with HPLC and electrochemical detection to enable rapid, near-real-time multiplexed neurotransmitter monitoring in behaving animals. For direct sampling, we developed rapid-pulse voltammetry coupled to machine learning. To address waveform design challenges, we developed a Bayesian optimization workflow to efficiently identify high-information waveforms. Our background-inclusive rapid-pulse voltammetry enables simultaneous in vivo monitoring of dopamine and serotonin, for example. We provide open-source software, including SeroWare—an end-to-end platform for data acquisition and analysis—that supports a wide range of voltammetry formats, from pulses to scans. These tools are applicable to a range of electrochemical analytes, forming a pipeline for optimizing multi-analyte detection and machine-learning analysis. Description: Long Swarms and Short Swarms at Volcanoes: Evidence for Different Processes (part 1) and Estimates of Water in the Hunga Tonga plume (part 2)

Presented by Dr. Steve McNutt | Professor, University of South Florida

Talk Abstract:

Volcanoes often show earthquake swarms of different durations. Long swarms (weeks to months) are characterized by a low b-value, suggesting increased pressure at depth. These are followed by short swarms (hours-days) with higher rates and 30-50 percent VLP events, suggesting pulses of magma injection. A case study of Hunga Tonga estimates the amount of water in the enormous plume and uses this to determine energetics of the eruption.

Biography:

Steve McNutt is a volcano seismologist who has spent over two decades working with the Alaska Volcano Observatory, studying some of the world's most active and unpredictable volcanic systems. His research spans an unusually wide range of volcanic phenomena, including the source and propagation of volcanic tremor, low-frequency events, and explosion earthquakes; the mechanical behavior of volcanoes (from eruption periodicity to how earth tides, sea level changes, and tectonic stress can trigger eruptions); volcano infrasound and volcanic lightning.

Category: Concerts & Performances, Social Gatherings, Readings
Organizer: Center for Creativity
Description: Share your talent or cheer on your friends at C4C's Open Mic Night! Whether you're a seasoned performer or stepping on stage for the very first time, everyone is welcome. No auditions or experience required: Just sign up for a performance slot and have fun in a supportive, creative atmosphere.

Perform spoken word, poetry, music, dance, monologues, skits, or almost any other creative act. Performance slots are up to 5 minutes and are available on a first-come, first-served basis.

Planning to perform? Arrive by 6:45 p.m. to sign up and participate in the 7 p.m. sound check. The show begins at 7:15 p.m. You can also sign up during the event if space remains, but performance slots often fill early. Microphones, a keyboard, acoustic and electric guitars, and amps are available. If you're bringing your own equipment or using a backing track, please arrive before 7 p.m. to test your setup.

Open to all Pitt students, faculty, and staff. Come to perform, discover new talent, meet fellow creatives, or simply enjoy an evening of live performances and community.

Registration is welcome but not required. Registering lets us know you're interested in attending. It does not reserve a performance slot or commit you to performing.

text:

Event: Mindset Matters Series
Date: Friday, November 13, 2026 at 8:30 AM to 8:50 AM
Venue: Online
Category: Trainings & Workshops, Virtual
Organizer: Office of Human Resources
Description: We often think that we need a vacation or large blocks of time in our days to feel refreshed, but it may just be that we need to learn how to capture small doses of well-being where we can in each day. Little “wins” can make a big difference and can be the catalyst to shift our mood/perspective in a positive direction.

The goal of these sessions is to use the time as a gentle nudge toward helping you explore your own interior world through the journal prompt of the day or time to just be still and enjoy the relaxing music. Instead of waiting for the world to stop so we can catch up, let’s slow down on purpose. Make a commitment to show up for yourself; to begin your day from a more centered place. Because, after all, mindset matters.

Testimonials:
“I was distracted this morning, but the music in the background and the deep breaths helped ease me into the day.”

“I was on vacation for over a week and really missed the journal prompts. They are great to really put things in perspective and make you think. Thank you!!"

Title: Reflections on a Career at the Intersection of AI and Medicine

Abstract: In this talk, I will summarize my research at the intersection of AI and medicine/biomedicine, highlighting the motivations, key results, and insights, and suggesting promising directions for future research. I will also reflect on lessons learned along the way.

Biosketch: Gregory Cooper, M.D., Ph.D., is Distinguished Professor Emeritus of Biomedical Informatics at the University of Pittsburgh. He was an active faculty member in the Intelligent Systems Program for 35 years and served for several years as its Co-Director. He received a B.S. in Computer Science from MIT and a Ph.D. in Medical Information Sciences and an M.D. from Stanford University.

His research develops and applies new methods in causal modeling, Bayesian statistics, machine learning, and artificial intelligence with the goal of improving clinical care and advancing biomedical discovery. text:

Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.

Description: The Center for Philosophy of Science at the University of Pittsburgh invites you to join us for our 67th Annual Lecture Series Talk. Attend in person in room 1008 in the Cathedral of Learning (10th Floor) or visit our live stream on YouTube at https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCrRp47ZMXD7NXO3a9Gyh2sg.

The Annual Lecture Series, the Center’s oldest program, was established in 1960, the year when Adolf Grünbaum founded the Center. Each year the series consists of six to eight lectures, about three quarters of which are given by philosophers, historians, and scientists from other universities.

Annual Leture Series – John Morrison

Friday, November 13th @ 3:30 pm - 5:30pm EDT

1008 Cathedral of Learning

Title: Do neural networks understand what they are doing?

Abstract:

It is often claimed that neural networks construct models of the world (“world models”) and do not merely exploit heuristics. In this sense, they are said to understand their tasks. But it is not always clear what having a world model amounts to, or what should count as evidence for or against. In the first half of the talk, I propose a minimal notion of a world model: a single, unified representation of a task that preserves its structural relations. I explain how this notion sits within a hierarchy of stronger ones, and argue that many disputes about world models are merely verbal. Description: About
Have you ever thought about DESIGNING A GAME? Even if you never considered designing a game, you are looking at this website and thinking, “I’m curious! I got this! I can totally do it!” And to add some icing to the cake, you can actually build something that has a positive social impact. Oh, yeah, and we recognize some games with awards! And there’s free food! And the event itself is free!

What is a game jam?
According to Wikipedia, a game jam is a gathering of people for the purpose of planning, designing, and creating one or more games within a short span of time, usually ranging between 24 and 72 hours. Participants are generally composed of programmers, game designers, artists, writers, and others in game development-related fields.

title: Mindset Matters Series (Monday, November 16, 2026)
text:
Mindset Matters Series takes place on Monday, November 16, 2026 at 8:30 AM at Online.
Event: Mindset Matters Series
Date: Monday, November 16, 2026 at 8:30 AM to 8:50 AM
Venue: Online
Category: Trainings & Workshops, Virtual
Organizer: Office of Human Resources
Description: We often think that we need a vacation or large blocks of time in our days to feel refreshed, but it may just be that we need to learn how to capture small doses of well-being where we can in each day. Little “wins” can make a big difference and can be the catalyst to shift our mood/perspective in a positive direction.

The goal of these sessions is to use the time as a gentle nudge toward helping you explore your own interior world through the journal prompt of the day or time to just be still and enjoy the relaxing music. Instead of waiting for the world to stop so we can catch up, let’s slow down on purpose. Make a commitment to show up for yourself; to begin your day from a more centered place. Because, after all, mindset matters.

Testimonials:
“I was distracted this morning, but the music in the background and the deep breaths helped ease me into the day.”

“I was on vacation for over a week and really missed the journal prompts. They are great to really put things in perspective and make you think. Thank you!!"

title: Art All Night: Artistic Expression of Bipolar Disorder — Opening and Reception (Monday, November 16, 2026)
text:
Art All Night: Artistic Expression of Bipolar Disorder — Opening and Reception takes place on Monday, November 16, 2026 at 5:00 PM at Alan Magee Scaife Hall, Falk Library.
Event: Art All Night: Artistic Expression of Bipolar Disorder — Opening and Reception
Date: Monday, November 16, 2026 at 5:00 PM to 6:30 PM
Venue: Alan Magee Scaife Hall, Falk Library, 3550 Terrace Street, Pittsburgh, PA 15261
Category: Exhibits
Organizer: Institute for Bioethics, Research, Ethics and Society Initiative, Health Sciences Library System
Description: All are welcome to join this official opening of an exhibit of the work of self-taught New York artist Norman Klenicki. The artist, who now resides in Connecticut, will join for this opening reception. For many years, Klenicki has used his artwork to express his experience of emotional distress, eventually diagnosed as bipolar disorder, and his treatment odyssey. Producing his art, often all night, has soothed his symptoms and resulted in a striking body of work that prompts discussion of mental illness, its causes, and its treatment. Joining Klenicki for this opening will be the show’s curator, Bridget Keown. The exhibit, curated by Bridget Keown, PhD, will have its “soft opening” in late-October and be on display through January 2027.

Sponsored by the University of Pittsburgh Master of Arts Program in Bioethics; Falk Library of the Health Sciences' History of Health Sciences Collection; Gender & Science Initiative of the Gender, Sexuality, and Women’s Studies Program; and the Research, Ethics and Society Initiative of Pitt Research.

Contact for additional information: PittResearchEthics@pitt.edu

Image: Emotional Self-Portrait #2 by Norman Klenicki

Description: Join the University of Pittsburgh’s Racial Equity Consciousness Institute (RECI) for our virtual learning community cohort!

This interactive program is designed for professionals, students, and community members who want to deepen their understanding of racial equity, explore personal and systemic biases, and build actionable strategies for change.

Through a combination of interactive workshops, reflective exercises, and peer discussions, participants will:

Description: The Center for Philosophy of Science at the University of Pittsburgh invites you to join us for our Lunch Time Talk. Attend in person at 1117 Cathedral of Learning or visit our live stream on YouTube at https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCrRp47ZMXD7NXO3a9Gyh2sg.

LTT: Alexander Paseau

Tuesday, November 17th @ 12:00 pm - 1:30 pm EST

Title: Is Historical Mathematics Largely True?

Abstract:

Historical mathematics is widely regarded as a repository of truths. It would seem unusually sceptical to deny that, say, ancient mathematical cultures established many truths about numbers and shapes, such as Pythagoras’ Theorem or instances of it for specific right-angled triangles.

My talk will list some of the ways in which this assumption might be tested. I’ll then focus on two case studies, both involving extra-mathematical beliefs that apparently ‘infect’, or in some way threaten, the truth of older mathematics. The first concerns 19th-century matricial algebra and the second 18th-century geometry.

This talk will also be available live streamed on:

YouTube at https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCrRp47ZMXD7NXO3a9Gyh2sg.

text:

Venue: Wesley W. Posvar Hall, 4303 - Center for Urban Education, 230 S Bouquet St, Pittsburgh, PA 15213
Category: Screenings
Organizer: Center for Urban Education
Description: Compromised: The Black Educator's Fight for Equity highlights the overlooked stories and advocacy work of Black educators who drove the fight for integration and Brown vs. the Board of Education yet faced disproportionate adverse outcomes relative to their white counterparts as school desegregation subsequently occurred absent their participation.

The movement for school integration was an essential force that would drive the broader Civil Rights Movement, offering the opportunity for Black communities, including parents, teachers, and administrators, to gather valuable organizing experience. The thought was that by having white and Black students share the same schools and resources, that an initial blow could be struck that would lead to the dissolution of American systemic racism. But while the victory of Brown v Board was rightly celebrated, the way that it was implemented, generally by all-white policy makers, saw Black schools closed, Black administrators demoted, Black teachers fired altogether, and Black students placed in hostile, traumatic situations far from their support networks. As white residents increasingly fled for the suburbs, once temporarily integrated schools changed to have predominantly Black student populations, only now the students were without anyone in a position of authority who looked like them or shared their experiences and cultural knowledge.

Description: Through music, visual art, and brief commentary, this concert will explore intergenerational trauma, mental health, and art. The REgenerate Music Project performs music of composers labeled degenerate artists and suppressed by the Nazis in 20th Century Germany. The string quartet, comprising musicians of the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra, seeks to keep those composers’ music alive and to honor their lives. In this concert, the quartet will perform pieces that resonate with the artwork of Norman Klenicki, a self-taught artist and son of Holocaust survivors, who uses his visual art to express and address the symptoms of his bipolar disorder triggered by the legacy of injuries his mother incurred at the hands of Nazi death camp guards.

In 2019, the University of Pittsburgh Center for Bioethics & Health Law created a virtual exhibition of his artwork: Experience, Integration, Expression: The Work of Norman Klenicki. In Fall 2026, the same curator, Bridget Keown, PhD, is mounting an in-person exhibit of Klenicki’s work in the gallery space of Scaife Hall, accessed from the Mezzanine (enter at Terrace and Lothrop Streets), that will be open November 2026 – February 2027. This concert celebrates the opening of this exhibit and the role of music and visual art in expressing and addressing the mental health challenges of intergenerational trauma. title: How Stigma Shapes Health for Sexual and Gender Minorities (Wednesday, November 18, 2026)
text:
How Stigma Shapes Health for Sexual and Gender Minorities takes place on Wednesday, November 18, 2026 at 12:00 PM at Public Health, A521.
Event: How Stigma Shapes Health for Sexual and Gender Minorities
Date: Wednesday, November 18, 2026 at 12:00 PM to 1:00 PM
Venue: Public Health, A521, 130 Desoto Street, Pittsburgh,  15261
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Center for LGBT Health Research, Department of Behavioral and Community Health Sciences 
Description: Presented by Michael Trujillo, assistant professor of psychology, Dietrich College of Humanities and Social Sciences, Carnegie Mellon University.

Stigma has been posited as a fundamental cause of health outcomes and health disparities, particularly among marginalized individuals such as sexual and gender minorities (SGM). It can motivate individuals to support or oppose public policies that directly and indirectly impact stigmatized individuals. Stigma also shapes the perceptions of daily events and how individuals with stigmatized identities respond to them, facilitating engagement in various strategies to cope with stigma related stress. In this talk, Dr. Trujillo will discuss a series of studies that examine the consequences of stigma for the health of SGM. The studies will highlight the negative consequences to policies protecting SGM, how responses to daily stress differ by sexual orientation, and internalized heterosexism as a potential pathway linking stigma to substance use. A discussion of his ongoing projects examining sexual stigma during dyadic interactions using dynamic psychophysiological measurement in SGM will follow.

text:

Date: Wednesday, November 18, 2026 at 2:00 PM to 3:00 PM
Venue: Chevron Science Center, 150, 219 Parkman Avenue, Pittsburgh, PA 15260
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Department of Chemistry
Description: This year's Kaufman Memorial Lecture speaker is Prof. Mark Johnson, Yale University.

Title: Decoding the spectral signatures of “excess” proton speciation and transport kinetics in water with cryogenic ion chemistry and spectroscopy

Abstract: Understanding the properties of protons released into water at the molecular level has proven to be surprisingly challenging. This occurs because the positively charged entity that is formed occurs with variable spatial extent surrounding a defect in the interlocking OH bonds that knit together the extended hydrogen bonded network. This talk will describe how these local structures were captured and characterized using specially designed experimental methods to isolate the vibrational spectra of specific molecular compositions at very low temperature. These instruments integrate cryogenic ion trapping techniques with mass spectrometry and laser spectroscopy. Once the structural information encoded in cold ion spectra was established, a second generation of experiments, one that is currently on-going, evolved that follow the kinetics of long-range proton migration, mediated by a precisely controlled number of water molecules. Simulations of this process, now anchored to experimental benchmarks, provide a microscopic picture of the “proton relay” paradigm envisioned long ago by Grotthuss and widely invoked to rationalize charge transport in aqueous media.

Description: Are you fluent in PubMed use but want to be able to use its advanced features? Level up with Advanced PubMed!

Structure and build more complex searches, including 3 & 4 concept clusters per searchDefine your search question as an answerable question using the PICO question formatDescribe the record structure undergirding PubMed, including MEDLINE recordsUtilize MeSH termsIncorporate more advanced nested Boolean searchesUtilize the Boolean operator "NOT" in searchesDetermine other potential databases to search in addition to PubMed based on your topicUtilize PubMed’s error notification systemLevel: Intermediate

Prerequisites:

Advanced PubMed has been designed as an additional step in the learning process for intermediate PubMed users. Note that if you have just completed our Painless PubMed class, you will likely need to practice using PubMed to develop fluency in the basics before arriving at the level at which you will be able to follow Advanced PubMed. Not sure if you’re ready for Advanced PubMed? Try the following exercise:

You are ready to take Advanced PubMed if you can perform these tasks without referencing guides:Run an author search; how many citations do you get?Set up a MyNCBI account and save a collection.Run a search on two concepts (fever in sore throat) using MeSH terms.Limit your search to English language results.Email the results of this search to yourself.

Description: Dr. Rocky Tuan, 8th Vice-Chancellor and President at The Chinese University of Hong Kong, will present "From Joint Regeneration to Joint-on-a-Chip (miniJoint)."

Abstract

Joint diseases such as osteoarthritis (OA) are highly prevalent and represent the primary cause of physical disability. Despite the success of restorative surgeries, functional biological reconstruction of diseased/traumatized articular joint tissues has not been achieved. This unmet medical need is primarily due to insufficient understanding of disease mechanisms and challenges in engineering functionally mature articular joint tissues. Recent technological advances have led to functional tissue engineering at both the macro- and micro-scales, with the former focusing on regenerative implants and the latter on disease modelling and drug testing. This lecture will provide an overview of the promises and challenges of stem cell- and smart biomaterial-based approaches in articular tissue engineering. Specific focus will be on development of the miniJoint, a human stem cell-derived joint-on-a-chip system, for studying OA pathogenesis, screening candidate therapeutics, and analysis of organ/system interactions. These studies illustrate the power of stem cell-based tissue engineering in generating functional biological implants and physiologically relevant OA models. text:

Venue: Thaw Hall, 104, 3943 O'Hara Street, Pittsburgh, PA 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Department of Geology and Environmental Science
Description: Evidence of Impact Melting in Iron Meteorites

Presented by Dr. Cari Corrigan | Research Geologist and Curator of Meteorites, Smithsonian Institution’s National Museum of Natural History

Talk Abstract:

Of the ~1250 recognized iron meteorites, ~10% are compositionally distinct, and thus termed “ungrouped”. Among these, iron meteorite impact melts are exceptionally rare, despite the fact that iron meteorite parent bodies, exposed cores of larger differentiated protoasteroids, must have experienced a violent impact history. While a few iron meteorites may exhibit impact melt features, others, including an anomalously high number of Antarctic iron meteorites, also contain anomalously low volatile siderophile element concentrations attributed to impact devolatilization. Here, we present results of a three-dimensional (3D) μXCT study of sulfide (troilite, FeS) inclusions in ungrouped irons that are suggestive of formation by diapiric rise of troilite through (partially?) molten metal after impact melting.

Biography:

Cari Corrigan is a Research Geologist and Curator of Meteorites at the Smithsonian Institution’s National Museum of Natural History in Washington DC. Standing on the shoulders of Pitt Professor Bill Cassidy and former Ph.D. student Ralph Harvey, she curates the US Antarctic Meteorite Collection and has classified over 7000 meteorites during her time at the Smithsonian. Description: Please join us for another exciting event in this season of Film and Media Studies Colloquia. Our program's series of talks explores a wide variety of topics related to film and media research, production, and teaching.

This talk, “Landscapes and Memories: Forming, Morphing, and Disappearing” will be led by Sarah Moore, Film & Media Studies Program. Please see a description below:

Living out West, Sarah Moore became obsessed with big landscapes and the nuances of memory. It wasn’t until she moved to Pittsburgh that landscape and memory would weave together in surprising ways. After her Dad developed early dementia five years ago, she found solace in a piece of land across from her house. Moore's films and creative work investigate ways landscapes can heal themselves while she simultaneously grapples with her Dad’s rapid memory deterioration.

Description: We often think that we need a vacation or large blocks of time in our days to feel refreshed, but it may just be that we need to learn how to capture small doses of well-being where we can in each day. Little “wins” can make a big difference and can be the catalyst to shift our mood/perspective in a positive direction.

The goal of these sessions is to use the time as a gentle nudge toward helping you explore your own interior world through the journal prompt of the day or time to just be still and enjoy the relaxing music. James McCommons, author of The Feathers Wars and Great Crusade to Save America’s Birds (2026), tells of the story of George Shiras III, a Pittsburgh lawyer, congressman, world’s first wildlife photographer and inventor of the trail camera, and the originator of what became the Migratory Bird Act, one of the most effective wildlife protection laws in American history. A member of a storied Pittsburgh family, Shiras joined the unlikely coalition of writers, photographers, conservationists, politicians, socialites, game wardens, business leaders, gunmakers, hunters and bird watchers who halted the decimation of wildlife and established the conservation movement to protect American wildlife.

James McCommons is a professor emeritus at Northern Michigan University in Marquette, Michigan where he taught journalism and nature writing for 20 years. A 1981 graduate of the University of Pittsburgh, majoring in English, McCommons worked as a newspaper and magazine journalist, professor, and author. Specializing in ecology, environmental and travel topics, he contributed to Better Homes and Gardens, Discover, Audubon, Wildlife Conservation, Organic Gardening, Backpacker, the Los Angeles Times, and the New York Times. He is the author of the narrative, non-fiction book: Waiting on a Train: The Embattled Future of Passenger Rail named by The Library Journal as a best nonfiction book of 2009. Organizer: Department of Computer Science
Description: Abstract: Software development is shaped by constant disruption—from open-source dependency abandonment to generative AI (GenAI) tools fundamentally reshaping how code is written.

In this talk, I'll present two lines of work, each examining a different disruption. First, I'll share my work on the disruption of open source dependency abandonment, revealing the unsupported challenges developers face when identifying and responding to abandonment, identifying factors that support successful downstream response, and demonstrating how theory-driven LLM-based systems can make those risks more visible. Second, I'll present findings from my recent collaboration with Microsoft Research about the disruption of GenAI adoption on development teams, demonstrating why adoption succeeds for some developers but stalls for others in seemingly similar contexts, showing the amplification effect organizational support mechanisms can have, and introducing the Productivity Pressure Paradox: a dynamic where increased productivity expectations without corresponding support can actually prevent developers from building the skills that would deliver those gains.

Finally, I'll outline my research vision for helping developers anticipate and navigate the disruptions of tomorrow—from building AI-powered tools for software supply chain resilience to studying how GenAI is reshaping development team practices and processes.

Bio: Courtney Miller is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at George Wash

text:
Mindset Matters Series takes place on Monday, November 23, 2026 at 8:30 AM at Online.
Event: Mindset Matters Series
Date: Monday, November 23, 2026 at 8:30 AM to 8:50 AM
Venue: Online
Category: Trainings & Workshops, Virtual
Organizer: Office of Human Resources
Description: We often think that we need a vacation or large blocks of time in our days to feel refreshed, but it may just be that we need to learn how to capture small doses of well-being where we can in each day. Little “wins” can make a big difference and can be the catalyst to shift our mood/perspective in a positive direction.

The goal of these sessions is to use the time as a gentle nudge toward helping you explore your own interior world through the journal prompt of the day or time to just be still and enjoy the relaxing music. Instead of waiting for the world to stop so we can catch up, let’s slow down on purpose. Make a commitment to show up for yourself; to begin your day from a more centered place. Because, after all, mindset matters.

Testimonials:
“I was distracted this morning, but the music in the background and the deep breaths helped ease me into the day.”

“I was on vacation for over a week and really missed the journal prompts. They are great to really put things in perspective and make you think. Thank you!!"

title: Mindset Matters Series (Monday, November 30, 2026)
text:
Mindset Matters Series takes place on Monday, November 30, 2026 at 8:30 AM at Online.
Event: Mindset Matters Series
Date: Monday, November 30, 2026 at 8:30 AM to 8:50 AM
Venue: Online
Category: Trainings & Workshops, Virtual
Organizer: Office of Human Resources
Description: We often think that we need a vacation or large blocks of time in our days to feel refreshed, but it may just be that we need to learn how to capture small doses of well-being where we can in each day. Little “wins” can make a big difference and can be the catalyst to shift our mood/perspective in a positive direction.

The goal of these sessions is to use the time as a gentle nudge toward helping you explore your own interior world through the journal prompt of the day or time to just be still and enjoy the relaxing music. Instead of waiting for the world to stop so we can catch up, let’s slow down on purpose. Make a commitment to show up for yourself; to begin your day from a more centered place. Because, after all, mindset matters.

Testimonials:
“I was distracted this morning, but the music in the background and the deep breaths helped ease me into the day.”

“I was on vacation for over a week and really missed the journal prompts. They are great to really put things in perspective and make you think. Thank you!!"

title: Pitt-CMU Colloquium: Andrey Kravtsov (University of Chicago) (Monday, November 30, 2026)
text:
Pitt-CMU Colloquium: Andrey Kravtsov (University of Chicago) takes place on Monday, November 30, 2026 at 3:30 PM at Thaw Hall, 102.
Event: Pitt-CMU Colloquium: Andrey Kravtsov (University of Chicago)
Date: Monday, November 30, 2026 at 3:30 PM
Venue: Thaw Hall, 102, 3943 O'Hara Street, Pittsburgh, PA 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Department of Physics and Astronomy
Description: Stress-testing LCDM structure formation paradigm on small scales

I will present a galaxy formation model within the Lambda Cold Dark Matter (LCDM) framework that is calibrated on the results of galaxy formation simulations and some of the empirical properties of nearby dwarf galaxies. I will then use the model to interpret a number of ostensible challenges to the LCDM framework, such as the "too-big-to-fail" problem, the Milky Way "plane of satellites" problem, and the "dark-matter-deficient" ultra-diffuse galaxies. I will show that none of these pose a serious challenge to LCDM paradigm within the current observational uncertainties because the corresponding observations can be explained within the standard galaxy formation modeling framework. At the same time, dwarf galaxies provide strong constraints on deviations from the LCDM power spectrum on small scales of up to k~100/Mpc and on the ultra-light wave dark matter models.

title: Becoming Radicals: Polish Jewish Women's Paths to the Spanish Civil War (Monday, November 30, 2026)
text:
Becoming Radicals: Polish Jewish Women's Paths to the Spanish Civil War takes place on Monday, November 30, 2026 at 4:00 PM at Carnegie Mellon University, Baker/Porter Hall, 246A.
Event: Becoming Radicals: Polish Jewish Women's Paths to the Spanish Civil War
Date: Monday, November 30, 2026 at 4:00 PM to 5:30 PM
Venue: Carnegie Mellon University, Baker/Porter Hall, 246A
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Center for Russian, East European, and Eurasian Studies, World History Center
Description: This lecture is part of the Socialist Studies Seminar.

Why did ordinary young women from interwar Poland leave everything behind to fight for Republican Spain? Through interconnected biographies, this paper examines how calss, gender, education, and ethnicity shaped women's paths toward political radicalization, socialism, and communism. Some encountered radical politics through universities, travel, and intellectual circles; others through hospitals, factories, poverty, and prison. Despite varied trajectories, their paths converged in Spain, where commitments to socialism, communism, and above all anti-fascism, gave political meaning to experiences shaped by inequality, care, and social change.

Co-sponsored by the World History Center at Pitt and the Carnegie Mellon University Department of History

title: The Afterlife of the World Trade Center (HAA Colloquium) (Wednesday, December 2, 2026)
text:
The Afterlife of the World Trade Center (HAA Colloquium) takes place on Wednesday, December 2, 2026 at 12:00 PM at Frick Fine Arts Building, 202.
Event: The Afterlife of the World Trade Center (HAA Colloquium)
Date: Wednesday, December 2, 2026 at 12:00 PM to 12:50 PM
Venue: Frick Fine Arts Building, 202, 650 Schenley Drive, Pittsburgh, PA 15260
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Department of History of Art and Architecture
Description: Over 1,800 pieces of steel salvaged from the World Trade Center are scattered across the U.S., incorporated into memorials that sit outside fire stations, on pedestrian malls, in median strips, and in other unexpected places. This presentation draws from the new book Scattered Steel: The Afterlife of the World Trade Center (Cornell, 2026) and investigates how twisted and bent beams were picked from the ruins at Ground Zero by a special curatorial team, archived for years in a hangar at JFK airport, and finally dispersed to communities around the country. While these pieces account for less than 5% of the steel recovered at the site (the vast majority was recycled overseas), the distribution remains one of the largest of its kind.

Drawing on the idea of the modern relic, Samuel Holleran explores how people who experienced the 9/11 attacks on television sought out corporeal forms of mourning and remembrance, receiving steel sections with honor guards and encouraging the laying of hands at anniversary ceremonies. He details the ‘gifting’ program established by the Port Authority, the interstate agency that owns the land on which the towers stood, that allowed civic groups, firehouses, and schools to obtain steel and build local memorials. Many of these were executed by first-time memorial-makers and craftspeople who established a genre of D.I.Y. memorialization that runs counter to the big budget commemorative projects produced during the same period. title: Fostering a Culture of Continuous Quality Improvement – webinar (Wednesday, December 2, 2026)
text:
Fostering a Culture of Continuous Quality Improvement – webinar takes place on Wednesday, December 2, 2026 at 12:00 PM at Online.
Event: Fostering a Culture of Continuous Quality Improvement – webinar
Date: Wednesday, December 2, 2026 at 12:00 PM to 1:30 PM
Venue: Online
Category: Trainings & Workshops, Virtual
Organizer: Mid-Atlantic Regional Public Health Training Center
Description: Continuous quality improvement (CQI) is essential for ensuring organizational agility and data-driven improvements in public health practice. This foundational webinar presents requisite elements and best practices for fostering a culture of CQI in public health agencies to tackle an ever-broadening array of public health challenges.

Learning Objectives
At the conclusion of this webinar, participants will be able to:

define continuous quality improvement (CQI) and its relevance to public health agencies;list three reasons why fostering a culture of CQI is necessary for public health agencies;describe the nature and types of communication needed to foster a culture of CQI in public health agencies;name two implementation strategies for public health agencies’ leaders to consider for the purpose of fostering a culture of CQI in public health agencies; anddescribe the time frame and desirable frequency of CQI ‘check-ins’ and the rationale for it, in the interest of fostering CQI in public health agencies.

Registration closes on Tuesday, December 1, 2026, at noon.

title: Bioengineering Seminar Series - Dr. Douglas Weber (Thursday, December 3, 2026)
text:
Bioengineering Seminar Series - Dr. Douglas Weber takes place on Thursday, December 3, 2026 at 4:00 PM at Benedum Hall, 157.
Event: Bioengineering Seminar Series - Dr. Douglas Weber
Date: Thursday, December 3, 2026 at 4:00 PM to 5:00 PM
Venue: Benedum Hall, 157, 3700 O'Hara Street, Pittsburgh, PA 15261
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Description: Dr. Douglas Weber, Akhtar and Bhutta Professor, Mechanical Engineering, Neuroscience Institute and Biomedical Engineering at Carnegie Melon University, will present "Bypassing, Augmenting, and Repairing Neuromotor Circuits to Restore Independence."

Abstract

The convergence of advancements in fundamental neuroscience and neural interface technologies have enabled clinically relevant technologies that measure and regulate neural signaling in the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves. These technologies provide new capabilities for studying basic mechanisms of information processing and control in the nervous system, while also creating new opportunities for restoring function lost to injury or disease. Neural sensors can measure the activity of motor neurons to enable direct neural control over prosthetic limbs and assistive technologies. Conversely, these neural interface technologies can stimulate activity in sensory and motor neurons to reanimate paralyzed muscles. Although many of these applications rely currently on devices that must be implanted into the body for precise targeting, ultra-miniaturized devices can be injected through the skin or vascular system to access deep structures without open surgery. This talk will focus on efforts to develop wearable and injectable neural interfaces for restoring or improving motor function in people with paralysis due to stroke, spinal cord injury, ALS, and other neurological disorders.

Description: What Do Observations of Exhumed Tectonic Plate Boundaries Tell Us About Subduction Zone Earthquakes?

Presented by Dr. Donald M. Fisher | Professor of Geosciences; Wilson Faculty Fellow, Penn State University

Talk Abstract:

The greatest earthquakes occur on the plate boundary of subduction zones and are typically associated with convergent margins where sediments blanket the downgoing plate. I argue here that geochemical processes increase cohesion in the sediment between plates and are responsible for interseismic strengthening (e.g., geochemical processes such as cementation and incongruent pressure solution (i.e., low grade metamorphic reactions)). Moreover, the loss of this cohesion during earthquakes is the primary mechanism for decreasing strength faster than the elastic strain can unload during slip initiation, a key prerequisite for slip intabilities associated with earthquakes. Interseismic increases in cohesion coincide with the growth of interseismic slip deficit. This talk will describe rocks deformed along the along the plate boundary at depths of seismogenesis and subsequently exhumed. Description: We often think that we need a vacation or large blocks of time in our days to feel refreshed, but it may just be that we need to learn how to capture small doses of well-being where we can in each day. Little “wins” can make a big difference and can be the catalyst to shift our mood/perspective in a positive direction.

The goal of these sessions is to use the time as a gentle nudge toward helping you explore your own interior world through the journal prompt of the day or time to just be still and enjoy the relaxing music. Instead of waiting for the world to stop so we can catch up, let’s slow down on purpose. Make a commitment to show up for yourself; to begin your day from a more centered place. Because, after all, mindset matters.

title: Mindset Matters Series (Monday, December 7, 2026)
text:
Mindset Matters Series takes place on Monday, December 7, 2026 at 8:30 AM at Online.
Event: Mindset Matters Series
Date: Monday, December 7, 2026 at 8:30 AM to 8:50 AM
Venue: Online
Category: Trainings & Workshops, Virtual
Organizer: Office of Human Resources
Description: We often think that we need a vacation or large blocks of time in our days to feel refreshed, but it may just be that we need to learn how to capture small doses of well-being where we can in each day. Little “wins” can make a big difference and can be the catalyst to shift our mood/perspective in a positive direction.

The goal of these sessions is to use the time as a gentle nudge toward helping you explore your own interior world through the journal prompt of the day or time to just be still and enjoy the relaxing music. Instead of waiting for the world to stop so we can catch up, let’s slow down on purpose. Make a commitment to show up for yourself; to begin your day from a more centered place. Because, after all, mindset matters.

Testimonials:
“I was distracted this morning, but the music in the background and the deep breaths helped ease me into the day.”

“I was on vacation for over a week and really missed the journal prompts. They are great to really put things in perspective and make you think. Thank you!!"

Description: Have you ever wanted to turn a real-world object into a detailed digital model? 3D scanning is a powerful technology that makes it possible, and it’s your first step into the world of digital creation.

In this hands-on workshop, you will learn the fundamentals of 3D scanning using our state-of-the-art equipment. We will guide you through the process of capturing an object's geometry, performing basic data cleanup, and exporting a finished model that's ready for 3D printing, animation, or further artistic refinement. You'll leave with a 3D file of the object you scanned and a new, powerful skill.

What you will learn:

The basic principles of structured light 3D scanning.How to operate the scanner and its software to capture a high-quality scan.Essential techniques for cleaning and finalizing your 3D model.How to export your model as an .obj or .stl file.Take your creation to the next level! This workshop is the perfect starting point for our "Digital Sculpting Essentials: An Introduction to ZBrush" session, where you can learn to artistically modify and sculpt the very model you create here. Attendance at both is highly encouraged for a complete project experience.

Can't make it to this workshop? You can always contact us with your questions about this or other digital scholarship and publishing topics! Read more about Digital Scholarship & Publishing support.

Description: Discussion of health literacy and the fight against health misinformation often centers around fact-checking or debunking written materials. Description: The Global Appalachia Faculty Reading Series brings Appalachia into conversation with regions around the world that share similar histories and challenges. Through fiction, history, and global scholarship, participants explore themes of extraction, economic transition, migration, environmental justice, Indigenous land rights, cultural identity, and the future of rural communities. The series encourages participants to consider what Appalachia can teach us about global challenges and what the experiences of communities elsewhere can teach us about Appalachia.

December 9 — Carbon Democracy by Timothy Mitchell
This discussion expands the conversation beyond Appalachia and Wales to consider the relationship between fossil fuels, workers, political power, and democracy. Mitchell provides a global framework for considering how energy systems have shaped political and economic life—and how the histories of Appalachia and South Wales fit within a much larger story.

A limited number of complimentary copies of each book are available to registered participants on a first-come, first-served basis.

title: Normalizing Rest for Advisors and Mentors (Thursday, December 10, 2026)
text:
Normalizing Rest for Advisors and Mentors takes place on Thursday, December 10, 2026 at 11:30 AM at Student Success Hub, 217 Langley Hall.
Event: Normalizing Rest for Advisors and Mentors
Date: Thursday, December 10, 2026 at 11:30 AM to 1:00 PM
Venue: Student Success Hub, 217 Langley Hall, 217 Langley Hall, Pittsburgh, 15260
Category: Trainings & Workshops
Organizer: Office of the Provost
Description: As advisors and mentors, we spend much of our time supporting others, yet conversations about our own need for rest can feel overlooked. In professions that value responsiveness and care for others, rest can feel difficult to prioritize and even harder to discuss openly.

This in-person, discussion-based workshop creates space for honest conversation about rest, restoration, and sustainability in advising and mentoring work. Using frameworks such as the 7 Types of Rest, Recovery Experience Theory, and Attention Restoration Theory (ART), participants will reflect on the different ways our work can deplete us, explore what feels restorative (and what doesn't), and how rest looks different across individuals, roles, and seasons of life. Rather than prescribing self-care strategies, this workshop focuses on normalizing rest as a necessary part of sustaining ourselves, our work, and our ability to support students and colleagues.

Facilitator: Mel Newcity, Program Manager for Advising Development, Office of the Provost

Register to attend by November 23. Lunch will be provided.

Event: RCR: The Publication Process: An Editor’s View

Venue: Online
Category: Trainings & Workshops
Organizer: Clinical and Translational Science Institute
Description: The Clinical and Translational Science Institute's (CTSI) Responsible Conduct of Research (RCR) Center serves as a resource for researchers at the University of Pittsburgh. Our objective is to provide education so that you can learn to effectively recognize and avoid research misconduct and understand the resources that are available to support your research. Click here for more information or to view upcoming workshops.

Presented by Bill Yates, PhD, Vice Chancellor for Research Protections and Professor of Otolaryngology and Neuroscience

In today’s competitive funding environment, productivity is extremely important. However, the peer review process has been compromised by time constraints of researchers. This session discusses the problems that may occur during peer review of manuscripts (including ethical concerns), and the steps that authors can take to address these problems. The session is intended to provide insights into how an author can best guide their paper successfully through the peer review process. (subject matter: responsible authorship)

Category: Trainings & Workshops
