Description: Consent forms should be written with language that facilitates the prospective participant's understanding of the reasons why one might or might not want to participate in research. title: Mindset Matters Series (Friday, December 18, 2026)
text:
Mindset Matters Series takes place on Friday, December 18, 2026 at 8:30 AM at Online.
Event: Mindset Matters Series
Date: Friday, December 18, 2026 at 8:30 AM to 8:50 AM
Venue: Online
Category: Trainings & Workshops, Virtual
Organizer: Office of Human Resources
Description: We often think that we need a vacation or large blocks of time in our days to feel refreshed, but it may just be that we need to learn how to capture small doses of well-being where we can in each day. Little “wins” can make a big difference and can be the catalyst to shift our mood/perspective in a positive direction.

The goal of these sessions is to use the time as a gentle nudge toward helping you explore your own interior world through the journal prompt of the day or time to just be still and enjoy the relaxing music. Instead of waiting for the world to stop so we can catch up, let’s slow down on purpose. Make a commitment to show up for yourself; to begin your day from a more centered place. Because, after all, mindset matters.

Testimonials:
“I was distracted this morning, but the music in the background and the deep breaths helped ease me into the day.”

“I was on vacation for over a week and really missed the journal prompts. They are great to really put things in perspective and make you think. Thank you!!"

*Any questions, please contact Ashley at BeWell@pitt.edu

Description: We often think that we need a vacation or large blocks of time in our days to feel refreshed, but it may just be that we need to learn how to capture small doses of well-being where we can in each day. title: The Neglected Soul: Ancient Monastic Teachings on Depression for the Modern World (Tuesday, January 12, 2027)
text:
The Neglected Soul: Ancient Monastic Teachings on Depression for the Modern World takes place on Tuesday, January 12, 2027 at 8:00 AM at Online.
Event: The Neglected Soul: Ancient Monastic Teachings on Depression for the Modern World
Date: Tuesday, January 12, 2027 at 8:00 AM to 9:00 AM
Venue: Online
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Institute for Bioethics
Description: Healthcare and Religion Lecture

Daniel Ibraheem
MD/MAR candidate
Yale University

Andreh Labib
DO candidate
Duquesne University Nasuti College of Medicine

This presentation describes how the 4th century theologian Evagrius Ponticus’s framework for the thoughts can help illuminate modern depression. Evagrius represents an ancient viewpoint on how people could experience various thought patterns parallel to depression and what could be done for them. Speaking primarily from a spiritual perspective, Evagrius offers wisdom that is useful for understanding spiritual elements of a condition that has been largely biologized. He demonstrates that spiritual considerations of depression are not in competition with biological models, but allow for multi-layered understandings of a disorder that impacts the whole human: body, soul, and mind.

Continuing medical education credit will be available for those in attendance.

Co-sponsored by the Department of Religious Studies, Jewish Studies Program, and Palliative and Supportive Institute

title: Poetic Citizenships: Feminist Writing as Political Acts (Thursday, January 14, 2027)
text:
Poetic Citizenships: Feminist Writing as Political Acts takes place on Thursday, January 14, 2027 at 12:30 PM at Cathedral of Learning, 602.
Event: Poetic Citizenships: Feminist Writing as Political Acts
Date: Thursday, January 14, 2027 at 12:30 PM to 2:00 PM
Venue: Cathedral of Learning, 602, Fifth Ave at Bigelow, Pittsburgh, 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Humanities Center
Description: Hosted by the Humanities Center and featuring faculty fellow, Ever Osorio Ruiz.

This paper re-examines the relationship between writing and politics in our contemporary transmedia landscape. Specifically, by analyzing the writing of feminist movements in Mexico (2010-2020) I explore how the creation of meaning and its inscription into a medium –banners, twitter, walls– operate as an expression of a general intellect, organizes political demands by codifying it in slogans, produces citizenship and expands the public space. A key aspect I explore is how brevity, as a literary and cultural form of these texts, is central for the expression and expansion of these writings and its transmedia circulation in moments of political effervescence.

Respondents include Elsie Campbell from French & Italian + Susana Draper, Professor of Comparative Literature, Princeton University . This event will be hybrid, so you can attend it either in person in 602 CL or via Zoom as you prefer. Precirculated material for this colloquium will be available here about two prior to the event.

title: Bioengineering Seminar Series - Dr. Russell Schwartz (Thursday, January 14, 2027)
text:
Bioengineering Seminar Series - Dr. Russell Schwartz takes place on Thursday, January 14, 2027 at 4:00 PM at Benedum Hall, 157.
Event: Bioengineering Seminar Series - Dr. Russell Schwartz
Date: Thursday, January 14, 2027 at 4:00 PM to 5:00 PM
Venue: Benedum Hall, 157, 3700 O'Hara Street, Pittsburgh, PA 15261
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Description: Dr. Russell Schwartz, Professor of Computational Biology and Biological Sciences at Carnegie Melon University, will present "Towards comprehensive portraits of somatic evolution and cancer progression via multimodal data integration."

Abstract

We have seen dramatic advances in biotechnology for probing genomics of complex tissues in fine spatial and temporal detail, advances that have been particularly impactful in understanding single-cell heterogeneity at play in complex tissues such as cancers undergoing a process of somatic evolution. The more we can observe, though, the more we appreciate the immense complexity of these processes. Genetic evolution of clonal cell populations unfolds in time and space in parallel with changing population dynamics of cell types and functional adaptation at the single-cell level of both tumor and non-tumor cell populations, with each part of this process shaping and shaped by the others. Producing a coherent picture of the complexity of the biology has depended on advances in computational tools concurrent with advances in biotechnology. This talk explores some of these computational directions as we work to integrate diverse data modalities, each giving a distinct window into the biology, to capture a more complete model of the process of somatic evolution and its functional consequences. title: Forensic Fragments: Documentary, Testimony, and Political Memory in India (Thursday, January 21, 2027)
text:
Forensic Fragments: Documentary, Testimony, and Political Memory in India takes place on Thursday, January 21, 2027 at 12:30 PM at Cathedral of Learning, 602.
Event: Forensic Fragments: Documentary, Testimony, and Political Memory in India
Date: Thursday, January 21, 2027 at 12:30 PM to 2:00 PM
Venue: Cathedral of Learning, 602, Fifth Ave at Bigelow, Pittsburgh, 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Humanities Center
Description: Hosted by the Humanities Center and featuring graduate fellow, Senjuti Mukherjee.

Radical documentary practices bear witness while catalysing political action, producing counter-hegemonic forms of memory and publicness amid disinformation and authoritarianism. Situated within Mukherjee’s dissertation on oppositional film and informal video cultures in post-1980s India, their project examines how forensic media fragments document, circulate, and mobilize evidence of state and communal violence. It compares two distinct media formations: early 2000s DigiCam footage preserved and annotated on the open-source archive PAD.MA, and contemporary smartphone videos and leaked CCTV footage circulated through Maktoob Media’s minority-rights platform. Bringing together archival research, digital ethnography, textual analysis, and interviews, the chapter traces shifts in circulation, permanence, authorship, and reuse across archival and algorithmic infrastructures. It argues that these fragments exceed their juridical status as evidence to function as documentary events that sustain counter-hegemonic memory, cultivate affective identification and solidarity, and reconfigure the political possibilities of documentary practice under contemporary authoritarianism.

Description: This professional development workshop series is designed for K-12 educators seeking to deepen their understanding of global issues through literature. This year, we will explore the theme of "Re-Centering Narratives: Indigenous and Island Peoples." Through global and regional perspectives, we will discuss narratives of Indigenous and Island Peoples, whose identities, spaces, and lived experiences are informed by global phenomena such as migration and displacement, economic and political struggles, environmental issues, human rights, and human conditions. By exploring compelling stories from diverse cultural perspectives, educators will gain insights into the complexities of this theme, its impact on individuals and communities, and how to engage students in meaningful discussions around these topics.

Each session features a carefully selected book, paired with historically contextualized presentations, interactive discussions, teaching strategies, and cross-disciplinary activities to inspire classroom implementation.

The workshop for January 21, 2027, will focus on the book, Factory Girl by Josanne La Valley

title: An Afternoon with Marisa Solomon (Thursday, February 4, 2027)
text:
An Afternoon with Marisa Solomon takes place on Thursday, February 4, 2027 at 12:30 PM at Cathedral of Learning, 602.
Event: An Afternoon with Marisa Solomon
Date: Thursday, February 4, 2027 at 12:30 PM to 2:00 PM
Venue: Cathedral of Learning, 602, Fifth Ave at Bigelow, Pittsburgh, 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Humanities Center
Description: Hosted by the Humanities Center and featuring visiting fellow, Marisa Solomon.

Marisa Solomon’s work looks at the durability of racism and its many material forms: toxicity’s movement through soil and bodies, the placement of landfills, waste infrastructure, and the technocratic planning and management of Black life and death. Attentive to the ways coloniality and anti-blackness are sedimented into the landscape, her work focuses on how Black improvisation with waste's form and meaning upend environmental thinking—including the raced, classed, and gendered stewards to whom the earth supposedly belongs.

She is the author of The Elsewhere is Black

This event will be hybrid, so you can attend it either in person in 602 CL or via Zoom as you prefer. Precirculated material for this colloquium will be available here about two prior to the event.

title: Plant-Human: Ecological Alterity in Black Surrealist Poetics (Thursday, February 11, 2027)
text:
Plant-Human: Ecological Alterity in Black Surrealist Poetics takes place on Thursday, February 11, 2027 at 12:30 PM at Cathedral of Learning, 602.
Event: Plant-Human: Ecological Alterity in Black Surrealist Poetics
Date: Thursday, February 11, 2027 at 12:30 PM to 2:00 PM
Venue: Cathedral of Learning, 602, Fifth Ave at Bigelow, Pittsburgh, 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Humanities Center
Description: Hosted by the Humanities Center and featuring faculty fellow, Joy Priest.

In her 1942 essay, “Malaise d’une civilisation” (“Malaise of a Civilization”), Suzanne Césaire introduces her counterhumanist concept of the “plant-human” as a surreal ontology of Black being. “Like a plant,” she writes, “he abandons himself to the rhythm of universal life. There is not the slightest effort to dominate nature.” Relatedly, in his book length poem, Cahier d’un retour au pays natal (“Notebook of a Return to the Native Land”), her partner, the poet Aimé Césaire, employs a perspective of inseparable relation between the combined consciousness of the landscape and the speaker that effects a shared subjectivity in opposition to the romantic lyric’s singular I-voice. In a work-in-progress that combines critical writing and the personal essay, Joy Priest traces a lineage from the Césaires’ counterhumanist poetics to recent books by Black poets and memoirists. Along with shared subjectivity, Priest considers other methods of ecological alterity in the works of Aracelis Girmay, Sarah Broom, and MaKshya Tolbert.

Respondents include Senjuti Mukherjee from Film & Media Studies + Dr. Sonya Posmentier, Associate Professor of English, Director of Graduate Studies, NYU . This event will be hybrid, so you can attend it either in person in 602 CL or via Zoom as you prefer. Precirculated material for this colloquium will be available here about two prior to the event.

title: A Black Geography of Pittsburgh's Civic Arena (Thursday, February 18, 2027)
text:
A Black Geography of Pittsburgh's Civic Arena takes place on Thursday, February 18, 2027 at 12:30 PM at Cathedral of Learning, 602.
Event: A Black Geography of Pittsburgh's Civic Arena
Date: Thursday, February 18, 2027 at 12:30 PM to 2:00 PM
Venue: Cathedral of Learning, 602, Fifth Ave at Bigelow, Pittsburgh, 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Humanities Center
Description: Hosted by the Humanities Center and featuring graduate fellow, Kale Doyen.

As a Black press photojournalist and lifelong Pittsburgher, Charles “Teenie” Harris photographed dramatic changes to his city during its mid-century urban renewal. Harris’s archive catalogs the demolition of Pittsburgh’s predominantly Black Hill District neighborhood, and the subsequent construction of an expressway interchange, luxury apartments, and the steel-domed Civic Arena. Through the conceptual framework of Black geography, this chapter analyzes the Civic Arena through its shared geography with historic ecological and cultural events—including industrial coal mining, the razing of a Native American burial mound for downtown urban development, and the site’s shifting land use as documented by Harris and his surviving communities. By reading this architectural biography alongside its racialized spatial history, the now-razed Arena and its contentious legacy can be understood within a historical pattern of racial capitalist extraction at the foot of Pittsburgh’s Hill.

Respondents include Diana Nguyen from English + Dr. Alaina Roberts, Associate Professor of History, University of Pittsburgh. This event will be hybrid, so you can attend it either in person in 602 CL or via Zoom as you prefer. Precirculated material for this colloquium will be available here about two prior to the event.

title: Book Launch and Poetry Reading with Joy Priest (Thursday, February 25, 2027)
text:
Book Launch and Poetry Reading with Joy Priest takes place on Thursday, February 25, 2027 at 12:30 PM at Cathedral of Learning, 602.
Event: Book Launch and Poetry Reading with Joy Priest
Date: Thursday, February 25, 2027 at 12:30 PM to 2:00 PM
Venue: Cathedral of Learning, 602, Fifth Ave at Bigelow, Pittsburgh, 15213
Category: Readings
Organizer: Humanities Center
Description: Join the Humanities Center as we celebrate the release of Joy Priest's newest book, The Black Outside.

The Black Outside is an ensemble of poems that archives personal and ancestral memory, contextualizing loss and longing in a world created by transatlantic slavery. In these poems, Black ecology is lived and thought across a range of sites, from the “interior gardens” to “grief’s aquatic caves.” At these sites, Priest’s speaker steps through a hole in the fabric of Western reality, a portal to a world outside, a surreal elsewhere. Here, she encounters musicians, philosophers, revolutionaries, and lovers who offer methods of escape and relation with nonhuman life. In an anti-pastoral gesture, Priest tarries around the landscape, refusing to look away and reflecting on her place in larger histories that have inaugurated our changing climate. In doing so, she invites us to understand loneliness as a communal experience, to emancipate ourselves from isolation.

Poet and scholar Joy Priest is the author of Horsepower (Pitt Poetry Series), selected by Natasha Trethewey as the winner of the Donald Hall Prize for Poetry, and the editor of Once a City Said: A Louisville Poets Anthology (Sarabande). Her other honors include a 2021 National Endowment for the Arts fellowship, a 2019-2020 Fine Arts Work Center fellowship, and the Stanley Kunitz Memorial Prize from the American Poetry Review.

This event will be both in-person in CL 602 and on zoom.

Books will be available for purchase.

title: Mushrooms and (Hu)men: A Radical Inquiry into Resistance and Decay (Thursday, March 4, 2027)
text:
Mushrooms and (Hu)men: A Radical Inquiry into Resistance and Decay takes place on Thursday, March 4, 2027 at 12:30 PM at Cathedral of Learning, 602.
Event: Mushrooms and (Hu)men: A Radical Inquiry into Resistance and Decay
Date: Thursday, March 4, 2027 at 12:30 PM to 2:00 PM
Venue: Cathedral of Learning, 602, Fifth Ave at Bigelow, Pittsburgh, 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Humanities Center
Description: Hosted by the Humanities Center and featuring our co-teaching fellows, Kaliane Ung and Diana Nguyen.

Nguyen and Ung are proposing a half-literary survey, half-creative writing workshop inspired by Anna Lowenhaupt Tsing’s The Mushroom at the End of the World: On the Possibility of Life in Capitalist Ruins. In Tsing’s seminal interdisciplinary work, the journey of the matsutake guides readers through the diverse lifeways of Asian diasporic communities shaped by its trade and consumption. Our hybrid course engages with ways of living, creating, reading, and writing inspired by fungal processes, emphasizing interconnectedness, transformation, and resilience. The first half of the class, taught by Dr. Ung, is a literature in translation survey that hones in on cultural productions staging life in a polluted world, drawing on a mixed-media corpus (novels, films, graphic novels, art) on questions of animality, trauma, displacement and migration. The second half, taught by Dr. Nguyen, is a creative writing workshop that utilizes decay as a (de)compositional model for assemblage. Creative prompts will be derived from course texts, and scaffolded assignments will include individual and collaborative experiments to encourage safety amid risk-taking and play.

Respondents include Kale Doyen from HAA, Joy Priest from English + Dr. Summer Kim Lee, Assistant Professor of English, University of California, Los Angeles . This event will be hybrid, so you can attend it either in person in 602

Description: We often think that we need a vacation or large blocks of time in our days to feel refreshed, but it may just be that we need to learn how to capture small doses of well-being where we can in each day. title: Political Appetites: Women as Culinary Activists and the Power of Food in Revolutionary America (Wednesday, March 17, 2027)
text:
Political Appetites: Women as Culinary Activists and the Power of Food in Revolutionary America takes place on Wednesday, March 17, 2027 at 5:30 PM at Cathedral of Learning, TBD.
Event: Political Appetites: Women as Culinary Activists and the Power of Food in Revolutionary America
Date: Wednesday, March 17, 2027 at 5:30 PM
Venue: Cathedral of Learning, TBD, Fifth Ave at Bigelow, Pittsburgh, 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Nationality Rooms and Intercultural Exchange Programs
Description: Led by Nancy Siegel, PhD, Professor of Art History & Culinary History, Towson University. She will provide a historical recipe tastings, specifically Liberty Tea; Federal Cake; Washington Pie; and Election Cake. Dr. Siegel will sign copies of her book Political Appetites: The Power of Food in Revolutionary America which will be available for purchase.

More information on Dr. Siegel and her work:

Food has long carried political meaning, and its significance in revolutionary America is no exception. In Political Appetites: Women as Culinary Activists and the Power of Food in Revolutionary America, art and culinary historian Nancy Siegel uncovers a richly layered story in which meals, ingredients, and even kitchenware helped Americans define what democracy should look—and taste—like. From tea boycotts and homemade Liberty Tea to Washington Pie, Election Cake, and Mammoth Cheese, ordinary foods became vehicles for protest, persuasion, and celebration in the years surrounding the Revolution and the Early Republic. Join us for this lecture which will trace the political meanings embedded in the meals people cooked, the gardens they nurtured, and the tableware they used as part of a vivid portrait of a dynamic society learning to express its ideals through the everyday acts of preparing and eating food.

Nancy Siegel is Assistant Dean and Professor of Art History & Culinary History at Towson University where she specializes in American landscape studies, underrepresented women art

title: Global Issues Through Literature:Re-Centering Narratives:Indigenous & Island Peoples:The Day Lasts More than a Hundred Years (Thursday, March 18, 2027)
text:
Global Issues Through Literature:Re-Centering Narratives:Indigenous & Island Peoples:The Day Lasts More than a Hundred Years takes place on Thursday, March 18, 2027 at 6:00 PM at Online.
Event: Global Issues Through Literature:Re-Centering Narratives:Indigenous & Island Peoples:The Day Lasts More than a Hundred Years
Date: Thursday, March 18, 2027 at 6:00 PM to 7:30 PM
Venue: Online
Category: Trainings & Workshops, Professional Development
Organizer: Global Studies Center, Center for Russian, East European, and Eurasian Studies
Description: This professional development workshop series is designed for K-12 educators seeking to deepen their understanding of global issues through literature. This year, we will explore the theme of "Re-Centering Narratives: Indigenous and Island Peoples." Through global and regional perspectives, we will discuss narratives of Indigenous and Island Peoples, whose identities, spaces, and lived experiences are informed by global phenomena such as migration and displacement, economic and political struggles, environmental issues, human rights, and human conditions. By exploring compelling stories from diverse cultural perspectives, educators will gain insights into the complexities of this theme, its impact on individuals and communities, and how to engage students in meaningful discussions around these topics.

Each session features a carefully selected book, paired with historically contextualized presentations, interactive discussions, teaching strategies, and cross-disciplinary activities to inspire classroom implementation.

The workshop for March 18, 2027, will focus on the book, The Day Lasts More than a Hundred Years by Chingiz Aitmatov

title: An Afternoon with Kameelah Janan Rasheed (Thursday, March 25, 2027)
text:
An Afternoon with Kameelah Janan Rasheed takes place on Thursday, March 25, 2027 at 12:30 PM at Cathedral of Learning, 602.
Event: An Afternoon with Kameelah Janan Rasheed
Date: Thursday, March 25, 2027 at 12:30 PM to 2:00 PM
Venue: Cathedral of Learning, 602, Fifth Ave at Bigelow, Pittsburgh, 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Humanities Center
Description: Hosted by the Humanities Center and featuring visiting fellow, Kameelah Janan Rasheed.

Kameelah Janan Rasheed is a learner and a death doula in training. She explores the poetics and politics of non-compliance and disobedience across written, spoken, and visual systems of communication. In doing so, she considers the radical possibilities of noise, unintelligibility, discrepancy, and refusing frictionless perception.

Across her practice at KJR Studios – an ecosystem spanning installation, publishing, pedagogy, performance, archival practice, and organizational care – she studies what regimes and institutions label “noise”: the communities, the bodies, the gestures, the utterances, and the forms of life that manage to exceed systems designed for certainty, extraction, and linearity.

This event will be hybrid, so you can attend it either in person in 602 CL or via Zoom as you prefer. Precirculated material for this colloquium will be available here about two prior to the event.

Description: We often think that we need a vacation or large blocks of time in our days to feel refreshed, but it may just be that we need to learn how to capture small doses of well-being where we can in each day. title: Tarot, Disorientation & Relational Self-Help: A Process Interview with Author and Social Worker Jessica Dore (Thursday, April 1, 2027)
text:
Tarot, Disorientation & Relational Self-Help: A Process Interview with Author and Social Worker Jessica Dore takes place on Thursday, April 1, 2027 at 12:30 PM at Cathedral of Learning, 602.
Event: Tarot, Disorientation & Relational Self-Help: A Process Interview with Author and Social Worker Jessica Dore
Date: Thursday, April 1, 2027 at 12:30 PM to 2:00 PM
Venue: Cathedral of Learning, 602, Fifth Ave at Bigelow, Pittsburgh, 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Humanities Center
Description: Hosted by the Humanities Center and featuring visiting fellow, Jessica Dore.

For many, the COVID-19 pandemic marked a permanent rupture in the experience of self as bounded and autonomous. That collective disorientation has amplified existing challenges to some of the foundational assumptions upon which the genre of self-help and the helping industries more generally are based. Self-help author, former editorial staff at self-help publisher New Harbinger Publications, and trained social worker Jessica Dore has experienced and written through the disorientation of that transition in the sense that Ami Harbin describes disorientation, as "to lose one’s bearings in relation to others, environments, and life projects” in such a way that involves “sustained uncertainty" and not knowing how to go on. In this colloquium, Dore will briefly present on pre-circulated material from a work in progress, a follow-up to her debut self-help title Tarot for Change: Using the Cards for Self-Care, Acceptance and Growth (Penguin Life, 2021). The new work is written from a distinctly un-expert position, and tentatively titled The Relational Tarot or Tarot for Becoming. Then, using a group interview model adapted from narrative therapy practice, Dore will be interviewed about her process and project by Carla Nappi, followed by brief interviews of audience members about their experiences of the interview.

title: Tarot Meeting: The Fool and the Major Arcana as “a school in the art of learning” (Friday, April 2, 2027)
text:
Tarot Meeting: The Fool and the Major Arcana as “a school in the art of learning” takes place on Friday, April 2, 2027 at 10:00 AM at Cathedral of Learning, 602.
Event: Tarot Meeting: The Fool and the Major Arcana as “a school in the art of learning”
Date: Friday, April 2, 2027 at 10:00 AM to 12:00 PM
Venue: Cathedral of Learning, 602, Fifth Ave at Bigelow, Pittsburgh, 15213
Category: Lectures, Symposia, Etc.
Organizer: Humanities Center
Description: Hosted by the Humanities Center and featuring visiting fellow, Jessica Dore.

Jessica Dore, author of Tarot for Change: Using the Cards for Self-Care, Acceptance and Growth (Penguin Life, 2021) will briefly introduce the major arcana of the tarot as "a school in the art of learning,” following the author of the anonymously and posthumously published Meditations on the Tarot. Then, we will look together at the arcanum that is numbered zero: The Fool. Participants will be invited to share their initial impressions of the card before a brief talk followed by a second round of participant shares. Considering tarot reader Selah Saterstrom's notion of arcana as archives, participants will be invited to share relevant poems, essays, articles, books, and other artworks towards the compilation of a Fool archive.

This event will be in person in CL 602.

Description: Hosted by the Humanities Center and featuring visiting fellow, Jamelle Bouie.

Based in Charlottesville, Virginia, Jamelle Bouie is a columnist for the New York Times. He covers history and politics. In addition, he co-hosts the Unclear and Present Danger podcast on the political and military thrillers of the 1990s.

In 2021, Jamelle received the Hillman Prize for Opinion & Analysis Journalism and in 2024 he was elected to the American Academy of Arts & Science. In 2025, he received the Carey McWilliams Award for a major journalistic contribution to the public's understanding of politics from the American Political Science Association. He also received the Tikkun Olam Prize for Promoting Public Historical Literacy from the American Historical Association.

Description: DataSci+AI Forum is HAIL’s annual get-together that packs a day of ideas, demos, and real conversations inspired by this year’s Server-Side Chats series. title: Global Issues Through Literature Series:Re-Centering Narratives: Indigenous & Island Peoples: The Island of Sea Women (Thursday, April 15, 2027)
text:
Global Issues Through Literature Series:Re-Centering Narratives: Indigenous & Island Peoples: The Island of Sea Women takes place on Thursday, April 15, 2027 at 6:00 PM at Online.
Event: Global Issues Through Literature Series:Re-Centering Narratives: Indigenous & Island Peoples: The Island of Sea Women
Date: Thursday, April 15, 2027 at 6:00 PM to 7:30 PM
Venue: Online
Category: Trainings & Workshops, Professional Development
Organizer: Global Studies Center, Asian Studies Center
Description: This professional development workshop series is designed for K-12 educators seeking to deepen their understanding of global issues through literature. This year, we will explore the theme of "Re-Centering Narratives: Indigenous and Island Peoples." Through global and regional perspectives, we will discuss narratives of Indigenous and Island Peoples, whose identities, spaces, and lived experiences are informed by global phenomena such as migration and displacement, economic and political struggles, environmental issues, human rights, and human conditions. By exploring compelling stories from diverse cultural perspectives, educators will gain insights into the complexities of this theme, its impact on individuals and communities, and how to engage students in meaningful discussions around these topics.

Each session features a carefully selected book, paired with historically contextualized presentations, interactive discussions, teaching strategies, and cross-disciplinary activities to inspire classroom implementation.

The workshop for April 15, 2027, will focus on the book, The Island of Sea Women by Lisa See

Description: We often think that we need a vacation or large blocks of time in our days to feel refreshed, but it may just be that we need to learn how to capture small doses of well-being where we can in each day. Little “wins” can make a big difference and can be the catalyst to shift our mood/perspective in a positive direction.

The goal of these sessions is to use the time as a gentle nudge toward helping you explore your own interior world through the journal prompt of the day or time to just be still and enjoy the relaxing music. Because, after all, mindset matters.

The goal of these sessions is to use the time as a gentle nudge toward helping you explore your own interior world through the journal prompt of the day or time to just be still and enjoy the relaxing music. Instead of waiting for the world to stop so we can catch up, let’s slow down on purpose. Make a commitment to show up for yourself; to begin your day from a more centered place. Because, after all, mindset matters.

Testimonials:
